entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Adolph Heisler
entries.content:
[00:00:01]
David Boder: (In English) This is Spool 81. Geneva, August 27th, 1946. The interview is with Adolph Heisler, eighteen (18) years old, from the Czech territory, which presumably has become Russian now. He carries a tattoo number A 4470. (A four, four ,seven, zero)

[00:00:29]
David Boder: Also, Herr Heisler, also wollen Sie uns noch einmal sagen Ihren ganzen Namen und wo sind Sie geboren. Sprechen Sie laut, langsam und ziemlich laut, nun?

[00:00:38]
Adolph Heisler: Also, mein Name ist Adolph Heisler und ich ....

[00:00:41]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:00:41]
Adolph Heisler: ...und ich komme aus der Tschechoslowakei, aus Karpathen Russland. Achtzehn (18) Jahre bin ich alt und ich bin deportiert worden später nach Auschwitz.

[00:00:51]
David Boder: Ja. Also erzählen Sie mir, wo waren Sie und was ist Ihnen passiert, wie der Krieg angefangen hat.

[00:01:00]
Adolph Heisler: Wenn der Krieg angefangen hat, hat man uns genommen in ein Ghetto and da hat man uns sehr mies behandelt. Und nach dem Ghetto ... in dem Ghetto waren wir ein Monat und nach einem Monat hat man uns deportiert mit dem Zug nach Auschwitz.

[00:01:15]
David Boder: Nun warten Sie mal. Ich will diese ganze Geschichte wissen. Das ist doch nicht so schnell gegangen. Wie hat man bekannt gemacht, wie ... Wer waren Ihre Eltern? Was war Ihr Vater und Ihre Mutter?

[00:01:27]
Adolph Heisler: Also wir hatten eine große Landwirtschaft und mein Vater hatte ein großes Holzunternehmen, da hat man in die Wälder ....

[00:01:36]
David Boder: Ja, nun?

[00:01:37]
Adolph Heisler: Alles ... und da hat man uns alles zugenommen ...

[00:01:42]
David Boder: Nun, Ihr Vater war ein Holzhändler und hatte .. war Landwirt?

[00:01:45]
Adolph Heisler: Ja und ...

[00:01:46]
David Boder: In der Stadt oder neben der Stadt?

[00:01:48]
Adolph Heisler: In der Nähe der Stadt.

[00:01:49]
David Boder: In der Nähe der Stadt. Und haben Sie Brüder und Schwestern gehabt?

[00:01:53]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, ich hatte zwei (2) Brüder. Ein Bruder lebt noch jetzt, er ist im russischen Territorium – bei der Tante lebt er.

[00:01:59]
David Boder: In Russland?

[00:02:00]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:02:01]
David Boder: Und der Andere?

[00:02:02]
Adolph Heisler: Der Andere .... von dem Anderen weiß ich nichts und von die Eltern weiß ich auch nichts.

[00:02:05]
David Boder: Sie wissen nichts von Ihren Eltern?

[00:02:07]
Adolph Heisler: Nein.

[00:02:07]
David Boder: Haben Sie von Ihrem Bruder im russischen Territorium einen Brief bekommen?

[00:02:12]
Adolph Heisler: Von meinem Bruder nicht, aber ein Mädel hat mir geschrieben, ein bekanntes Mädel, sie wohnte nah bei, hm, neben uns, sie hat mir geschrieben, dass sie hat gesprochen mit meinem Bruder. Und ich hab auch einmal telegraphiert und alles, aber Antwort hab ich nicht bekommen. Ich weiß nicht ... ich kann nicht in Verbindung kommen mit Russland und ich weiß auch nicht wies ihm geht und alles.

[00:02:35]
David Boder: Ja, nun also in der Stadt gelebt, wie hat die Stadt geheißen?

[00:02:41]
Adolph Heisler: Chynadiyovo.

[00:02:42]
David Boder: Chynadiyovo.

[00:02:43]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:02:44]
David Boder: Wie schreibt man das?

[00:02:45]
Adolph Heisler: C.

[00:02:47]
David Boder: Ah, C.

[00:02:48]
Adolph Heisler: Z

[00:02:49]
David Boder: Czyna ....

[00:02:50]
Adolph Heisler: Chynadiyovo.

[00:02:51]
David Boder: Chynadiyovo.

[00:02:52]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, das ist eine tschechische Stadt bei (unverständlich).

[00:02:53]
David Boder: Nun, als erzählen Sie mir, die Deutschen sind dorthin gekommen. Wie sind sie da rein gekommen?

[00:03:01]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, also sie sind sofort hereingekommen, wir haben gesehen die deutsche Besetzung mit dem Militär und es ist auf einmal schwarz geworden vor den Juden ihre Augen. Und nach zwei (2) Wochen am Morgen sind sie gekommen und man hat nichts gewusst, sie besetzen die Häuser und das war dann in 2 Stunden alles zusammen gepackt und deportiert worden. Man hat nicht gewusst wohin. Wir wurden geführt zu einem Haus, in diesem Haus hat man zusammen getrieben und man ... alle mit den Autos in das Ghetto.

[00:03:33]
David Boder: Ja. Wo ... wo war das Ghetto? Wie hat man das Ghetto gemacht?

[00:03:37]
Adolph Heisler: Das Mukachevo Ghetto. Das waren große Barracken von einer Ziegelfabrik. Dort waren große Barracken von Holz, die voll waren mit Ziegel, die man dort gelagert. Und es war sehr (unverständlich) konnte es nicht aushalten, denn es waren schrecklich viele Menschen. In einer Baracke wohnten drei tausend (3000) Mann, da war kein Platz und schrecklich viele Menschen und ...

[00:04:01]
David Boder: Männer und Frauen und Kinder alles zusammen?

[00:04:03]
Adolph Heisler: Alles zusammen. Die Familien waren ... dort waren noch die Familien zusammen.

[00:04:07]
David Boder: Ja, nun, und Sie waren der Ältes....., ja, sie haben einen Bruder und eine ...

[00:04:12]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, zwei Brüder.

[00:04:13]
David Boder: Zwei Brüder haben Sie gehabt?

[00:04:14]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:04:14]
David Boder: Waren die älter oder jünger?

[00:04:16]
Adolph Heisler: Jüngere Brüder.

[00:04:17]
David Boder: Jüngere Brüder. Nun, und, hm, wie lange sind Sie gewesen dort in dieser Ziegelfabrik?

[00:04:23]
Adolph Heisler: In der Ziegelfabrik waren wir vier, vier (4) Wochen.

[00:04:26]
David Boder: Ja, und wer hat Ihnen zu Essen gegeben, was hat man zu Essen gegeben?

[00:04:30]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, die Kehille haben sich selbst ausgehalten noch von dieser Verpflegung, weil wir haben gehabt die Lebensmittel und alles haben sie weg transportieren von zu Hause. Die Operation hat alles zugenommen und ....

[00:04:41]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:04:43]
Adolph Heisler: ... und es war nicht genug, was man gebracht hat von der Stadt.

[00:04:47]
David Boder: Ja. Und wer war die Kehille?

[00:04:51]
Adolph Heisler: Das war die jüdische Gemeinde, weil die haben gesagt, dass man soll (unverständlich) haben noch nicht zugenommen das Geld, Protektion und sie waren (unverständlich) zum Transportieren Lebensmittel.

[00:05:04]
David Boder: Lebensmittel. Nun, und nach, hm, .....das hat gedauert, sagen Sie, vier (4) Wochen?

[00:05:09]
Adolph Heisler: Vier (4) Wochen.

[00:05:10]
David Boder: Und was ist dann passiert? Sagen Sie mir die ganzen Einzelheiten, wie es war.

[00:05:15]
Adolph Heisler: Also sie kommen an einem Morgen und sie haben gesagt, wer die Rechte hat von dieser Stadt, die Zugehörigkeit, dann ist es möglich, dass er da bleiben darf und ... dass er nach Hause gelassen werden. Und so haben wir gebracht alle Papiere, wir haben auch gezeigt Papiere, alles gute Papiere. Und sie haben die zugenommen. Und auf einmal sieht man ein großes Feuer von den Papieren. Sie haben sie nur über uns Spaß gemacht. Und am anderen Tag .....

[00:05:41]
David Boder: Also Sie sagen, man hat die Papiere gesammelt und was hat man dann getan?

[00:05:45]
Adolph Heisler: Man hat sie verbrennt, weil sie wollen selber, dass sie damit wir nicht haben um auszureisen ....

[00:05:51]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:05:52]
Adolph Heisler: ... und am anderen Tag an Morgen hat man nicht erlaubt, dass man verlässt die Baracke und man soll hinein kommen in einen Haufen Wagons. Und dann haben sie gepackt diese Wagonen zu hundert (100) hat man in einen Wagon, ohne Essen, ohne Allem und man hat uns transportiert ... wir wurden transportiert, wohin aber hat niemand gewusst. Wir fahren .... wir fahren zwei (2) Wochen auf dem Zug. Und dann sind wir rausgekommen nach Auschwitz. Wir wussten nicht ......

[00:06:17]
David Boder: Ja, noch ....

[00:06:18]
Adolph Heisler: Wir wussten nichts von Auschwitz .... von der Vernich...., weil wir haben gesehen, die Arbeiter ... Leute in Häftlingskleider, aber wir haben nicht gewusst, was das bedeutet. Dann aber ... dann haben wir die ganze Geschichte gehört.

[00:06:31]
David Boder: Also, wollen wir ein bisserl zurück gehen. Man hat sie auf ....alle hinein gesetzt in die Wagons.

[00:06:37]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:06:37]
David Boder: Was für Wagons waren das?

[00:06:38]
Adolph Heisler: Das waren Lastwagen Wagons für die Vieh. Sehr viele Personen waren da, es war sehr voll gestopft, ohne Wasser. Man hat kein Wasser uns nicht gegeben. Das Essen war gar nichts, weil von zu Hause hat man nicht mehr, wir waren doch schon vier (4) Wochen in dem Ghetto, alles was wir hatten war weg.

[00:06:57]
David Boder: Und wie viele Personen waren in einem Wagon?

[00:07:00]
Adolph Heisler: Wir waren ein hundert (100) Leute in einem Wagon.

[00:07:02]
David Boder: Waren dort Stühle, waren dort Bänke ......

[00:07:05]
Adolph Heisler: Nein, nein, da waren keine. Die Decken hat man zugenommen, alles hat man zugenommen, wir liegen auf die Holzbretter.

[00:07:11]
David Boder: Waren Ihre Mutter und Ihr Vater mit Ihnen?

[00:07:13]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, war noch in dem Wagon auch, aber .....

[00:07:15]
David Boder: Und die zwei (2) Brüder?

[00:07:16]
Adolph Heisler: Auch, also alle waren zusammen. Nur in Auschwitz – wie wir sind dran gekommen, hat man uns verteilt alle.

[00:07:22]
David Boder: Ein Moment .... also hat man sie reingeschoben in die Wagons. War da eine Toilette?

[00:07:29]
Adolph Heisler: Nichts, nichts.

[00:07:30]
David Boder: So wie hat man das getan, wenn man hat wollen gehen ... zum, hm, zum ... Bidet oder?

[00:07:36]
Adolph Heisler: Wir hatten einige Töpfe, so hatten wir ....

[00:07:39]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:07:39]
Adolph Heisler: ... Toiletten gemacht und dann ausgeschüttet.

[00:07:42]
David Boder: Ausgeschüttet wo?

[00:07:44]
Adolph Heisler: Hinaus aus dem Wagon.

[00:07:45]
David Boder: Waren die Wagons offen?

[00:07:47]
Adolph Heisler: Da war eine kleine Öffnung, durch das Fenster....

[00:07:50]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:07:50]
Adolph Heisler: ... und mit Draht ...

[00:07:51]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:07:52]
Adolph Heisler: ... und da hat man kaum die Hand durch.

[00:07:54]
David Boder: Und wie haben die Männer und Frauen ... die Frauen diese Töpfe benutzt?

[00:07:58]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, da war alles gleich, egal ... man hat da nicht sehr viel geschaut, da.

[00:08:02]
David Boder: Ja, also und wir lange sind man gefahren?

[00:08:08]
Adolph Heisler: Zwei (2) Wochen.

[00:08:09]
David Boder: Zwei (2) Wochen?

[00:08:10]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:08:11]
David Boder: Und hat man die Wagons da jeden Tag los gemacht?

[00:08:13]
Adolph Heisler: Nein.

[00:08:15]
David Boder: Und Wasser?

[00:08:17]
Adolph Heisler: Auch nicht. Wir hatten ... jeder hat sich noch mitgenommen vom Ghetto einen Eimer Wasser und wir haben bekommen Brot, das heißt zwei (2) Kilo Brot und mit diesem hat man gelebt die ganze Zeit ...

[00:08:27]
David Boder: Also?

[00:08:27]
Adolph Heisler: ... pro Person.

[00:08:28]
David Boder: Haben Sie und Ihre Familie genug zu essen gehabt?

[00:08:32]
Adolph Heisler: Von genug ist leider da nicht, aber was kann man machen?

[00:08:35]
David Boder: Ja, nun .... sind sie alle .... was haben die Menschen den ganzen Tag im Wagon getan?

[00:08:42]
Adolph Heisler: Gar nichts. Wir haben uns gesetzt, Einer hat gesagt, das passiert. Und Einer hat gesagt, das wird sein. Wir haben absolut nichts gewusst und wir waren ganz nervös. Wir waren alle nicht mehr normal von der Geschichte was ist vorher gegangen.

[00:08:56]
David Boder: Aha. Und nun wann sind Sie angekommen und wann? In Auschwitz?

[00:08:59]
Adolph Heisler: In Auschwitz.

[00:09:00]
David Boder: Erzählen Sie, wenn der Zug ist angekommen, was ist dann passiert? Also was hat dort passiert?

[00:09:06]
Adolph Heisler: Also wir sind dort angekommen.

[00:09:08]
David Boder: (Lärm im Mikrophon) Also warten Sie mal .............nun?

[00:09:10]
Adolph Heisler: Wir sind dort angekommen nach Auschwitz. Es ist dort gestanden ein SS Sturm Führer und der hat aussortiert die alten Menschen und die Kinder auf eine Seite und die Arbeitsfähigen, die die sehr gut und arbeitsfähig ausgesehen haben, die hat er auf die andere Seite. Die Anderen, die haben sie weg geführt und wohin wir haben nicht gewusst. Nur am anderen Tag haben wir gesehen die große Flamme mit Rauch vom Krematorium, wo man hat sie verbrannt. Und wir sind gegangen in Baracken.

[00:09:37]
David Boder: Wer sind das: wir?

[00:09:39]
Adolph Heisler: Wir – die Arbeitsfähigen, ich war auch unter ihnen und ich habe ...

[00:09:43]
David Boder: Also was ist passiert mit Ihrer Familie, wenn sie kamen nach Auschwitz?

[00:09:47]
Adolph Heisler: Zu meiner Familie hat passiert, dass mein Bruder und ich sind wir gestanden auf einer Seite und die Übrigen sind gestanden ....

[00:09:54]
David Boder: Wer war die Übrigen?

[00:09:55]
Adolph Heisler: Die Mutter. Der Vater war nicht da, denn den Vater hat man zugenommen zum, hm, Dienst, zum militärischen Dienst, noch zu Hause.

[00:10:04]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:10:05]
Adolph Heisler: Und die Mutter mit dem kleinen Bruder ist, hm, ..... ist gegang ... wurde genommen auf die andere Seite mit ... so mit den nicht Arbeitsfähigen.

[00:10:13]
David Boder: Also das habe ich nicht gewusst! Ihr Vater ist nicht mit Ihnen gewählt worden, Ihr Vater wurde genommen zum militärischen Dienst. War Ihr Vater mit Ihnen im Ghetto dabei?

[00:10:23]
Adolph Heisler: Nein.

[00:10:23]
David Boder: Nein, also wo war er da? War er in der ungarischen Armee?

[00:10:27]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:10:27]
David Boder: Hm, war er in der tschechischen Armee?

[00:10:29]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, er war in der tschechischen Armee. Und da wurde er einberufen und diese starken Menschen, die gut arbeitsfähig waren zu graben, Schützengraben zu graben.

[00:10:39]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:10:40]
Adolph Heisler: Und er ist auch dort geblieben. Und wir waren im Ghetto.

[00:10:43]
David Boder: Aha. Und Sie haben ihn nicht .... er hat sie nicht gesehen bevor Sie weggefahren sind.

[00:10:47]
Adolph Heisler: Nein.

[00:10:47]
David Boder: Ja und Sie haben nichts von ihm gehört.

[00:10:49]
Adolph Heisler: Nein.

[00:10:49]
David Boder: Also die Mutter und der kleine Junge haben sie in Auschwitz auf die andere Seite gestellt?

[00:10:53]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:10:54]
David Boder: Nun, also weiter.

[00:10:56]
Adolph Heisler: Und der Bruder und ich sind gegangen – wie sagt man – baden.

[00:11:01]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:11:01]
Adolph Heisler: Und nach dem Baden hat man abgeschoren alles und hat man uns geführt in eine Baracke.

[00:11:06]
David Boder: Was meinen Sie, man hat abgeschoren alles? War das ....

[00:11:08]
Adolph Heisler: Die Haare und alles abgeschoren.

[00:11:09]
David Boder: Am ganzen Körper.

[00:11:10]
Adolph Heisler: Am ganzen Körper.

[00:11:11]
David Boder: Also weiter (Läuten, wie ein Telefon) Dr. Boder (in English): that was a telephone interruption. (Auf deutsch): Nun?

[00:11:16]
Adolph Heisler: Und dann hat man uns - nach dem Abscheren und nach dem Bad - hat man uns angezogen die Häftlingsanzüge, sie waren so wie die Anderen. Wir haben nicht gewusst, was da los ist. Und wie wir sind rausgekommen, haben wir gesehen, wie die Stecken geflogen sind bei die Häftling über die Rücken und Köpfe.

[00:11:34]
David Boder: Also wer hat sie geschlagen?

[00:11:35]
Adolph Heisler: Es waren die SS und es waren die deutschen Kriegs... nicht Kriegsverbrecher, sondern Verbrecher, die im sechs und dreißiger (36) Jahr noch nicht in den Konzentrationslagern waren und die waren noch ärger als die SS selbst.

[00:11:51]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:11:52]
Adolph Heisler: Und diese hat man genommen als ‚capos’, das heißt sie haben absolute Kraft über die Häftlinge gehabt in dem Lager, selbst haben das gehabt bei dem Kommando, sie haben gehabt (unverständlich).

[00:12:04]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:12:06]
Adolph Heisler: Und dann hat man uns getrieben in die Baracken. Und dann wenn kommt der andere Tag – auch nichts zu essen und schlafen haben wir überhaupt nicht können, denn es war kalt und es waren die Steine, eine Baracke von Steine und da ....

[00:12:22]
David Boder: Ein Steinboden?

[00:12:24]
Adolph Heisler: Ja. Und da sind wir gesessen. Das war in Birkenau selbst.

[00:12:28]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:12:28]
Adolph Heisler: Das war noch nicht in Auschwitz, das war, hm, das Quarantäne Lager für Auschwitz.

[00:12:32]
David Boder: Ja. Das war was für ein Lager?

[00:12:34]
Adolph Heisler: Quarantäne Lager.

[00:12:35]
David Boder: Ein Quarantäne Lager für Auschwitz?

[00:12:36]
Adolph Heisler: Die Leute wurden dort gebadet und abgeschoren und angezogen. Und Auschwitz war schon ....es war nahe von Auschwitz und Auschwitz war ein Arbeitslager.

[00:12:44]
David Boder: Ja, nun?

[00:12:46]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort hat man uns dann gefragt, was wir (unverständlich) und sie haben gesagt, wir müssen arbeiten.

[00:12:54]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:12:55]
Adolph Heisler: Und so habe ich gesagt, ich bin ein Schlosser, denn ich habe gewusst, dass es immer besser ist zu sagen, dass man irgend eine Arbeit hat, als im Feld zu arbeiten, aber ...

[00:13:04]
David Boder: Haben Sie verstanden Schlosserei?

[00:13:06]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, ich bin dort in die Schule und zu Haus ich habe immer gern gehabt, so mit dieser Sache herum zu spielen.

[00:13:10]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:13:10]
Adolph Heisler: Und ich wusste ganz genau, dass sie gebraucht haben einen Schlosser da, .... und da habe ich eine Ahnung und so habe ich mich dazu beworben.

[00:13:20]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:13:21]
Adolph Heisler: Und so habe ich mich dazu beworben. Also, ich habe selber kein Glück gehabt für das, weil ....weil ich bin ... sie haben mich nicht zugenommen dazu.

[00:13:29]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:13:30]
Adolph Heisler: Und am nächsten Tag hat man uns hinaus gerufen. Wir haben .... wir haben schon gehabt die .... die Nummern haben wir noch nicht gehabt.

[00:13:38]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:13:38]
Adolph Heisler: Und wir wurden heraus gerufen und man hat uns geführt nach Auschwitz, zum Lager Auschwitz. Dort wie wir sind angekommen hat man uns gegeben eine Supp zu essen. Es war schon am dritten (3.) Tag und so wir haben bekommen einen (1) Liter Supp und man hat uns geführt zum nummerieren.

[00:13:57]
David Boder: Zum Tätowieren.

[00:13:58]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:13:58]
David Boder: Wenn jeder hat bekommen einen (1) Liter Supp, worin hat man die Supp gegeben?

[00:14:02]
Adolph Heisler: Das waren solche Schüssel, die Schüssel ... zerbrochene Schüssel, was waren von die Transporte zusammen geholt, weil sie mitgenommen haben die Töpfe ...

[00:14:10]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:14:10]
Adolph Heisler: ... von den Wagonen ....

[00:14:11]
David Boder: Ja, nun?

[00:14:12]
Adolph Heisler: ... und die haben sie zusammen gesammelt und haben in diesen die Suppe gegeben ...

[00:14:16]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:14:16]
Adolph Heisler: ... zu essen.

[00:14:17]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:14:18]
Adolph Heisler: Und nachdem wir bekommen haben die Suppe, und danach tätowiert. Wir sind dann noch geblieben zwei (2) Tage und am dritten (3.) Tag hat man uns weg genommen und man hat geteilt vom Bruder und ich mich hat man weggenommen in einer Kohlengrube zu arbeiten. Das war acht (8) Kilometer von Auschwitz, in Jawischowitz (Jawiszowice).

[00:14:36]
David Boder: Jawischowitz?

[00:14:37]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:14:37]
David Boder: In einer Kohlengrube.

[00:14:38]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:14:39]
David Boder: Und hat man Ihnen gegeben Hammer und hat man Ihnen gegeben ....

[00:14:42]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, so wie jeder .... wie jeder Arbeiter hab ich ......

[00:14:44]
David Boder: Und eine Lampe auf dem Kopf?

[00:14:46]
Adolph Heisler: Nicht auf dem .... wir haben gehabt in die Hände Lampen. Und zwar hat sechs (6) Kilo die Lampe und selbst haben wir getragen.

[00:14:53]
David Boder: Warum, warum war die Lampe so schwer? Was war das?

[00:14:56]
Adolph Heisler: Es war ... ich weiß nicht, es waren die ... die Karbid – nicht Karbid Lampen, aber ....

[00:15:01]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:15:01]
Adolph Heisler: ... solche Laternen, elektrische Akkumulator-Laterne.

[00:15:05]
David Boder: Oh, das waren ... ja.

[00:15:06]
Adolph Heisler: Und das waren ....

[00:15:06]
David Boder: Mit Batterien?

[00:15:07]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:15:08]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:15:08]
Adolph Heisler: Das waren solche Lampen damit sie es auch aushalten zwölf (12) Stunden, weil wir haben acht (8) Stunden Arbeit ...

[00:15:15]
David Boder: Aha.

[00:15:15]
Adolph Heisler: ... aber (unverständlich) musste leuchten, weil wir ...

[00:15:20]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:15:20]
Adolph Heisler: ... die Appells hatten und das und das.

[00:15:22]

[00:28:46]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:28:46]
Adolph Heisler: Wenn es war ein Guter und er hat geredet, dann hat man ihn gefragt, wo man führt uns hin.

[00:28:50]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:28:50]
Adolph Heisler: Und er hat gesagt, er weiß das selbst nicht. Eben er hat auch einen Befehl vom (unverständlich) bekommen und mehr und wohin weiß er auch nicht.

[00:28:58]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:28:59]
Adolph Heisler: Also dann haben wir gesehen, dass wir kommen nach Buchenwald – wie wir sind angekommen.

[00:29:02]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:29:03]
Adolph Heisler: Das war nach acht (8) Tagen auf dem Zug gefahren ...

[00:29:06]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:29:07]
Adolph Heisler: ...wir sind nach Buchenwald und wir waren noch sehr schwach so von der Reise.

[00:29:11]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:29:12]
Adolph Heisler: Mir selbst hat es den Kopf auch verdreht nach dem Bad. Wir haben uns dort selbst gebadet, weil sie haben die Deutschen, die gekommen sind, in ein anderes Lager ... hat man gebadet.

[00:29:22]
David Boder: Nun, also was soll das bedeuten.....

[00:29:23]
Adolph Heisler: Zur Desinfektion.

[00:29:24]
David Boder: ... und Sie sagen Ihr Kopf war verdreht?

[00:29:25]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, ich hab mich da selbst .... ich bin nicht zu mir da selbst gekommen.

[00:29:28]
David Boder: Was soll das heißen?

[00:29:29]
Adolph Heisler: Ich war schwach geworden nach dem Baden. Ich war sehr schwach und habe ein heißes Bad bekommen....

[00:29:34]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:29:34]
Adolph Heisler: ... und das hat mich, mein Beine zerstört, denn ich war doch ganz erfroren.

[00:29:38]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:29:39]
Adolph Heisler: Ich hab kaum können zum Bad zu gehen.

[00:29:41]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:29:42]
Adolph Heisler: Und danach bin ich ... nach dem heißen Bad, hat es mir den Kopf verdreht.

[00:00:00]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:29:45]
Adolph Heisler: Also, dann habe ich mich ein wenig hin gesetzt und bin zu mir ein bisschen gekommen.

[00:29:49]
David Boder: Aha.

[00:29:50]
Adolph Heisler: Und dann hat man und dann geschickt.... nach dem Bad wieder geschickt und die Haare wurden noch einmal abgeschoren alles. Die ganzen Haare abgeschoren, ja, .... und dann hat man uns geführt in Blocken in die Baracken. Und dort waren wir einige ... zwei (2) Tage in den Baracken. Und dann haben wir gehört, wir gehen wieder in die Arbeit - irgendwo anderen Platz. Und auf dem anderen Platz hat man uns heraus getrieben einen Morgen Tag in den Schnee (unverständlich). Und man hat uns nicht gesagt wohin man geht und das war auch ein kalter Tag und man hat uns hinaus gepackt in Wagons. Und wir sind gefahren einen Tag, es war gut, dass es war nicht mehr.

[00:30:31]
David Boder: Wieder von Buchenwald?

[00:30:32]
Adolph Heisler: Von Buchenwald, Deutschland zu einem anderen ... das war in Thüringen.

[00:30:36]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:30:36]
Adolph Heisler: Trawniki.

[00:30:37]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:30:38]
Adolph Heisler: Und wir sind angekommen im Lager. Also das war noch viel ärger wie die Kohlengruben.

[00:30:43]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:30:44]
Adolph Heisler: Das war ein Lager in (unverständlich) und dort waren Depots von Munition und im Keller haben wir gewohnt – unter die Erde in Bunkern.

[00:00:00]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:30:52]
Adolph Heisler: In einem Wald.

[00:30:53]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:30:54]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort war das ... das Behandeln noch viel ärger wie überall.

[00:30:58]
David Boder: Warum?

[00:30:59]
Adolph Heisler: Weil da hat man nicht gebadet. In anderen Lagern da konnte man da vielleicht noch baden. Wir haben kein Wasser gehabt. Das hat gedauert – in 3 Monaten also wir haben nicht gehabt kein Wasser auf dem Gesicht überhaupt – für waschen sich. Und die Läuse haben uns aufgegessen im Ganzen.

[00:31:14]
David Boder: Und was haben Sie dort denn getan?

[00:31:16]
Adolph Heisler: Gearbeitet, gegraben verschiedene Graben, Munition geladen.

[00:31:21]
David Boder: Aha.

[00:31:21]
Adolph Heisler: Und sie haben gebaut eine große Fabrik in einem ... unter dem Wald.

[00:31:25]
David Boder: Schon in fünf und vierzig (45)?

[00:31:27]
Adolph Heisler: In fünf und vierzig (45).

[00:31:27]
David Boder: Eine unterirdische Fabrik ....

[00:31:29]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:31:29]
David Boder: ... haben sie gebaut. Nun?

[00:31:31]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort war es doch was Schreckliches. Ich habe dort unterhalten mit Leuten, sie waren Einige von Polen, die waren sechs (6) Jahre schon darin. Haben sie gesagt, dass sie in die ärgsten Lager so wie Majdanek, Treblinka waren, aber in so einem Lager waren sie noch nicht.

[00:31:48]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:31:48]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort waren wir ... und dann bin ich auch noch krank geworden von die vielen Läuse – die letzten zwei (2) Woche bevor die Befreiung.

[00:31:57]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:31:58]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort bin ich krank geworden und bin ich ganze Zeit beim Arzt – acht (8) Tage. Ich bin hingegangen jeden Abend und hab gesagt, ich kann nicht arbeiten, aber er wollte mir nicht glauben.

[00:32:07]
David Boder: War es ein jüdischer Arzt?

[00:32:09]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:32:09]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:32:10]
Adolph Heisler: Von Polen, ein Jude. Das war ein sehr ein Schlechter. Da waren unter die Juden auch sehr schlechte Menschen, weil sie haben sehr .... sehr gemeine Leute.

[00:32:19]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:32:21]
Adolph Heisler: Und hat er mich dann.... er hat mich geschoben, ich war damals jung – ich war siebzehn (17) Jahre alt – und er hat mich dann gegeben ins Spital, das im Revier. Dort war ich acht (8) Tage. Da hat man mich geschickt dann - mit einem Transport auch nach (unverständlich).

[00:32:41]
David Boder: Wo waren die Krematorien denn?

[00:32:43]
Adolph Heisler: Das war in der Nähe – acht (8) Kilometer weiter von dort war auch ein Lager, ein großes Lager Ohrdorf. Und dort haben sie auch gehabt ein Krematorium hergerichtet.

[00:32:53]
David Boder: Haben sie dort die Leute vergast?

[00:32:55]
Adolph Heisler: Nein, sie haben sie nur getötet, aus .... sie waren sowieso schon halb tot. Sie haben sie tot geschlagen mit Gewehr oder was sonst, hm, ...................... aber das war unser Glück, dass die Amerikaner sind schon ....

[00:33:10]
David Boder: Nun wo waren Sie, wenn die Amerikaner sind gekommen?

[00:33:14]
Adolph Heisler: Wir waren da in diesem .....in diesem Lager, wo man hat uns genommen zum Pulver .... zum Vergasen. Und wir ....

[00:33:21]
David Boder: Was heißt das Lager ... welches Lager war das?

[00:33:23]
Adolph Heisler: Das war in Ohrdorf. Nachdem ich krank war, hat man mich weg geführt von dort.

[00:33:27]
David Boder: Wohin?

[00:33:28]
Adolph Heisler: Acht (8) Kilometer weiter war das Lager wo die Leute sollen .... war ein Krematorium. Die Leute waren... die dort hin kamen waren viele krank, weil .... es war schrecklich dort ...

[00:33:37]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:33:38]
Adolph Heisler: Die hat man getötet und verbrannt.

[00:33:41]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:33:43]
Adolph Heisler: Und ... und wie wir sind gekommen schon, das war schon der letzte Transport. Sie haben nicht mehr Zeit gehabt, dass ... dafür. Sie waren schon mit sich selbst zu tun, weil die Amerikaner haben sich schon genähert da.

[00:33:53]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:33:54]
Adolph Heisler: Und wir sind hier gelegen wieder acht (8) Tage. Und es hat geheißen, dass wir bleiben dort bis sie erschießen die ganzen Leute, aufschießen oder explodieren das Lager, oder was immer.

[00:34:09]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:34:09]
Adolph Heisler: Und zum Glück hat man uns genommen nach, hm, ... transportiert nach Buchenwald.

[00:34:16]
David Boder: Zurück transportiert nach Buchenwald?

[00:34:16]
Adolph Heisler: Ja, aber ...

[00:34:18]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:34:19]
Adolph Heisler: Es war aber ein besonderes Glück mit mir, dass – ich weiß nicht – wie ich das (unverständlich) die ganze Geschichte, weil .... uns alle hat man transportiert mit die Wagon, .....mit ....... zu Fuß.

[00:34:31]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:34:32]
Adolph Heisler: Und ich hab mir gesagt – da waren auch andere kranke Menschen – ich gehe nicht mehr zu Fuß; sie sollen mich hier töten. Ich soll zu Fuß gehen und dann sterben? Hab mich hierher gestellt, um hier zu sterben auf diesem Platz.

[00:34:43]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:34:44]
Adolph Heisler: Und dann ist gekommen im letzten Moment Autobus und so die Kranken wurden ein .... eingeladen in die Autos und hat man sie weggeführt.

[00:34:52]
David Boder: Nach Buchenwald?

[00:34:53]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:34:54]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:34:54]
Adolph Heisler: Und das war unser Glück. Wie wir sind gekommen nach Buchenwald ... da haben wir geglaubt .... In Buchenwald hat man uns in die Nähe des Krematoriums und so haben wir geglaubt, dass wir ins das Krematorium genommen werden, aber zum Glück ....

[00:35:06]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:35:07]
Adolph Heisler: ... hat man uns doch nicht ins Krematorium gebracht, sondern in dem alten Lager dort von die Menschen, die gekommen waren in Quarantäne. Und dort hat man uns gehalten einige Tage.

[00:35:19]
David Boder: Und dann?

[00:35:20]
Adolph Heisler: Wir haben gewusst, dass die Amerikaner sind schon nahe, weil sie sind schnell vorwärts, wir haben jede Nacht gehört die Schießerei. Und von Buchenwald hat man auch angefangen zu evakuieren .... weg zu führen viele Leute.

[00:35:32]
David Boder: Wohin?

[00:35:34]
Adolph Heisler: Also ich weiß nicht wohin.

[00:35:36]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:35:36]
Adolph Heisler: Weil ich bin dort geblieben und es hat geheißen, dass die ... wer kann gehen, kann gehen und wer nicht gehen kann, der ... denn das Lager wird zerstört.

[00:35:45]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:35:45]
Adolph Heisler: In letzter Stunde.

[00:35:46]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:35:47]
Adolph Heisler: Und ... die gesunden Leute sind gegangen, aber unser Block hat gesagt, wir gehen nicht. Und sie sollen uns töten, wir werden hier bleiben.

[00:35:56]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:35:57]
Adolph Heisler: Und ... die SS ist gekommen am anderen Tag ... es war ein Sonntag ... da sind gekommen die SS und sie haben angefangen hinaus zu schmeißen aus die Fenster und zu treiben.

[00:36:08]
David Boder: Hinaus zu schmeißen – was?

[00:36:10]
Adolph Heisler: Durch die Fenster.

[00:36:12]
David Boder: Ja, sie haben die Menschen raus geschmissen ....

[00:36:13]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:36:13]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:36:14]
Adolph Heisler: Durch die Fenster. Und sie haben angefangen sie zu treiben auf den Appell Platz und von dort hat man uns wollen evakuieren.

[00:36:20]
David Boder: Auf welchem Stock war es?

[00:36:22]
Adolph Heisler: Es war ... es waren nicht mit Stockwerk.

[00:36:25]
David Boder: Warum durch die Fenster, warum nicht durch die Türen?

[00:36:28]
Adolph Heisler: Weil niemand hat nicht wollen gehen!

[00:36:30]
David Boder: Aha, und?

[00:36:31]
Adolph Heisler: Jeder hat sich geweigert vor der Evakuierung.

[00:36:33]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:36:34]
Adolph Heisler: Und sie haben geschüttet Wasser über die Menschen. Niemand hat .... sie haben aber nichts ausgeführt. Die Leute haben sich gesagt, dass ..... sollen sie (unverständlich) ... sollen sie schießen.

[00:36:44]
David Boder: Nun?

[00:36:44]
Adolph Heisler: Und sie haben doch nicht geschossen, ich weiß nicht warum. Und am anderen Tag – wieder die selbe Geschichte. Und dann doch haben sie heraus gekriegt und haben die Leute versammelt am Appell Platz.

[00:36:56]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:36:57]
Adolph Heisler: Und ich bin auch dort hinaus gekommen. Und hab ich gesehen, dass da ein Transport steht mit Jugendliche.

[00:37:03]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:37:03]
Adolph Heisler: Und das war der Grund, sie wurden aussortiert – sie bleiben hier im Lager – sie sind nicht transportfähig. Und dann habe ich mich dorthin zu gestellt. Ich war ja auch Junge.

[00:37:13]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:37:14]
Adolph Heisler: Und hab mich hinzu gestellt und hab mich rein gemischt und bin zurück gegangen ins Lager C und die andere Leute sind weg mit den Transport. Und das war Dienstag schon. Und Mittwoch ... das war der achte Tage wo wir waren ganz ohne Essen. Am Mittwoch hat man gehört eine große Schießerei und um zehn (10) haben wir gehört den Feind-Alarm, der kam an, weil da kam ein amerikanischer Tank. Sie sind zurück gefahren und um elf (11) Uhr haben wir gehört die Flieger. Und um halb vier (4) sind wir befreit worden von die Amerikaner, das waren die ersten Amerikaner. Die ganzen Deutschen haben verlassen das ganze Lager.

[00:37:57]
David Boder: Und wann haben die Deutschen das Lager verlassen?

[00:38:00]
Adolph Heisler: Sie haben es verlassen um ein (1) Uhr Nachmittag.

[00:38:02]
David Boder: Und was haben sie gesagt?

[00:38:03]
Adolph Heisler: Nichts, man hat nur gesehen sie laufen sie weg von der Wache. Es war so. Wir haben nachher dann gewusst ... gehört, dass der von Weimar, der Lager Kommandant hat, hm, telefoniert, sie sollen sprengen die Lager – eine Stunde nach der Befreiung. Er hat noch nicht gewusst damals, dass das Lager ist befreit worden. Es war halb fünf. Und der Lager Älteste – es war ein Häftling – hat geantwortet: ‚Ja, ja, wir werden zersprengen ihre Köpfe.’ Also, wenn wir eine Stunde vorher noch nicht befreit gewesen wären, hätten sie gesprengt das Lager.

[00:38:39]
David Boder: Was hat er ihm geantwortet?

[00:38:41]
Adolph Heisler: Dass es, hm, dass er telefonieren sollte zum Heiland und nicht zu uns hier.

[00:38:46]
David Boder: Aha, nun?

[00:38:48]
Adolph Heisler: Und das war die Befreiung. Und nach der Befreiung die Menschen haben sich vorgestellt dann so Geschichten, ganze Beglückung, aber viele sind auch gestorben nach der Befreiung, weil sie haben bekommen das Essen, das Fett und die ganze Nahrung und haben sich verdorben den Magen. Und sie haben bekommen Bauchschmerzen und sind gestorben davon auch.

[00:39:08]
David Boder: Ja. Und dann wurde ...

[00:39:12]
Adolph Heisler: Und dann hat man mich weg genommen von dem jugendlichen Block, dort war ich eine Zeit lang. Dann bin ich krank geworden mit Fleck-Typhus.

[00:39:22]
David Boder: Nach der Befreiung haben Sie Fleck-Typhus bekommen?

[00:39:24]
Adolph Heisler: Ja.

[00:39:24]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:39:25]
Adolph Heisler: Und dort bin ich gelegen vier (4) Wochen krank. Und dann habe ich gehört von dem Transport in die Schweiz und hab ich mich auch gemeldet dafür zu fahren in die Schweiz.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Alexander Gertner
entries.content:
[00:00:00]
David Boder: Wait a moment. Stay there. [Music.] [In English:] Geneva, Switzerland. August the 26th, 1946, at a community house of displaced people, a religious, Jewish group, and the interviewee is Mr. Alexander Gertner.

[00:00:44]
David Boder: How old are you?

[00:00:45]
Alexander Gertner: I’ll soon be twenty.

[00:00:47]
David Boder: Twenty.

[00:00:48]
Alexander Gertner: I’ll be soon.

[00:00:48]
David Boder: He is twenty years [old]. He will be twenty next November.

[00:00:52]
David Boder: And so, Mr. Gertner, tell us again your name, Alexander Gertner.

[00:00:57]
Alexander Gertner: Alexander Gertner.

[00:00:58]
David Boder: And how old are you?

[00:00:59]
Alexander Gertner: Born on the 16th of November, ’26...1926.

[00:01:03]
David Boder: Yes. And where were you born, Mr. Gertner?

[00:01:06]
Alexander Gertner: In Roumania. [Name not clear] is the name of the place...

[00:01:08]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:01:09]
Alexander Gertner: ...province [of] Maramures [?] in Roumania.

[00:01:12]
David Boder: Roumania?

[00:01:13]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:01:13]
David Boder: Write down for me the name of the place.

[00:01:15]
Alexander Gertner: The place...

[00:01:17]
David Boder: And so, Mr. Gertner, you speak Yiddish. Do you want to speak Yiddish or German?

[00:01:20]
Alexander Gertner: Yiddish, yes, Yiddish.

[00:01:21]
David Boder: Yiddish. [In Yiddish:] And so, I want you to tell me everything.

[00:01:25]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:01:25]
David Boder: Where you have been when the war started and what happened to you. Make yourself comfortable and start telling.

[00:01:33]
Alexander Gertner: From the beginning.

[00:01:34]
David Boder: Don’t omit details.

[00:01:35]
Alexander Gertner: Yes?

[00:01:35]
David Boder: We want to know everything that happened.

[00:01:41]
Alexander Gertner: And so from the beginning. And so in recent times when I...in 1944...1944...[correction] in 1943 I came to Grosswardein [Roumanian name: Oradea], that was a town in Roumania...

[00:01:51]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:01:52]
Alexander Gertner: There I started learning carpentry. And I was learning there for a few months, and then it came about that I couldn’t learn any more, because there was no stuff...

[00:02:02]
David Boder: What does it mean, ‘no stuff’?

[00:02:03]
Alexander Gertner: No...no material.

[00:02:05]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:02:06]
Alexander Gertner: No material. And so I was compelled...I started learning another trade, glove knitting.

[00:02:12]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:02:12]
Alexander Gertner: You understand? And that also lasted a few months, and then stopped coming the supplies, the material from Budapest.

[00:02:21]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:02:21]
Alexander Gertner: So I remained in Grosswardein till 1944, till before Pesach [Jewish Easter]. In 1944 before Pesach I wanted to journey to my parents home in [not clear]...

[00:02:31]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:02:31]
Alexander Gertner: ...for Pesach. I believed that I would go home eight days before Pesach. Why do I have to go home two weeks before Pesach. Shall I speak louder?

[00:02:38]
David Boder: No...

[00:02:38]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:02:39]
David Boder: I will tell you. As soon as you see that this [the neon light indicator] lights up now and then, that means it is loud enough. Let’s go on.

[00:02:45]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:02:45]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:02:46]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:02:47]
David Boder: Go on [?].

[00:02:48]
Alexander Gertner: And so I figured on going home only eight days before Pesach, to go home. So eight days, ten days before Pesach the trains were barred for Jews. So Jews were not allowed to travel by trains.

[00:03:00]
David Boder: On the railroads.

[00:03:02]
Alexander Gertner: On the railroads.

[00:03:03]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:03:03]
Alexander Gertner: And so I forgot [to tell you]. On the 5th of March the Germans came [into our town]. On the 5th of March, 1944, the Germans entered.

[00:03:10]
David Boder: ’44.

[00:03:11]
Alexander Gertner: Yes, ’44, and we began right away wearing yellow stars.

[00:03:16]
David Boder: Yellow patches.

[00:03:16]
Alexander Gertner: Yellow patches.

[00:03:18]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:03:19]
Alexander Gertner: And...and so before Pesach I wanted to go home. One couldn’t. And after Pesach...and so I had to remain in Grosswardein. Right after Pesach, two weeks after Pesach, they began to assemble the Ghetto. And the Ghetto lasted [words not clear].

[00:03:32]
David Boder: So you did not go home?

[00:03:33]
Alexander Gertner: No. I remained in there. The parents wanted me home, and the mother and the father, because they weren’t in the same place, and I wanted to go home, and I couldn’t any more.

[00:03:42]
David Boder: Why...why weren’t your father and mother in the same place?

[00:03:45]
Alexander Gertner: Because they lived in that place where I was born, understand?

[00:03:48]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:03:48]
Alexander Gertner: And I went to [name not clear] to live there.

[00:03:51]
David Boder: Nu, but your father and mother lived together?

[00:03:53]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:03:53]
David Boder: Oh, yes. Do you have any brothers and sisters?

[00:03:55]
Alexander Gertner: No. I had one sister, younger than I.

[00:03:58]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:03:59]
Alexander Gertner: And so...

[00:03:59]
David Boder: Why do you say you ‘had’?

[00:04:01]
Alexander Gertner: I don’t know whether she is alive.

[00:04:02]
David Boder: [00:04:03]
Alexander Gertner: I am ninety per cent certain, alas, that she isn’t.

[00:04:05]
David Boder: And about your parents?

[00:04:06]
Alexander Gertner: Also. Even more [certain].

[00:04:07]
David Boder: Hm. Nu, and so you couldn’t go back.

[00:04:12]
Alexander Gertner: No. And so I remained in Grosswardein in the Ghetto. It was...the Ghetto was assembled two weeks after Pesach. It took four days till the Ghetto was built. It was shut. Nobody could go out, out of the house, and...

[00:04:24]
David Boder: There in the little town?

[00:04:25]
Alexander Gertner: No, Grosswardein was a bigger town of about a hundred and twenty thousand inhabitants.

[00:04:29]
David Boder: Write down for me the name of the town.

[00:04:30]
Alexander Gertner: Grosswardein.

[00:04:33]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:04:34]
Alexander Gertner: And the Ghetto began to be built. I have...I remained in a house there where I lived...well, in my room.

[00:04:41]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:04:42]
Alexander Gertner: And I...I didn’t have anything to eat, because I was not prepared [did not stock up]. I wanted in the morning to go to work like always at five o’clock. I got up to go for prayer and from there straight to work. So I got up. I see police already standing in the...every ten meters on the street, and the policeman tells me, ‘Shut the door again, and go back into the house.’ And so four days I was shut in the house. I couldn’t go out. We nearly died of hunger. And so then we were permitted to go out. Later already was...

[00:05:07]
David Boder: And so four days you were in the house.

[00:05:10]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:05:10]
David Boder: With whom were you in there?

[00:05:12]
Alexander Gertner: I was alone, because I lived privately [by myself]...

[00:05:14]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:05:14]
Alexander Gertner: ...in a room. Well, there were Jews there in the house, but every body thought about himself, but yet one did help out another.

[00:05:21]
David Boder: You got something to eat?

[00:05:23]
Alexander Gertner: Nothing special, but one could get something.

[00:05:25]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:05:25]
Alexander Gertner: Very little, you can imagine. And then after the four days was Saturday. I wanted to go out to....I had relatives there in Grosswardein. I wanted to go out to my relatives. So I was instantly caught to work. I didn’t even have time...

[00:05:37]
David Boder: The Germans caught you to work?

[00:05:38]
Alexander Gertner: The Germans caught [people] on the street to work. I was brought to a...to a...to a food factory. There we had to unload wagons with potatoes and German clothing in to a storehouse. I unloaded the same, and it lasted till the evening. We didn’t eat anything since the morning, and in the evening a pot of potatoes was cooked for us, and we were given it. That was the...till the evening. In the evening there arrived the SS superior group leader [an officer]. He saw that the work wasn’t finished yet. He began to throw around the potatoes and [he] wanted to devour everybody. And so...so the Ghetto...

[00:06:12]
David Boder: And so from this work, where did you go?

[00:06:15]
Alexander Gertner: Went back to the relatives. I didn’t go back to the old place where I lived, on that street. I went back to my relatives, and I have...

[00:06:22]
David Boder: Your relatives lived in the Ghetto?

[00:06:24]
Alexander Gertner: Oh, yes, they lived in the Ghetto.

[00:06:25]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:25]
Alexander Gertner: And so I went there to eat something [?]. From the Ghetto...

[00:06:28]
David Boder: Excuse me. Tell me, how is a Ghetto made? How did they make the Ghetto?

[00:06:32]
Alexander Gertner: How they made the Ghetto? First they made a plan. There were in the town thirty thousand Jews. They made a plan. All Jews should...for instance, in...in the Jewish region they intended to blockade all the streets. They blockaded, and they told the Gentiles to move out of these streets, and the streets were barricaded with boards two meters high, and all the Jews from the whole town were sent into...into these few streets. And even from the surrounding towns the Jews were brought...who lived in the surrounding towns were brought in.

[00:06:59]
David Boder: And who decided where one was going to live?

[00:07:04]
Alexander Gertner: The Germans. Everything [by] the Germans.

[00:07:05]
David Boder: The Germans.

[00:07:05]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:07:06]
David Boder: Did they say, ‘You go in here, and you go in there?’

[00:07:09]
Alexander Gertner: No. They said here the Jews have to live, on this piece of ground.

[00:07:12]
David Boder: All right, but...

[00:07:13]
Alexander Gertner: All the Jews were sent in. The Germans brought [them] with trucks. The whole town was sent in by trucks, thrown into the Ghetto, on this piece of ground.

[00:07:20]
David Boder: On the few streets.

[00:07:20]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. Now then...yes. And everyone...among us there were already appointed Jewish police and all kinds of different...Hungarian police. [Word not clear] it is called in Hungarian.

[00:07:30]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:07:30]
Alexander Gertner: And then they pushed in....In one house has to be...in one room had to be nine people, in one room of twelve meters. No, well, in one room of...in a bigger room nine people had to live.

[00:07:41]
David Boder: Let’s take a room like this.

[00:07:43]
Alexander Gertner: In a room like this approximately twenty people had to live.

[00:07:46]
David Boder: How big do you think this room is? How many meters square are here?

[00:07:50]
Alexander Gertner: In this room? Approximately eight by eight, eight by nine.

[00:07:56]
David Boder: Eight by nine. And so in a room eight by nine approximately how many had to live?

[00:08:01]
Alexander Gertner: Twenty to twenty-five people had to live.

[00:08:03]
David Boder: People...

[00:08:03]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:08:03]
David Boder: How, men and women...

[00:08:04]
Alexander Gertner: Men and wives together with children, everything. They were thrown together with the things, with all the belongings that they possessed.

[00:08:10]
David Boder: The policemen did that?

[00:08:11]
Alexander Gertner: The policemen, yes. And then one did...the...the Ghetto...When they began to move them in trucks, they were thrown on the streets. And then, when all those people were already in the Ghetto, he began to distribute everybody. In this house live so many. In this house....One was missing a child. One was missing a sack with things. One was missing that. One was missing that. It was a calamity! And everybody was on guard, because the grabbed for work on various things, in various places. And we...then when we had been already distributed, we already were pushed together. I lived with my relatives. There I lived. Then everybody was allotted....The food in the Ghetto consisted of a fifth...it was twenty-five dekas of bread. That is...how much is that in grams? Twenty-five dekagrams of bread and a liter of soup.

[00:08:57]
David Boder: Two hundred and fifty grams.

[00:08:58]
Alexander Gertner: Two hundred and fifty grams and...heavy bread. It was heavy bread [of inferior flour badly baked], and there was a liter of soup at dinner time — sometimes even a little more, and in the morning black coffee, but no sugar.

[00:09:07]
David Boder: Now wait a moment. Wait a moment. You say ‘a liter of soup.’ Did everybody go from home to the...

[00:09:13]
Alexander Gertner: No. One [person] went from a house. For instance, from a family that had five people it was said...it was recorded that every family has so many, and he was given for so many.

[00:09:22]
David Boder: So many liters of soup.

[00:09:23]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:09:23]
David Boder: Where was it cooked?

[00:09:24]
Alexander Gertner: There was a field kitchen. At first there was one big field kitchen. Then it was seen that it was not enough. There were four, five kitchens established.

[00:09:31]
David Boder: You have a tattoo number...

[00:09:32]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:09:32]
David Boder: What is the number?

[00:09:33]
Alexander Gertner: Twelve thousand two hundred sixty-nine [12,269].

[00:09:36]
David Boder: And the letter ‘A.’ ‘A,’ what is it for?

[00:09:38]
Alexander Gertner: ‘A’? It began...it was like this. At first it was made till two hundred [two hundred thousand?], and then they completed two hundred. So they began again from one, and the made an ‘A’ [possibly a triangle].

[00:09:46]
David Boder: Hm. All right.

[00:09:48]
Alexander Gertner: You understand?

[00:09:49]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:09:49]
Alexander Gertner: And then...I want to continue...So dinner was distributed in the Ghetto. A little soup was given. It was only watter. And we who had [something] added a little cooking at home, and whoever didn’t...So the Ghetto lasted four...

[00:10:03]
David Boder: [00:10:04]
Alexander Gertner: The number six is already worn off. It was like this...

[00:10:07]
David Boder: Why is it worn off?

[00:10:08]
Alexander Gertner: It came about by itself.

[00:10:09]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:10:09]
Alexander Gertner: It wasn’t written well at the beginning...

[00:10:11]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:10:11]
Alexander Gertner: ...because it was done quickly.

[00:10:12]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:10:13]
Alexander Gertner: [00:10:15]
David Boder: Sixty-nine or sixty-five?

[00:10:17]
Alexander Gertner: Sixty-nine.

[00:10:17]
David Boder: Hm, nu? And so?

[00:10:20]
Alexander Gertner: And so we...and everybody was given the little food. The Ghetto became thus. During the time of the Ghetto everybody had to work. They caught young boys and also girls. We had to work hard. For instance, in a bakery that was there, we had to carry eighty-five-kilo sacks to the second floor [in Europe the third.] Boys came home with lung infections, with shooting pains, with different [word not clear].

[00:10:37]
David Boder: What?

[00:10:39]
Alexander Gertner: With diseases boys came home, from carrying the heavy sacks to the second floor.

[00:10:44]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:10:44]
Alexander Gertner: You understand?

[00:10:45]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:10:45]
Alexander Gertner: And then the Ghetto played [existed] like this for four weeks. One was grabbed, one was beaten at work, and we didn’t know what was happening. And then in the Ghetto was installed in the large Beth Hamidrosh [an annex of the synagogue; term also used synonimously with synagogue]....There was a [word not clear] Beth Hamidrosh in Grosswardein in the synagogue. It was vacated. All the things that were in there were thrown out, and it was made into a Ghetto...a Jewish...a Ghetto hospital.

[00:11:08]
David Boder: A Ghetto hospital?

[00:11:09]
Alexander Gertner: A Ghetto hospital.

[00:11:10]
David Boder: Who did that?

[00:11:11]
Alexander Gertner: That was made...that was ordered by the Germans. It was made by the Jews themselves...it was made.

[00:11:15]
David Boder: Why?

[00:11:16]
Alexander Gertner: They had to. It was ordered.

[00:11:16]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:11:17]
Alexander Gertner: There were so many sick that we didn’t know where to put the sick.

[00:11:20]
David Boder: Were you allowed to carry out the Sefer Torahs [the Holy Scrolls]?

[00:11:22]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. We had to, not that we were just allowed.

[00:11:24]
David Boder: But yes, but they weren’t thrown out.

[00:11:26]
Alexander Gertner: No, they were carried out. We received the order. And then we have...they threw into the hospital....The synagogue annex was very big. People were carried in there who had wasted away [?]. Nobody paid attention to a person. Surely there were Jewish doctors. They were, of course, their people. One didn’t know what to do. They [the Germans] didn’t give any medicaments. They didn’t give any supplies with which to treat. One held out. One, two, on the third day he was already dead. My...my uncle also lay there with pneumonia, usually a light illness. Then he developed pleurisy. He did not receive any care. Then he caught pleurisy, and so with the pleurisy he came to Auschwitz. And, of course, you know what happened there. And like this it was. And so the Ghetto lived thus for four weeks. And then began the deportations. It was on the second day, well, a day after Shevuoth [the Feast of the Tabernacles] in ’44. It started on the 1st of June....No, on the 1st of June I went...it means approximately on the 6th, on the 25th of May.

[00:12:25]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:12:28]
Alexander Gertner: They began to send transports. The first transport took place on the Saturday after the Feast of the Tabernacles.

[00:12:32]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:12:32]
Alexander Gertner: Then, after the first transport was sent away...

[00:12:35]
David Boder: Now wait a moment. How was the first transport selected? How was the transport assembled?

[00:12:40]
Alexander Gertner: It was done like this. One street was taken in the morning, a certain street. It was arranged that every street had a number, a district number.

[00:12:47]
David Boder: Hm. Yes.

[00:12:47]
Alexander Gertner: The first street was taken, for instance, Kopetino [?] Street, and Khotin [?] Street, which were there.

[00:12:51]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:12:52]
Alexander Gertner: These [streets] were taken. There were three thousand people. They were loaded into wagons [RR-cars], and they were taken away.

[00:12:58]
David Boder: Men, women, and children?

[00:12:58]
Alexander Gertner: Men, women, children, everything.

[00:13:00]
David Boder: Those who could work, also?

[00:13:02]
Alexander Gertner: Did not matter. Everything, everything. From young to old.

[00:13:04]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:13:05]
Alexander Gertner: Sick people, too.

[00:13:06]
David Boder: And where were they transported to?

[00:13:07]
Alexander Gertner: They...we were told that we are taken ito deep Hungary to a lager.

[00:13:11]
David Boder: You were on that transport?

[00:13:13]
Alexander Gertner: We were told so [?].

[00:13:14]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:13:14]
Alexander Gertner: And then we were....Where they were taken to, one knows — to Auschwitz. To Auschwitz we were taken. I, too, went there.

[00:13:20]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:13:20]
Alexander Gertner: And then we came...and so it was. The first transport was taken away. I was caught to work. It was on the first day of Saturday [obviously Shevouth]. In the houses from which the Jews were taken away the SS have...the Hungarian gendarmes...the gendarmerie...

[00:13:34]
David Boder: You said you were born in Roumania?

[00:13:36]
Alexander Gertner: Yes, but in the year ’40 we were handed over by the Germans [?]—I forgot to tell you — to Hungary. You surely heard about it.

[00:13:40]
David Boder: Yes, well...

[00:13:41]
Alexander Gertner: The district of [?] Transylvania...

[00:13:43]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:13:43]
Alexander Gertner: ...was occupied by Hungary in the year ’40, in September.

[00:13:46]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:13:46]
Alexander Gertner: You surely heard about it.

[00:13:47]
David Boder: Yes, yes, yes. Nu?

[00:13:48]
Alexander Gertner: And I was born as a Roumanian and went to a Roumanian school.

[00:13:52]
David Boder: And then you became a Hungarian.

[00:13:53]
Alexander Gertner: Became....The Hungarians handed us over to Auschwitz, because the Roumanians did not hand any Jews over to Auschwitz.

[00:13:58]
David Boder: Oh! The Roumanians did not hand over the Jews?

[00:14:00]
Alexander Gertner: No. The Roumanians did not. They gave them trouble [harrasments] in the country. Jews were killed off there and slaughtered and sent to Dniestr, but directly to Auschwitz in transports...

[00:14:07]
David Boder: Where did you say they were sent to?

[00:14:09]
Alexander Gertner: To Dniestr. There to the Ukraine.

[00:14:11]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:14:11]
Alexander Gertner: To Dniestr.

[00:14:12]
David Boder: To Dniestr.

[00:14:12]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:14:13]
David Boder: But you were not handed over to Auschwitz.

[00:14:14]
Alexander Gertner: No direct transports like in Hungary, where they took from young to old on a transport.

[00:14:18]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:14:18]
Alexander Gertner: The people were not taken in Roumania.

[00:14:19]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:14:19]
Alexander Gertner: Only in Hungary.

[00:14:20]
David Boder: And so you were taken to work after the first transport.

[00:14:23]
Alexander Gertner: No. I was taken directly to these houses to remove the furnishings. I saw that there are in these houses Prayer Shawls, Phylacteries. Everything was strewn about. I pictured to myself how it must be [now] in our house, too. And so the transports went in this manner. There were six transports: Saturday the first, then Sunday, Monday, Tuesday...on Tuesday there did not depart a transport, so we already thought that...that...

[00:14:44]
David Boder: That it will be enough.

[00:14:45]
Alexander Gertner: That it will be enough. In the meantime there were no wagons [available]. Next day they took again. Wednesday I came into transp-...my turn [came], that is, I and my housemates [?]. And so we were taken on a transport and quickly....We didn’t know anything on the evening [before] that tomorrow we are going on a transport, because we knew that another district was going. In the morning comes in the...the gendarmerie, the Hungarian, and yell, ‘Quick, in half an hour everybody has to be with his bundles in the street.’ And my...my aunt begins to cry. The uncle lies in the hospital sick, helpless. And she has to go away, and the hospital still remains. And so, well, he didn’t...she was not permitted to take leave of him. And so we came. We stood in the street, five in a row, and then suddenly they counted up, counted up. Right before us it stopped. Thus there were already enough. Three thousand could only be taken at one time. And we remained behind, two hundred and fifty people. We remained behind, because it was...we could not be taken any more on this transport.

[00:15:36]
David Boder: And your aunt also remained behind?

[00:15:37]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. My aunt and my uncle, and another friend, too. And then we were taken into the synagogue annex. There was a big synagogue annex.

[00:15:46]
David Boder: [00:15:48]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:15:49]
David Boder: So three thousand were taken.

[00:15:50]
Alexander Gertner: Three thousand. They took more, because they did not know how many were in the district [?]. So they counted off the three thousand, and two hundred and fifty remained. There were too many.

[00:15:58]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:15:59]
Alexander Gertner: We were brought back. We were brought into that house. We were locked in the big synagogue. There was a big, [word not clear] synagogue. We were locked in. We were not permitted to go out [words not clear].

[00:16:09]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:16:10]
Alexander Gertner: And there we were brought something to eat from the kitchen. They admitted it [the food], barely admitted it. We had to stay there overnight. You can imagine! Two hundred and fifty people had to stay there overnight on the benches, and...

[00:16:21]
David Boder: Women and children?

[00:16:21]
Alexander Gertner: Women and children and old and sick. It was a...a...and then in the morning exactly at five arrived a transport of gendarmerie, the Hungarians, who took us to fall in also in fives, and we were again...we were taken to the wagons.

[00:16:38]
David Boder: Well, you said that you...

[00:16:40]
Alexander Gertner: Already the next day...the next day...already on Thursday.

[00:16:41]
David Boder: Oh! So you were spared it only for one day.

[00:16:45]
Alexander Gertner: What?

[00:16:46]
David Boder: For one...your deportation was put off for one day. For one day.

[00:16:51]
Alexander Gertner: No. We have...we went away Wednesday.

[00:16:54]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:16:54]
Alexander Gertner: In the meantime there were too many, so we were sent away Thursday.

[00:16:57]
David Boder: Nu, nu?

[00:16:58]
Alexander Gertner: You understand?

[00:16:58]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:16:59]
Alexander Gertner: And then in turn [?] on Thursday morning we were taken again and led to the trains. We were taken. There already stood...

[00:17:04]
David Boder: To the rainroad.

[00:17:05]
Alexander Gertner: The railroad.

[00:17:06]
David Boder: Were there other people?

[00:17:07]
Alexander Gertner: Other...well, crowds of people behind us.

[00:17:10]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:17:10]
Alexander Gertner: We were the first, becasue we were the rest from yesterday.

[00:17:13]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:17:13]
Alexander Gertner: You understand? We were taken right away to the wagons. There we already saw whole [many] wagons were standing, maybe dozens [?] of wagons. And the SS distrubute [the people into] the wagons. There was a superior group leader with a few SS officers. They counted up the [people for the] wagons, and they did....I went into the first wagon. We were counted off eighty people, and...and we went into the wagon.

[00:17:35]
David Boder: What kind of wagons were they?

[00:17:37]
Alexander Gertner: They were freight wagons...

[00:17:39]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:17:39]
Alexander Gertner: ...used for transportation of cattle.

[00:17:41]
David Boder: A freight wagon.

[00:17:42]
Alexander Gertner: Freight wagon, freight wagons.

[00:17:43]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:17:44]
Alexander Gertner: They were small wagons. We entered eighty, eighty-five people into one wagon, and we were locked in. They said, ‘Who is missing...if one will be missing, then the whole wagon will be shot.’ So said the Hungarian gendarmerie. They said that.

[00:17:57]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:17:58]
Alexander Gertner: And then someone was made the leader of the wagon. He should supervise.

[00:18:04]
David Boder: A Jew?

[00:18:04]
Alexander Gertner: Also a Jew. There were only Jews there.

[00:18:06]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:18:07]
Alexander Gertner: And we were locked in there. On Thursday at twelve o’clock...

[00:18:12]
David Boder: You were there with whom?

[00:18:14]
Alexander Gertner: I was...by accident I was able to be with my...with my relatives, [word not clear] only with the aunt, because the uncle remained in the hospital. She alone—the others were thrown into another wagon. One couldn’t choose.

[00:18:24]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:18:24]
Alexander Gertner: We remained there with strangers, such from the same city, acquantainces. And eighty people in a wagon, a small wagon. For the whole wagon was...was...was allotted a jar of water, and a half a bread to each.

[00:18:37]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:18:37]
Alexander Gertner: A small piece [?] of black bread. This was for the whole journey, and we had nothing prepared [?].

[00:18:42]
David Boder: Were you told where you were being taken?

[00:18:44]
Alexander Gertner: We were told nothing. Absolutely nothing was said. The train started moving Thursday noon at twelve o’clock, and we went...

[00:18:51]
David Boder: Nu, a convenience...

[00:18:53]
Alexander Gertner: There was nothing.

[00:18:54]
David Boder: ...a toilet.

[00:18:54]
Alexander Gertner: There were in the wagons absolutely no toilets. Absolutely nothing. It was...we went out [releaved ourselves] ...one...it was...impossible to tell.

[00:19:01]
David Boder: Tell it...how was it?

[00:19:04]
Alexander Gertner: We went out. We had containers or such. We poured it out through the window. One saw another...we couldn’t...we took a dress, covered there a corner of the wagon and there. When one came out another went in. So in a line...

[00:19:17]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:19:17]
Alexander Gertner: We didn’t have any water to wash one’s self and such.

[00:19:20]
David Boder: Hm. One made it on the [in English:] floor...[in German:] on the floor?

[00:19:24]
Alexander Gertner: Right on the floor. The children screamed. They had no water, and the...on the first day there was still water that had been given, and we could [get] a little on the way. And then on the second day there was absolutely no water. The children—it was a pity—the children cried. The parents did not drink any water so that it should remain for the children.

[00:19:42]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:19:43]
Alexander Gertner: So we journeyed for four days and four nights till...till Sunday evening.

[00:19:49]
David Boder: Yes. Where did you come to?

[00:19:51]
Alexander Gertner: Sunday evening we came to...to Birkenau, to Auschwitz. This is near Auschwitz.

[00:19:55]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:19:56]
Alexander Gertner: And so in the wagons was...we thought we shall perish from thirst. There were terrible heat spells then, and...

[00:20:02]
David Boder: Just a moment. [Words not clear.]

[00:20:04]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. It was terribly hot, and the wagons were closed...

[00:20:09]
David Boder: When was it? In June or May?

[00:20:10]
Alexander Gertner: June. The first of June.

[00:20:12]
David Boder: The first of June. Nu?

[00:20:13]
Alexander Gertner: We couldn’t stand it. We said, ‘If we go another night, then...’ We were all undressed, naked, only in the trousers, because of the heat. We arrived on the first of June. We arrived at...

[00:20:26]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:20:28]
Alexander Gertner: On the first of June we arrived in Auschwitz.

[00:20:30]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:20:30]
Alexander Gertner: Birkenau it is called. Auschwitz one could...but Birkenau was the extermination camp. And there we detrained. And so says...says my aunt, ‘Do they take away the things?’ All the things which we had brought. So one there says, ...There were other Jews, Polish, who had unloaded us, who had been in the lager a long time, who cleaned out the RR-cars. They said, ‘The soul is taken away, too, not only the things!’

[00:20:54]
David Boder: Nu.

[00:20:55]
Alexander Gertner: We went down...we were immediately, right away, told to fall in fives, men separately and women separately. We couldn’t...I didn’t even have time to bid good bye to the relatives, to the friends. We were told to hurry. The SS were standing. We were lined up by the SS [?]. We were ordered to fall in. First the women fell in and then the men. We fell in. There was standing an SS chief doctor and was showing with his finger: left and right, left and right.

[00:21:21]
David Boder: Why did he point? What did it mean?

[00:21:23]
Alexander Gertner: Those...those whose face he saw looked young and was healthy for work, that he can work...some he asked, ‘How old are you?’ One...seldom he asked the age...if he was in doubt. And left [he pointed] when he was old [?]. Right away he said, ‘Left, right, left, right.’

[00:21:38]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:21:39]
Alexander Gertner: And those...those on the left, about those, we know where they went. They went into the gas chamber right away. And we, the others, went to bathe. We were taken away to...we were sorted out. From such a transport there could have been sorted out approximately two hundred to two hundred and fifty men.

[00:21:55]
David Boder: One couldn’t see the crematories in Birkenau? In Birkenau...

[00:21:58]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. In Birkenau were the crematories. There we saw them. It was so...

[00:22:02]
David Boder: Where were you? In Auschwitz or Birkenau?

[00:22:03]
Alexander Gertner: In Birkenau. In Auschwitz there were no crematories.

[00:22:06]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:22:07]
Alexander Gertner: And so, it was so. When we came there were arriving many transports, because they hurried...

[00:22:11]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:22:11]
Alexander Gertner: There arrived in a day fifteen thousand to twenty thousand people.

[00:22:15]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:22:16]
Alexander Gertner: They arrived...they did not have time to burn them in the crematories, because in a crematory went thirty-six people [at one time]. There were thirty-six...[correction] six crematories. In a crematory were six ovens.

[00:22:26]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:22:26]
Alexander Gertner: In every oven one man. So in a few minutes thirty-six people could burn. That means that in six crematories could [be burned] a few hundred people in a few minutes. That is not...but this was not enough.

[00:22:36]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:22:36]
Alexander Gertner: Because so many people were arriving. So they took, in the forest...There was a forest there.

[00:22:40]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:22:40]
Alexander Gertner: They took and made pits.

[00:22:43]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:22:43]
Alexander Gertner: These were dug out and wood was packed in. And when the people were brought out from the gas chamber...

[00:22:49]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:22:49]
Alexander Gertner: And so all the people had been gassed.

[00:22:51]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:22:52]
Alexander Gertner: They were still alive, because in eight minutes one can still...one still had the soul in him [was still alive]. They were immediately transported in RR-cars from the gas chamber, when taken out from there [?], and right away in RR-cars the people were sent over to the pits. The people were thrown in there, more wood was thrown on top, and fire set to it. And we were...

[00:23:07]
David Boder: With what was it lit?

[00:23:09]
Alexander Gertner: Probably with gasoline.

[00:23:10]
David Boder: Did you see it?

[00:23:11]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. The flames were seen. So we asked, ‘What are the flames there?’ This we saw first when we didn’t know anything about the crematories. So we asked, ‘What are the flames?’ So we were told by the others who had been there. They said, ‘The old things are being burned that people brought along.’ And then a day later we found out about the flames. We...we felt the stench. We didn’t know what it was...

[00:23:31]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:23:31]
Alexander Gertner: ...what was stinking. And so we were led — I know what happened — to the others [?]. And we were taken, the two hundred men. We were led into a bathhouse on the other side. Going on the road...

[00:23:44]
David Boder: How old were you then?

[00:23:45]
Alexander Gertner: Then? It was two years ago.

[00:23:47]
David Boder: So?

[00:23:48]
Alexander Gertner: I was...

[00:23:49]
David Boder: Eighteen...

[00:23:49]
Alexander Gertner: Eighteen. Seventeen and a half years approximately.

[00:23:51]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:23:53]
Alexander Gertner: And so on the road, when I...when all the things were taken away, I took with me...there was a bread lying on the ground, so I picked up a bread. I saw that it is necessary to have a bread with oneself. Whatever is taken away that...and the Phylacteries I took along with me. And on the way...there were very many camps. There were women’s lagers. There were on the road leading to the bathhouse...I see women there standing there and begging. Other people are throwing them something to eat. They fall one on top of the other and fight over the food. So I took the bread and threw it in [to them]. So I saw they threw themselves, maybe five, ten, or fifteen women, maybe more, on that bread.

[00:24:28]
David Boder: Were these the women who had been in the lager, or women...

[00:24:30]
Alexander Gertner: In the lager, the lager. They were already behind fences. And from afar I saw an SS woman who was managing them. [She] saw that...that they are grabbing bread, so she chased them away. She beat them. So I said [understood] then, I already knew, I already saw that there is a hunger, because they were grabbing....We didn’t know where we were...

[00:24:47]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:24:48]
Alexander Gertner: We were bewildered. We were led to the baths. And so we were all thirsty. We waited till we came to water so that we could fill up with water. And in the meantime we could not go out [satisfy our needs]. Already for a few days we had not gone out, you know what I mean, in the toilet.

[00:25:02]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:25:02]
Alexander Gertner: And we...we...

[00:25:03]
David Boder: You mean you have kept back?

[00:25:04]
Alexander Gertner: We kept back with all our strength. We didn’t eat in the RR-cars, so that we shouldn’t have to go, because it was embarrassing. And...and one couldn’t stand it, a crowd [?] of eighty people, when every person should go out.

[00:25:15]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:25:15]
Alexander Gertner: You understand? And then we were...when we were...

[00:25:21]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:25:21]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. When we went to the bath, and there first of all there was a ditch, so everybody went and relieved himself. We didn’t know what...we didn’t know if it was permitted or it was not permitted. We were told to undress nude. We waited in the nude. It was already in the evening. It was cold. We shivered. And they closed...we went inside, and we went to bathe. We entered the bath hall. We were all...we were all told to go into such a water, such a gasoline, that disinfects the body.

[00:25:53]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:25:53]
Alexander Gertner: And then we were showered. And so we were crowded in with thousands of people...

[00:25:57]
David Boder: What does it mean, you had to walk into gasoline? What was it, a tub?

[00:26:00]
Alexander Gertner: Yes, in such a bathtub that is...that is...gasoline...there was something. I don’t know if it is gasoline or such. It disinfects.

[00:26:06]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:26:06]
Alexander Gertner: There shouldn’t be...something, different things...

[00:26:09]
David Boder: Diseases.

[00:26:10]
Alexander Gertner: Diseases.

[00:26:11]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:26:11]
Alexander Gertner: We went in, and there we were showered. And when we went under the shower, we drank up more water than...than we used for bathing, because we are very thirsty.

[00:26:21]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:26:22]
Alexander Gertner: And then, when we came out, everybody was given a [pair of] pants, these prisoner’s pants, striped, and a jacket and a shirt and a cap. This...

[00:26:29]
David Boder: And a cap?

[00:26:30]
Alexander Gertner: And a cap.

[00:26:30]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:26:31]
Alexander Gertner: And then, when we came out, no one could recognize the other. We absolutely couldn’t recognize...

[00:26:36]
David Boder: Why?

[00:26:37]
Alexander Gertner: Because we were other, because we were dressed most differently, with a cap, with a...in such...in such a suit.

[00:26:43]
David Boder: The hair wasn’t cut?

[00:26:45]
Alexander Gertner: The hair was completely cut off, from head to feet.

[00:26:47]
David Boder: When?

[00:26:48]
Alexander Gertner: Before entering the bath.

[00:26:49]
David Boder: Oh!

[00:26:50]
Alexander Gertner: There stood barbers. They shore us from head to feet, wherever [?]...

[00:26:53]
David Boder: What kind of barbers? With what did they cut?

[00:26:55]
Alexander Gertner: With scissors, with different...they tore it together with the flesh.

[00:26:59]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:26:59]
Alexander Gertner: You understand? And then, when we had been...finished, when we were finished up with the machines, we went in small groups, still in a line, into...into the bath hall.

[00:27:10]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:27:10]
Alexander Gertner: When we came out, we absolutely couldn’t recognize one another. And here we see how...how one comes out. He shows that he has a blue back, that he had been beaten in...still in the Ghetto, because in the Ghetto it was still so, till that, for instance, the rich people, who were known in town to be rich...

[00:27:26]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:27:27]
Alexander Gertner: ...and were known as rich people, they were beaten [by] the Hungarian soldiers of the Hungarian army, that they should hand over the gold and the money that they had hidden.

[00:27:35]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:27:35]
Alexander Gertner: They were beaten. There was such a mangler.

[00:27:37]
David Boder: A what?

[00:27:37]
Alexander Gertner: A mangler. That was a house, such a house that was called a mangler [a barn housing a mangling machine for cold pressing of clothes].

[00:27:41]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:27:41]
Alexander Gertner: They were taken in there, and they were beaten till [near] death [so] they should tell...to tell everything, where one hid the money and the gold. There was still such a Jew who had been there, in that mangler. In the same...

[00:27:52]
David Boder: Mangler was called the place?

[00:27:54]
Alexander Gertner: That house was called mangler, yes.

[00:27:55]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:27:56]
Alexander Gertner: And so he showed what a blue back he had from the beating.

[00:28:01]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:28:01]
Alexander Gertner: An incident [?]. And then, when we had been bathed, we had...it was already late at night. It was already approxiamtely twelve at night. We...we were put in a row, and we were led, and...

[00:28:14]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:28:15]
Alexander Gertner: Dark—we did not see anything. We were led. What do we see? We saw only the flames...flames, huge flames, maybe up to fifty meters in height. We saw flames and smoke.

[00:28:24]
David Boder: From where? From the pits or...

[00:28:26]
Alexander Gertner: From...from the pits. From the crematories such flames didn’t come out, because they had a chimney.

[00:28:30]
David Boder: Yes...

[00:28:30]
Alexander Gertner: And the...

[00:28:31]
David Boder: ...a smokestack.

[00:28:32]
Alexander Gertner: Yes, a smokestack.

[00:28:33]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:28:34]
Alexander Gertner: When we came back, we were taken into a block, into a wooden block, there in the Gypsy lager.

[00:28:40]
David Boder: All right. Why was it called the Gypsy lager? Yes?

[00:28:44]
Alexander Gertner: In the Gypsy lager there were Gypsies. They had been already longer in camp. And they...they supervised us. They beat with...every little Gypsy was beating. He had a big stick. Such a small child, and he beat...

[00:28:57]
David Boder: Whom did he beat?

[00:28:58]
Alexander Gertner: Everybody, whoever was close he had the right to beat.

[00:29:02]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:29:02]
Alexander Gertner: So we...we came in at twelve o’clock at night into that lager. We didn’t know anything. So there came in one Gypsy, a tall one, with a club. He says, ‘Whoever has money hidden on him, or gold, should immediately hand it over!’ If it should be found on someone he will shoot him immediately. And we...we said...

[00:29:22]
David Boder: What language did he speak?

[00:29:24]
Alexander Gertner: German.

[00:29:25]
David Boder: German. A Gypsy.

[00:29:26]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:29:26]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:29:27]
Alexander Gertner: And he went...

[00:29:27]
David Boder: Why was it called the Gypsy lager?

[00:29:30]
Alexander Gertner: Because...because...because there lived Gypsies. There were like this: Lager ‘A’, Lager ‘B’, Lager ‘C’. There were numbers, and this was a Gypsy lager.

[00:29:37]
David Boder: And the little ones lived there...

[00:29:39]
Alexander Gertner: Yes.

[00:29:39]
David Boder: ...with them?

[00:29:39]
Alexander Gertner: Yes, as prisoners, too.

[00:29:40]
David Boder: They were...

[00:29:41]
Alexander Gertner: They were there together with the women and children. They could live together with the women and children.

[00:29:46]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:29:48]
Alexander Gertner: And so at night...

[00:29:49]
David Boder: And they...they were assigned over you?

[00:29:52]
Alexander Gertner: Yes. They were assigned over us. They were the block elders and room elders, and so forth.

[00:29:56]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:29:57]
Alexander Gertner: At night...it was already around three, four. And so we were harangued that we should hand over quickly, and before going to sleep, everybody should hand over everything.
