So that at night we had to get out a little to catch fresh air. And indeed, on the night when we went out we met a young man who asked about a [his] father, about an entire family. [00:16:51] David Boder: Yes? [00:16:52] Benjamin Piskorz: And he mentioned the name. We said that we didn’t know him, and that same ‘comrade’ noticed where we were hiding, and next morning he come in again with gendarmerie and betrayed us. When I came out of the cellar the gendarmerie immediately had me. [00:17:07] David Boder: Have you know him? Did you know who he was? [00:17:09] Benjamin Piskorz: I didn’t know him, because he was not a Jew from Warsaw. And even from Warsaw one can’t know all the Jews. [00:17:15] David Boder: Hm. [00:17:15] Benjamin Piskorz: And this really was...from his pronunciation one recognized that he was a Galitian. [00:17:20] David Boder: Hm. [00:17:21] Benjamin Piskorz: Because the Galitian Jews have such...such a...a [peculiar] pronunciation in...in Jewish. [00:17:26] David Boder: Hm. [00:17:27] Benjamin Piskorz: And the Jews that...that Jew persuaded us. We should come out. We are going to work [he told us]. He was caught at night. He found an excuse that he was caught this night and he had to show where the Jews were hidden. If not, he was going to be shot. But as we knew from before, all these people who talked that way were the real Gestapo work...employees. That Jew promised us that we were going to go to work and nothing would be done to us. When I came out of the cellar I hid the gun that I had and the ammunition in a...in a barrel, in a real barrel with water, thrown in. When I came out, I was immediately taken to the side and my hands were manacled. After that... [00:18:05] David Boder: You were in the SS uniform. [00:18:07] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, because I was in the SS uniform. [00:18:09] David Boder: Nu? [00:18:10] Benjamin Piskorz: Then the Ukrainians built a huge fire of charcoal. They gathered charcoal. They built a huge fire and began asking questions. Where is my family? I didn’t want to disclose that I have family here, [claiming] that the mother is a stranger to me. But my mother spoke up. She thought that I would be...that I would be...that with this she would save me, if she says that I still have a mother they won’t do anything to me. And so the mother was tied with another few people, among [them] also that cousin, and they were burned alive. I was standing before the fire, approximately twelve to fifteen meters away. Afterwards I was...while I was standing my nerves, my whole consciousness became as if entirely lost. What does lost mean? I didn’t know what to do. Around and around have...near me stood SS men and guarded me with their weapons. If I take one step forward I will be immediately shot. Should I throw myself on the fire? I am also a dead one, so I have...the...the...I was so...I grew into the ground, I can say. I couldn’t [take] one step forwards or one step backwards. I remained standing. Afterwards...so when...when I saw that the mother was fainting already in the fire, she does not know already what she is doing, and the last cry from my mother, ‘My child, stay alive. [01:02:36] Benjamin Piskorz: And he freed me, the general. [01:02:38] David Boder: Nu? [01:02:39] Benjamin Piskorz: Because I told him that I am nervous. I told him the whole story at the trial. I showed him the tongue. I showed him the number. I...I presented various facts, that how I can be normal in such a moment when I have only been liberated for five months, that I should again fall in a... [01:02:55] David Boder: Yes. [01:02:55] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . in a jail. And so he judged me right, and he freed me. [01:02:59] David Boder: Hm. [01:02:59] Benjamin Piskorz: And so during the trial six people testified against me, the lager leader, the major, the lager leader, a Greek, the Englishmen [?] who had beaten me, the Englishman, a Negro who was the interpreter... [01:03:11] David Boder: Hm. A Negro an interpreter? [01:03:12] Benjamin Piskorz: A Negro an interpreter. From German into English for that major. [01:03:16] David Boder: Yes. [01:03:16] Benjamin Piskorz: By that lager leader and the...a Ukrai-...two, three Ukrainian policemen... [01:03:21] David Boder: What did they testify? [01:03:22] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . two Ukrainian policemen. That I broke a bed. [01:03:25] David Boder: Hm. [01:03:26] Benjamin Piskorz: That I broke a bed. And for that I beat up an Englishman, and such things. And so I was...he freed me, the general. [01:03:35] David Boder: Hm. [01:03:36] Benjamin Piskorz: The general freed me, and also he asked that I should come to him privately to his house, that he would give a report, a report of everything I went through. He took everything down, and he also photographed me. He attached the photograph to the papers that I had reported. He made a little newspaper article of this... [01:03:55] David Boder: Hm. [01:03:55] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . of everything that I had told him. The same [things] that I am telling now is about what I told him. [01:04:00] David Boder: Nu? [01:04:02] Benjamin Piskorz: And later on I left. I still worked in an English kitchen there. The major later on found me a job in the kitchen. [01:04:11] David Boder: The same major? [01:04:11] Benjamin Piskorz: The same major. We became the best of friends. Afterwards he helped me. And he also fixed me up with a wedding. I got married in Judenburg. [01:04:20] David Boder: To whom? [01:04:21] Benjamin Piskorz: To a woman...to a girl from Poland, from Upper Silesia. [01:04:25] David Boder: Where did you meet her? [01:04:26] Benjamin Piskorz: In Budapest, in Hungary. [01:04:28] David Boder: Not one of the eight girls? [01:04:30] Benjamin Piskorz: No, no, the Rumanian girls remained... [01:04:32] David Boder: Nu? [01:04:32] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . in Rumania. [01:04:33] David Boder: Then your girl right away left with you? [01:04:37] Benjamin Piskorz: The girl...I have known this girl five months before the wedding. [01:04:40] David Boder: Nu? [01:04:41] Benjamin Piskorz: And so we like a girl and a boy we got acquainted. We fell in love. And so it was decided to remain. The fact remains that we got married, and we remained with one another. We left later on. [01:04:56] David Boder: Where to? [01:04:57] Benjamin Piskorz: From Austria to Italy. [01:04:59] David Boder: Wait a moment. Did the girl come afterwards to look for you in...in the lager, or was she with you all the time? [01:05:07] Benjamin Piskorz: The girl was in Budapest in the lager. [01:05:10] David Boder: Oh, nu? [01:05:11] Benjamin Piskorz: And I met this girl, and together we came to the lager in Austria. [01:05:14] David Boder: Yes. Oh, you came together. [01:05:16] Benjamin Piskorz: Came together. [01:05:16] David Boder: When you had that affair with the... [01:05:18] Benjamin Piskorz: Then she was in the lager, and she also brought a change of clothes and food to the prison. [01:05:23] David Boder: Nu, nu, and? [01:05:25] Benjamin Piskorz: And afterwards I came out, and I really saw that she worries about me, that she indeed loves me, and after a certain time we got married. [01:05:35] David Boder: Did you get married there in the lager? [01:05:36] Benjamin Piskorz: In the lager, yes. The major himself arranged the wedding. [01:05:40] David Boder: Hm. [01:05:40] Benjamin Piskorz: A very nice wedding, and we both got married. [01:05:43] David Boder: What does it mean, a nice wedding? [01:05:45] Benjamin Piskorz: Nu. So what does it mean, a wedding? The way things were in the lager there was nothing to eat. [01:05:50] David Boder: Yes? [01:05:50] Benjamin Piskorz: And on my wedding there was enough to eat. [01:05:52] David Boder: Aha. [01:05:52] Benjamin Piskorz: I received cigarettes for the wedding. I received clothing from the UNRRA. [01:05:56] David Boder: Hm. [01:05:57] Benjamin Piskorz: So that the wedding was called a really nice wedding according to conditions after the war. [01:06:01] David Boder: Yes. [01:06:02] Benjamin Piskorz: And for such a boy like me without funds, without anything... [01:06:04] David Boder: Hm. [01:06:05] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . this wedding was a nice wedding. [01:06:06] David Boder: Where are the parents of the girl? [01:06:08] Benjamin Piskorz: The parents of the girl have...have been killed in the lager, in Auschwitz. [01:06:12] David Boder: Oh. She was alone? [01:06:13] Benjamin Piskorz: Alone, yes. [01:06:14] David Boder: Aha. [01:06:14] Benjamin Piskorz: And she is now up in the hospital. We have a little baby. [01:06:17] David Boder: Now? [01:06:17] Benjamin Piskorz: Newly born, yes. [01:06:18] David Boder: How old is the baby [?]? [01:06:19] Benjamin Piskorz: The baby is now five days old. [01:06:20] David Boder: Five days old? A boy or a girl? [01:06:25] Benjamin Piskorz: A girl. [01:06:26] David Boder: Aha. [01:06:27] Benjamin Piskorz: And I have also given her a name after the mother. [01:06:29] David Boder: Aha. What is the name of the baby? [01:06:31] Benjamin Piskorz: Sara. [01:06:32] David Boder: Aha. Nu? [01:06:33] Benjamin Piskorz: And now I am in Italy, and thus I am living here in Italy. [01:06:38] David Boder: How did you come over to Italy? When did you attach yourself to a Kibbutz? [01:06:44] Benjamin Piskorz: To a Kibbutz. All the time while I was in Austria...twelve months I was in a Kibbutz. [01:06:48] David Boder: What was the... [01:06:49] Benjamin Piskorz: Kibbutz Dror Habonim. [01:06:51] David Boder: Oh, that is the... [01:06:52] Benjamin Piskorz: [01:06:54] David Boder: That man who is sitting there at the doorway, did he come together with you? [01:06:58] Benjamin Piskorz: He came with me, but he wasn’t with me... [01:07:01] David Boder: That is Mr... [01:07:03] Benjamin Piskorz: Isaac Wolf. [01:07:05] David Boder: Wolf, yes. [01:07:06] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, Wolf. [01:07:06] David Boder: Isaac came together with you? [01:07:07] Benjamin Piskorz: Together with me, yes. [01:07:08] David Boder: Nu? [01:07:09] Benjamin Piskorz: And Wolf was in another lager. Wolf was in Traffaya [?]. [01:07:13] David Boder: Yes? [01:07:14] Benjamin Piskorz: And I was in Judenburg. It is a hundred [?] eighty-odd kilometers from here [?]? [01:07:18] David Boder: Yes. And when did you get together? Where? [01:07:20] Benjamin Piskorz: We got together in Judenburg. [01:07:23] David Boder: In Judenburg? [01:07:24] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. [01:07:25] David Boder: And... [01:07:25] Benjamin Piskorz: Because the lager there was liquidated for certain reasons. They made investigations. Englishmen came with Austrian police. Raids were carried out. People were stealing there. The Austrians came to search if we didn’t have many English cigarettes or such things, whether people didn’t do business. In the meantime they took away for themselves felt boots, gloves, that we had received from the UNRRA. The Austrian police took away... [01:07:49] David Boder: Hm. [01:07:49] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . for themselves. They said this is forbidden to own. They took it away. And so after a certain time I arrived in Italy. [01:07:57] David Boder: Hm. [01:07:58] Benjamin Piskorz: And thus I am now in Italy and am waiting till I will be able to go to Eretz Israel. [01:08:03] David Boder: Nu? [01:08:03] Benjamin Piskorz: And I have also family in Argentina, in Buenos Aires and Rio de Janeiro. I have received from them a few letters lately. Now for nine weeks I did not receive any letters from them, and I do not know what to...I have a grandmother there... [01:08:13] David Boder: Oh. [01:08:13] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . and brothers and sisters of my father. [01:08:18] David Boder: A grandmother? [01:08:19] Benjamin Piskorz: A grandmother, yes. [01:08:20] David Boder: Nu? [01:08:20] Benjamin Piskorz: And brothers and sisters of my father. [01:08:23] David Boder: Yes? [01:08:23] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, and so I do not know what is... [01:08:25] David Boder: What did you say happened to your father? [01:08:28] Benjamin Piskorz: What? The father was taken away still in the year ’41. [We are] without any word from him. I don’t know what happened to him. [01:08:33] David Boder: He was taken alone. The family... [01:08:35] Benjamin Piskorz: Alone. [01:08:36] David Boder: . . . remained. [01:08:37] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, yes. The whole family was in Argentina. [01:08:39] David Boder: No, I mean your family. The father was taken away... [01:08:42] Benjamin Piskorz: My...my father was taken away. The mother was burned and the cousin... [01:08:46] David Boder: The cousin, yes. [01:08:47] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . and...and another brother. There was another brother of the father, an upholsterer, who worked in Poland, escaped to Russia, and from him I have lately received words that he is alive in Russia. [01:08:56] David Boder: He is alive in Russia. [01:08:57] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. [01:08:57] David Boder: A brother. [01:08:57] Benjamin Piskorz: A brother of my father. [01:08:59] David Boder: Oh. And did the Argentine people [relatives] send you something? [01:09:03] Benjamin Piskorz: They sent me something like...ten pounds they sent me through a bank, but... [01:09:09] David Boder: Ten pounds in money. [01:09:10] Benjamin Piskorz: Ten pounds in money, but through a bank. But here it is very hard even with the ten pounds. [01:09:17] David Boder: Aha. [01:09:17] Benjamin Piskorz: Because we have to buy additionally [to the provisions of the camp]. And now we have a baby. And we don’t received enough aid for the baby, and coming...I came without clothes. I had to buy [?] myself something from the UNRRA. I hardly received anything. The clothes that I had received there on the wedding are torn in the meantime, and they got soiled, because I did not have any other clothes for work, because I arrived with only a handbag, a piece of soap, a toothbrush, toothpaste, things that one needs for the road. So I did not have what to wear. They had torn. When I received the ten pounds I had to buy a suit. [01:09:46] David Boder: Aha. [01:09:47] Benjamin Piskorz: And I had to buy myself a shirt. I had to buy for the wife some clothes. [01:09:51] David Boder: Did you have to exchange it through the bank, the ten pounds? [01:09:53] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, through the bank. [01:09:54] David Boder: How many liras did you receive for it? [01:09:56] Benjamin Piskorz: I received nine thousand liras [the official exchange was very low]. [01:09:58] David Boder: For each pound. [01:09:58] Benjamin Piskorz: No, nine hundred liras for a pound. [01:10:01] David Boder: Nine hundred liras. [01:10:01] Benjamin Piskorz: Nine hundred liras for a pound. [01:10:03] David Boder: Aha. [01:10:04] Benjamin Piskorz: And also it was deducted...three hundred and thirty-odd liras were deducted by the bank for the exchange. [01:10:13] David Boder: Yes. [01:10:13] Benjamin Piskorz: So that I received eight hundred and sixty-odd...six hundred and a few liras. And for this I bought myself...I had to buy a suit, for four thousand liras a suit. I am wearing the suit now. [01:10:24] David Boder: Aha, yes. [01:10:25] Benjamin Piskorz: Because now again I don’t have anything to wear. And I had to buy myself a shirt, because I didn’t have any change. For the wife I had to buy clothes. I didn’t have anything to wear for the wife. Now again I have a baby so that I will again have to. I have no money. And from the uncles I don’t receive any letters for nine weeks. For as long as I am here in... [01:10:43] David Boder: Send it by air mail. Send it... [01:10:49] Benjamin Piskorz: I send. I have already sent away around fifteen letters. Every week I send away three, four letters, two letters, one letter. I cannot send too many. Every letter has to cost me the minimum, a hundred liras, a hundred and eight liras. And how many such ‘hundred and eight liras’ do I have? [01:11:03] David Boder: Aha. Tell me this. The...when your wife will return...She is here in the hospital? [01:11:11] Benjamin Piskorz: In the hospital in Tradate. [01:11:13] David Boder: In Tradate. Do you have a room for yourself? [01:11:16] Benjamin Piskorz: Here I have a room for myself. I have received now a room for myself. [01:11:20] David Boder: Oh. And how were you before? [01:11:22] Benjamin Piskorz: Before we were in Cremona in a lager. [01:11:24] David Boder: With... [01:11:24] Benjamin Piskorz: With seventy people together. [01:11:26] David Boder: What does it mean, with seventy people? Men and women? [01:11:28] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, men and women together in one room, because there was no possibility of living in any other way. Because it was one Kvutzah [?], one Kibbutz, a group that lived collectively. One did not eat without [?] the other. Whatever we could, whatever we got. None of us had any funds. These were all people who trod the same road of the...the...the Fighter Groups of the Warsaw Ghetto, the Socialist workers. [01:11:52] David Boder: Tell me this. Why is not the Kibbutz arranged so that the men and women would not be in the same room[Footnote: I remember seeing in Tradate a room housing more than thirty couples, many couples having one bed for the two, without curtains or any separation from the others. The Menonites in Feldafing lived about in the same manner.]? [01:12:01] Benjamin Piskorz: And so in that lager it was impossible. The...the captain of a lager leader did not take too much interest in it. Lately the lager leader was changed, and he did take interest. [01:12:14] David Boder: Who is the lager leader? [01:12:15] Benjamin Piskorz: I do not know his name. An Englishman. [01:12:18] David Boder: An Englishman. [01:12:19] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. [01:12:20] David Boder: A Jew? [01:12:20] Benjamin Piskorz: No. [01:12:21] David Boder: Nu? [01:12:22] Benjamin Piskorz: And the Englishman lately did take an interest. He procured more rooms there. He changed...he made...there was a synagogue in that lager, so he took over the synagogue. He did not allow having a synagogue there. Instead, in the synagogue husbands and wives... [01:12:37] David Boder: Aha. [01:12:38] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . slept together. And so it was made there...it was not only husbands and wives. There were girls, unmarried ones, and unmarried boys, and also families. For instance, my wife, a pregnant woman was together with a girl who was not even married. [01:12:55] David Boder: A girl? [01:12:56] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. So that the circumstances...the conditions were not such as could be wished for. [01:13:02] David Boder: Yes? [01:13:03] Benjamin Piskorz: And the people...and so after a period of time the comrades who work in Milan organized a Hachshara, which organizes kvuthot of the organized groups. Such Kibbutzim... [00:00:00] David Boder: Yes. [01:13:17] Benjamin Piskorz: They transferred us to Tradate. And now we are here in Tradate. [01:13:22] David Boder: And when do you think you will be in Eretz Yisroeil? [01:13:26] Benjamin Piskorz: This...this is up to the powers that give the certificates. This is up to the [name of a special bureau]. [01:13:32] David Boder: Do not people travel without certificates? [01:13:35] Benjamin Piskorz: People travel without certificates. I don’t know how one goes. This is already... [01:13:40] David Boder: Oh. [01:13:40] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . a different thing. I do not concern myself with it, with such things. I hear it. I do not know if people travel without certificates, but according to rumors [?], when I read the papers, the Austrian, the Swiss newspapers...I read the Italian newspapers, because I have already learned a little Italian during this time. And I have comrades who know Italian well. They translate for me that comrades arrive who were...who went illegally. Otherwise I do not know about it. [He seems a bit secretive] [01:14:03] David Boder: Yes, it is understood. [01:14:05] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. [01:14:06] David Boder: And how are the conditions here? How long have you been here? [01:14:10] Benjamin Piskorz: Here I am already three months. [01:14:12] David Boder: And how many people are there here? [01:14:14] Benjamin Piskorz: Here? I do not know so exactly. This I do not know. [01:14:18] David Boder: Nu, yes, but there are many people here? [01:14:21] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes, there are many people here. [01:14:23] David Boder: Yes. People eat in two, three [shifts]. [01:14:25] Benjamin Piskorz: Now the conditions demand that people have to eat...go to eat two, three times [in shifts], so that sometimes, towards the end [last shift], there is a shortage of food. [01:14:35] David Boder: Not enough food left. [01:14:36] Benjamin Piskorz: Because it is so: With us here in Tradate it is so: It is collective. Collective means this, that everybody comes over to the table and finds his food on the table. [01:14:45] David Boder: Yes? [01:14:46] Benjamin Piskorz: And when he finishes eating, he leaves and makes room for someone else. And occasionally one who has eaten and is still hungry goes to eat again. [01:14:55] David Boder: Oh, oh. That... [01:14:56] Benjamin Piskorz: No. This is...nothing can be done about that, because they are hungry. The aid received is perhaps enough, according to the view that is figured out on the...the minimum prices, but when they go to buy it, it is sometimes more expensive and sometimes this is cheaper. [01:15:12] David Boder: Yes. [01:15:12] Benjamin Piskorz: It is possible that it evens up, but the food is very meager. [01:15:15] David Boder: Is not enough. [01:15:15] Benjamin Piskorz: For a man who has returned from the woods, a partisan, or a man who has returned from a lager, from a concentration camp, who for three, four years was in a camp, starved out, without a little fat, he should have to live now on this it is very little. [01:15:29] David Boder: Yes. [01:15:30] Benjamin Piskorz: It is very meager. [01:15:32] David Boder: So, nu, so what does one do? [01:15:34] Benjamin Piskorz: And what does one do? Whatever one can to get something. If he has some things that he had brought from Germany, he sells them and eats. So again he has nothing. [01:15:43] David Boder: Where does he sell it? [01:15:44] Benjamin Piskorz: He sells. He goes to Milan. There are people who need such things for themselves, so they buy them. [01:15:50] David Boder: Aha. [01:15:50] Benjamin Piskorz: So for such things one has to... [01:15:54] David Boder: Nu, [an unfinished word]... [01:15:54] Benjamin Piskorz: So [words not clear]. [01:15:58] David Boder: When the baby arrived, did you get anything extra for... [01:16:03] Benjamin Piskorz: For the baby I received... [01:16:05] David Boder: Yes? [01:16:05] Benjamin Piskorz: For the baby I received a package, some underwear. [01:16:07] David Boder: From whom? [01:16:08] Benjamin Piskorz: This was given by the Joint. [01:16:10] David Boder: Yes? [01:16:10] Benjamin Piskorz: The Joint gave a package. And to this package I have to buy another such ten. [01:16:14] David Boder: Why? [01:16:15] Benjamin Piskorz: Because a child uses up. And such things, for instance, diapers for the child to change, one need things to change. One cannot change a child with the same diapers. And secondly, [words not clear]. I do not get help so that I should be able to buy for money. I do not have... [01:16:31] David Boder: From Argentina you did not get anything? [01:16:33] Benjamin Piskorz: I received the ten pounds. It is very little. The uncles...it is very little, what I received. During all the time that I am in Italy, five months, I received ten pounds. And what is nine thousand liras? How can one live on it? [01:16:46] David Boder: Hm. [01:16:47] Benjamin Piskorz: When we lived in a lager [for DPs] we had to buy additional food. So the major portion that was spent was spent for food. Not for clothes, but for food it went in the lager. Here maybe it is [more] stable. A person gets used [adjusted]. He straightens himself out. He does not go two, three times [to eat the same meal]. These are single cases, that one does go twice to eat [eats in more than one shift so that others get nothing]. You understand? Singe, single cases. A man who has not...does not know about that. He does not realize that it is somebody else’s food. [01:17:12] David Boder: Now... [01:17:13] Benjamin Piskorz: A man who is... [01:17:15] David Boder: I do not understand too well the counting in dekas. Last night I ate here, too. [01:17:26] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes? [01:17:27] David Boder: How many dekas of bread was it? [01:17:30] Benjamin Piskorz: How much bread do we receive daily? [01:17:34] David Boder: It was in the evening. [01:17:37] Benjamin Piskorz: In the evening, a bun. [01:17:39] David Boder: How much do you... [01:17:40] Benjamin Piskorz: Eight dekas. [01:17:41] David Boder: I think... [01:17:42] Benjamin Piskorz: Eight dekas. [00:00:00] David Boder: It weighed eight dekas? [00:00:00] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. [01:17:42] David Boder: And now many dekas of bread do you receive daily? [01:17:45] Benjamin Piskorz: Half a kilo. [01:17:46] David Boder: Oh. That is how much? Fifty dekas? [01:17:49] Benjamin Piskorz: Fifty dekas. [01:17:50] David Boder: And when does one receive the other two dekas [42 dekas]? [01:17:53] Benjamin Piskorz: It is this way. The...the...we get it this way. In the morning we get a bun. [01:17:59] David Boder: Hm. [00:00:00] Benjamin Piskorz: A bun. Such a bun can weigh...it depends how the bun is baked. [00:00:00] David Boder: Hm. [00:00:00] Benjamin Piskorz: There are about six buns to a kilo... [00:00:00] David Boder: Hm. [00:00:00] Benjamin Piskorz: . . . to a kilo. [00:00:00] David Boder: Yes. [00:00:00] Benjamin Piskorz: Sometimes we get three buns and sometimes four buns. It depends. [01:18:12] David Boder: Oh, per day? [01:18:14] Benjamin Piskorz: Per day. [01:18:15] David Boder: Per day. [01:18:15] Benjamin Piskorz: Yes. Such a bun for a meal is very little, so that one cannot be... [01:18:19] David Boder: Yes. I did not want to eat it. It does not taste good. [01:18:24] Benjamin Piskorz: No. [01:18:25] David Boder: When I was in Switzerland I saw that they got more, although not in all places. In some places...And those who eat Kosher, do they have more or what? [01:18:37] Benjamin Piskorz: Those who eat Kosher? [01:18:39] David Boder: Yes. [01:18:39] Benjamin Piskorz: I do not know. I did not meet any people yet who eat Kosher. [01:18:43] David Boder: Here.... . . is there a separate Kosher group here? [01:18:46] Benjamin Piskorz: I don’t know. I do not pay attention to it. First, I am already so that what I am given I eat and I am satisfied, because to get something special is impossible. Because on someone else’s money and on someone else’s means I cannot live on [a few words not clear]. [01:19:05] David Boder: Alright. This concludes Spool...this concludes Spool 103, the second spool of Benjamin Piskorz with the story of the Warsaw Ghetto and the story of liberation. He has no...[ends abruptly]

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews David Lea
entries.content:
[00:00:03]
David Boder: Paris, ah, August 12, 1946 at the headquarters of the American Joint Distribution Committee. The interviewee is David Lea with tattoo number 120930 of Auschwitz.

[00:00:21]
David Boder: Äh...Also Herr Lea, wollen Sie mir sagen, wo sind sie geboren?

[00:00:26]
David Lea: In Saloniki.

[00:00:27]
David Boder: Sie sind geboren in?

[00:00:29]
David Lea: In Saloniki.

[00:00:29]
David Boder: In Saloniki.

[00:00:30]
David Lea: Griechenland [Unterbricht]

[00:00:31]
David Boder: In Griechenland. Und, äh, was für ein Staatsangehöriger sind sie? I mean, äh, von welchem Lande sind sie ein Staatsangehöriger? Äh, ich meine, äh, sind sie ein Grieche oder sind sie ein Spanier, oder was sind sie?

[00:00:49]
David Lea: Grieche.

[00:00:50]
David Boder: Sie sind Grieche, all right. Und sie sind in Saloniki geboren?

[00:00:54]
David Lea: Jawohl.

[00:00:54]
David Boder: Nun erzählen sie mich, äh, was hat dort passiert, wenn der Krieg angefangen hat?

[00:01:01]

[00:36:13]

En el 44, a la fin del 44, en noviembre, en el campo de Birkenau, en septiembre, octubre o noviembre, 600.000 hungareses judíos vinieron en Birkenau. Después que los crematorios no daban abasto para quemar a los judíos, los SS ordenaron 3000 hombres que hagan unos pozos.

[00:36:50]
David Boder: ¿Cómo dijo?

[00:36:52]
David Lea: Pozos, pozos. [El entrevistado dice algo en otro idioma para hacerse entender].

[00:36:55]
David Boder: Ah...agujas...

[00:37:02]
David Lea: Sí. Agujas.

[00:37:03]
David Boder: Agujeros

[00:37:03]
David Lea: Sí. Y quemaron en 27 días 600.000 judíos vivos. Los vimos nosotros, nosotros porque yo laboraba [ininteligible] comando al crematorio, y los vía por del frente, los quemaron vivos con leña y bencina. Los transportes que venían, había veces

[00:37:24]
David Boder: Los quemaban en agujeros, no en los...

[00:37:26]
David Lea: No los quemaron...No los quemaron en los hornos porque no tenían tiempo.

[00:37:31]
David Boder: Sí. No los pasaron en el chambre...cámara de gas

[00:37:36]
David Lea: No. No los pasaron en la cámara de gas porque no tenían tiempo los alemanes.

[00:37:41]
David Boder: ¿Entonces qué?

[00:37:41]
David Lea: Los quemaron en los...en los pozos que hicimos nosotros, con leña y con essence

[00:37:47]
David Boder: ¿Con qué?

[00:37:48]
David Lea: Con essence, bencina.

[00:37:50]
David Boder: Bencina.

[00:37:50]
David Lea: Bencina.

[00:37:51]
David Boder: Bueno. ¿Les mataron anteriormente o qué?

[00:37:52]
David Lea: Los quemaron vivos. No los mataron, los quemaron vivos.

[00:37:56]
David Boder: ¿Los quemaron vivos?

[00:37:57]
David Lea: Vivos. Seiscientos mil hungareses judíos, al noviembre o al septiembre. No me acuerdo exactamente la data y el día, mas me acuerdo que yo vide esto [ininteligible]

[00:38:06]
David Boder: ¿Cómo?

[00:38:09]
David Lea: lo vi esto como si la [ininteligible] fuera mía.

[00:38:12]
David Boder: Bueno.

[00:38:13]
David Lea: Los transportes que venían ahí estaban guardados por miles de SS y en todo el convoy había como 20 a 25 o 50 [ininteligible]. Y en el último que vi había una Jeep alemana, decían que era la Croix Rouge. Y los judíos, cuando les...los metían al convoy, les decían que los iban a ir al hospital y los judíos lo creían porque veían que estaban acompañados por el [ininteligible]

[00:38:36]
David Boder: ¿El [ininteligible] tenía qué? ¿Una cruz roja?

[00:38:42]
David Lea: El [ininteligible] tenía la Croix Rouge y tenía...

[00:38:46]
David Boder: ¿Qué es “Croix Rouge”?

[00:38:47]
David Lea: La Cruz Roja

[00:38:47]
David Boder: ¿La Cruz Roja?

[00:38:49]
David Lea: Sí. Tenía en la [ininteligible], tenía una bandera blanca con la Cruz Roja y decía que lo vamos a llevar al hospital a mirar, y lo vamos a llevar [ininteligible]. Después, allí...adentro de allí abría los gases.

[00:39:06]
David Boder: Ajá.

[00:39:06]
David Lea: Mas [ininteligible] sabía de eso, el transporte [ininteligible]. Mesmo nosotros mismos [ininteligible]. Mas después de un mes, dos meses, tres meses que laboré al crematorio, ya supimos que contiene. El gas lo traen con la Cruz Roja. Con el [ininteligible], con la coche de la Cruz Roja.

[00:39:26]
David Boder: De la Cruz Roja. Sí.

[00:39:27]
David Lea: De la Cruz Roja. Esto como estoy explicando...yo lo estoy explicando que [ininteligible] si no lo puedo explicar, caros hermanos [ininteligible] y no vas a poder sentir. Es la más desgracia, la más grande que hubo en el crematorio. [ininteligible] nuestros hermanos. Seis millones de judíos murieron en los campos, cuales maltratados, cuales de hambre, cuales [ininteligible] para pasar a la chambre a gas, fillos y padres. No podían más resistir la sufriencia y la hambrera y el piojo, ni el trabajo y se iban voluntarios a la chambre a gas.

[00:40:09]
David Boder: Bueno, dígame...eh...¿qué es que dijo usted de los...?

[00:40:15]
David Lea: ¿De la esterilización?

[00:40:18]
David Boder: Bueno, sí.

[00:40:21]
David Lea: En el campo de Auschwitz, que es la misma dirección que el campo de Birkenau, es unos veinte minutos a pie, esterilizaban a las mujeres de 18 años y hasta 27 años. Las esterilizaban en el Bloco 10 de Auschwitz. En Berkinau, esterilizaban de 22 años fita 30 años a los jóvenes, en el Bloco...

[00:40:48]
David Boder: ¿A los hombres?

[00:40:49]
David Lea: Hombres, hombres.

[00:40:50]
David Boder: ¿Cómo los esterilizaban?

[00:40:51]
David Lea: Los llevaban allí y con inyecciones, los esterilizaban. Con inyecciones los esterilizaban. Al Bloco 26. Esto paso al Juin, al 4, 7, 8 de Juin.

[00:41:09]
David Boder: ¿Qué mes?

[00:41:10]
David Lea: Juin

[00:41:11]
David Boder: Mes de junio

[00:41:14]
David Lea: Junio. Sí. De 1943. Después que hacían esto, que esterilizaban a mujeres y hombres, se echaban los SS, había unas chambres especialitas para los hombres, los jóvenes y las mujeres en edad, se echaban ahí juntos...si querían tener los doctores de las SS...si podían prevenir a realizar otra raza. Y la más parte, no parirían. La más parte, el 95% no parirían.

[00:41:48]
David Boder: Bueno. Los otros...que...¿se pusieron embarazadas? ¿o cómo? Eh...¿Qué quiere decir 95% no podían...eh no...?

[00:42:00]
David Lea: Los 95% no volvían, a poder, a quitar los espermas.

[00:42:04]
David Boder: Oh. No podían volver a tener acto sexual.

[00:42:07]
David Lea: No podían tener el acto sexual.

[00:42:09]
David Boder: Bueno. Entonces, metieron juntos los hombres con las mujeres.

[00:42:14]
David Lea: Juntos con las mujeres y no podían hacer nada. Mas a notar que les daban buena comida a estos hombres para ver si podían hacer cosas, mas normalmente mesmo que les dieran toda la comida del mundo era imposible de arribar porque estaban bien esterilizados.

[00:42:29]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:42:30]
David Lea: Y cada día, en el campo de Birkenau había una selección de hombres, de 2000 a 3000 hombres quemaban cada noche, deportados que estaban en el campo [ininteligible] tres meses o cinco meses o un año. Como [ininteligible] judíos, como judíos sefaradí, como judíos lituanos, como hungareses y los llevaban al crematorio.

[00:42:55]
David Boder: Dígame otra vez el caso cuando pidieron permiso...permiso de rezar sobre los muertos.

[00:43:08]
David Lea: ¿Sobre?

[00:43:10]
David Boder: Que dijo usted que los que quemaron a los muertos pidieron permiso que podían rezar, que podían...eh...Dijo usted anteriormente que no les permitían de decir sus...

[00:43:24]
David Lea: Ah, sí. Me topé en Landberg, al 45 en Baviera. Trabajaba en un comando de quince hombres judíos y yo, dieciséis.

[00:43:41]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:43:41]
David Lea: Un día, de los comandos que trabajaba, murió la hermana en el campo de concentración número 7. Naturalmente, nosotros como judíos, llamemos un joven que tenía un amigo, un compañero, para [ininteligible] a excavar.

[00:43:58]
David Boder: .

[00:44:02]
David Lea: . Y entonces, cuando hicimos la excavación, el SS viene y nos dice “¿qué están haciendo sucios judíos con un libro?”. Le dice el hombre...

[00:44:15]
David Boder: Ah, ¿tenían un libro?

[00:44:16]
David Lea: Sí. Teníamos un libro...los hungareses y los poloneses judíos...cuando los hungareses al 44 que los deportaron, traían libros [ininteligible] y [ininteligible]. Y nosotros guardábamos en la tierra, en los pantalones, guardábamos los libros de la ley para [ininteligible].

[00:44:35]
David Boder: Para rezar.

[00:44:37]
David Lea: Para rezar. Cuando le ve, dice...di...dice “¿qué es ese sucio libro que tienes judío?”, pero me dice a mí...

[00:44:44]
David Boder: Hable más despacio.

[00:44:45]
David Lea: “¿Qué es ese sucio libro que tienes?”. Mi compañero se alzó y le dijo que “es mi hermana y quería rezar”. Y dice “para los sucios no necesita [ininteligible]”. Tomó la pala, levantó la pala y le dio en la cabeza y el hombre, al momento murió. Y nosotros lo enterramos con la hermana, con 400 más en una fora. En cada fora que hacíamos, 300, 350, 400, 450. Después de dos metros y cuarenta centímetros de hondura, echábamos la tierra y antes de cubrirlos echábamos [ininteligible] o cal para que no diera [ininteligible]

[00:45:29]
David Boder: ¿Para que no diera qué?

[00:45:30]
David Lea: [00:45:31]
David Boder: Ah.

[00:45:32]
David Lea: Y entonces, echábamos piedra y tierra, y enterrábamos la fosa y nos íbamos. Al otro día, hacíamos el mismo trabajo, porque era un campo de cuarentena. Era un campo para matar con las inyecciones a los judíos. Las inyecciones que echábamos, mesmo en el brazo, mesmo en el pie, después de tres a cuatro minutos, la sangre le subía a [ininteligible]

[00:45:59]
David Boder: ¿A dónde?

[00:46:00]
David Lea: Cuando echaba la inyección, la sangre le subía [ininteligible], ya estaba preto

[00:46:04]
David Boder: ¿Quiénes echaban las inyecciones? ¿Ustedes?

[00:46:07]
David Lea: No. Los SS.

[00:46:08]
David Boder: Los SS.

[00:46:09]
David Lea: Y en muchos campos, los SS daban orden a los judíos que echaran inyecciones, pero los judíos obligatoriamente lo hacían porque si no lo hacían, el SS estaba con la metralleta y ya estaba detrás de él y “si no haces esto te mato”.

[00:46:23]
David Boder: ¿Y?

[00:46:24]
David Lea: Y claro, el judío que era venir, le echaban la inyección.

[00:46:30]
David Boder: Pero dígame. ¿De dónde la sangre aparecía?

[00:46:33]
David Lea: En la [ininteligible]

[00:46:34]
David Boder: Aquí en el...

[00:46:35]
David Lea: Y preto y aquí.

[00:46:37]
David Boder: ¿Parecía salir?

[00:46:39]
David Lea: No. Se veía todo preto, el meollo de la [ininteligible] se hacía preta con dos puntos, tres puntos y ya...al momento se morían. Mas después de dos a tres puntos,...

[00:46:52]
David Boder: ¿Quiénes hacían los tres puntos?

[00:46:54]
David Lea: Tres minutos

[00:46:56]
David Boder: ¿Tres minutos?

[00:46:57]
David Lea: De dos a tres minutos, después se hacía todo preto. El [ininteligible] preto. Y nosotros los tomábamos y los echábamos en una [ininteligible] y los enterrábamos. Después, en el campo 1 en Landberg, había el grande SS medical. El nombre era Blanca, tenía nombre español, un alto, moreno. Era como yo de grande.

[00:47:27]
David Boder: ¿Una mujer?

[00:47:28]
David Lea: No. Un hombre. Se llamaba Blanca. Un alto moreno, alrededor de 35 a 34 años. Este no podía ver a los judíos, mesmo a los judíos querían trabajar, que estaban en buena salud, unos cuantos, él ordenaba echarles inyecciones. Este fue matado, este mismo, tenía una criatura y una mujer. Fue...se mató

[00:47:59]
David Boder: ¿Cómo una criatura?

[00:48:00]
David Lea: Un pequeño.

[00:48:02]
David Boder: Ajá. ¿Un niño?

[00:48:03]
David Lea: Un niño. Un pequeño. Tenía un pequeño y una mujer con él.

[00:48:07]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:48:07]
David Lea: Cuando los americanos se estaban acercando del Lager 1, él ya vio que se estaban acercando, no tenía más para hacer, nada para salvar...tomó al pequeño, lo mandó a la [ininteligible], tomó una inyección, mató [ininteligible] a la mujer suya en primero, después [ininteligible] y él. Y un compañero mío que se topa actualmente en París le quitó la hora y el anillo de la mano y...cuando vio que 2ya estaba muerto, le quitó el anillo y la hora de la mano.

[00:48:44]
David Boder: ¿Cómo se llama la hora? ¿El reloj?

[00:48:46]
David Lea: El reloj. La hora y el anillo. Este camarado se topa actualmente en París y nos vemos cada día y cada noche.

[00:48:56]
David Boder: Bueno

[00:48:57]
David Lea: Quería...

[00:48:58]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:49:00]
David Lea: En el campo 5, en el campo 5, después de la ocupación,

[00:49:10]
David Boder: ¿El campo 5 de qué?

[00:49:10]
David Lea: El campo 5 de Landsberg, Baviera, después de la ocupación, estábamos trabajando en unos comandos muy duros de árboles, para cortar árboles, para [ininteligible] nosotros, no podíamos hacer trabajo porque no teníamos comida y diríamos “si quieres que trabajemos, danos comida”, sino no [ininteligible] necesidad. No podemos trabajar 14 horas en el día, matándonos es mejor. Los SS no nos querían matar.

[00:49:38]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:49:39]
David Lea: No nos querían matar. Los vamos a hacer penar, los vamos a maltratar de leña y después los vamos a matar cuando nos place y nos gusta a nosotros. Esto aconteció en el Lager de Landsberg. En el Lager 5, en el Lager 6, en el Lager 7, en el Lager 8, en el Lager 9, en el Lager 10 y en el Lager 11. Laborábamos a la estación [ininteligible], ese era el comando

[00:50:09]
David Boder: ¿[Ininteligible]? [El entrevistador confirma el nombre del comando en alemán]

[00:50:13]
David Lea: . Yo laboraba al Lager 7 al Tot comando. El nombre mío...

[00:50:22]
David Boder: ¿Tot comando?

[00:50:23]
David Lea: Tot comando, sí.

[00:50:23]
David Boder: That was bad. ¿Qué era esto?

[00:50:26]
David Lea: Tot comando era un comando especialista para enterrar los muertos, porque en Alemania era prohibido de hacer crematorios y de quemar a los muertos, porque la más parte de la población civil alemana ignoraba que había crematorios y fornos. Muchas veces veníamos de...nos encontrábamos con civiles alemanes y les explicábamos. Y los civiles decían: “esa barbaridad, el pueblo alemán no la hace nunca”. Pero nosotros, les dijimos: que un día, nosotros ya sabemos que [ininteligible] los alemanes, mas va a saber la historia, o [ininteligible], o mesmo [ininteligible], que existió crematorios en Alemania”.

[00:51:07]
David Lea: El más lungo y cruel crematorio fue en el campo de Buchenwald, el cual tengo un compañero que dormimos todos juntos en el [ininteligible] en la Maison de la Rue [ininteligible]. 9 Rue [ininteligible], París. Somos 4 de ellos, 4 judíos. Los tres son del campo de Buchenwald, el uno es del campo de Dachau [ininteligible]. Uno se llama [ininteligible], el otro se llama Henry Suchami, actualmente labora en la American [ininteligible]. Henry Suchami es el primer transporte sefardí de Grecia en Auschwitz. 109957, el número [ininteligible] 109957 primo transporte de Grecia, el cual perdió padre, madre, familia, tres criaturas de cinco años, de siete años y de once años, y mujer. Y la mujer, preñada.

[00:52:15]
David Lea: , un joven de alrededor de 35 años, perdió una criatura y su mujer. Y está escrito a la migración palestiniana y no hay posibilidad de partir, no hay inda posibilidad de partir. El [ininteligible] palestiniano de París, que se topa en la calle 83 Avenue [ininteligible], le dice “mañana, después de mañana, de aquí a cinco meses, de aquí a un mes, de aquí a tres meses, te vas a ir”. Este joven tiene parientes en Palestina, mas como es flaco, no puede irse ilegal, se espanta, se está quedando conmigo...

[00:52:56]
David Boder: Es que es flaco...

[00:52:58]
David Lea: Del campo [ininteligible]. Como está [ininteligible] el campo, [ininteligible] ni trabajar puede, ni nada. Naturalmente, es que espera de mí, un compañero que estuvimos al campo tres años, un bocado de pan o una calza que le va a dar una [ininteligible] para él se meter. Si no le da una calza, un calzado, no tiene para meter, que...y no puede trabajar. Tiene flaco, tiene [ininteligible] los pulmones. No es sólo este caso de los déportés, hay muchos déportés aquí en Francia, el cual...

[00:53:29]
David Boder: Por supuesto.

[00:53:30]
David Lea: Hay muchos déportés aquí en Francia, que estamos sufriendo ainda. Mesmo que nos queremos ir en Palestina y estamos viendo la barbarie del inglés, que si nosotros...la juventud que salimos de los campos, si nos vamos en Palestina, nunca empezaríamos a trabajar. Yo, lebanés que le estoy hablando, no pensaría nunca a trabajar en Palestina, pensaría en tomar el fusil o la metralleta y demandar la libertad. Si no la toma la libertad con la guerra...si no tengo la libertad con la política, la va a tomar con la guerra. Nunca pensaría a trabajar. Si me muero en Palestina, algún día mis hijos o mis hermanos van a venir. Porque ya vi el campo cuando estuve tres años, ya vi la exterminación de 6000 judíos y no me gustaría nunca esta política inglesa. Nosotros, los rescatés de los campos, queremos ir presto a batirnos contra esos...sucia raz...sucia política inglesa y no tenemos la posibilidad por esto de donde estamos. Que nos topamos en Fra...actualmente en Francia muchos jóvenes judíos y que están migrando ilegal.

[00:54:41]
David Boder: Emigrando a Francia

[00:54:44]
David Lea: No. Está emigrando a la Palestina.

[00:54:46]
David Boder: Sí.

[00:54:46]
David Lea: Y un día la Palestina...un día, la Palestina la tomaremos y mesmo si se morirían 50.000 judíos en Palestina en combate o 100.000 judíos. No es lo importante.

[00:54:58]
David Boder: This ends Spool 42 of Mr. David Lea.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Hadassah Marcus
entries.content:
[00:00:02]
David Boder: France. September the 13th, 1946, at Henonville, fifty kilometers from Paris, in a home for displaced Jews which consists of a large Kibbutz and also of a Lithuanian Yeshiva which is here temporarily. And the person to be interviewed is Mrs. Hadassah Marcus, tattoo number 48543 and a triangle.

[00:00:40]
David Boder: And so, Mrs. Marcus, tell us again your name and where you are from.

[00:00:44]
Hadassah Marcus: My name is Hadassah Marcus, born in Warsaw and all my years [I] have spent in Warsaw.

[00:00:51]
David Boder: Now, Mrs. Marcus, how old are you now?

[00:00:54]
Hadassah Marcus: I am thirty-two years old.

[00:00:57]
David Boder: Thirty-two years.

[00:00:58]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:00:58]
David Boder: Do you have a family?

[00:01:00]
Hadassah Marcus: I have no family.

[00:01:02]
David Boder: Your husband is not with you?

[00:01:03]
Hadassah Marcus: My husband isn’t with me for a long time.

[00:01:06]
David Boder: And you are alone here in the Kibbutz?

[00:01:07]
Hadassah Marcus: I [am] alone in the Kibbutz.

[00:01:09]
David Boder: And so. Nu, Mrs. Marcus, would you tell me where you were and what happened to you when the war began?

[00:01:18]
Hadassah Marcus: The war started by us in the first minute [at first] in the year 1939.

[00:01:24]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:01:24]
Hadassah Marcus: I was at that time with five small children and with my husband, and with a very large family. Our family consisted of over five hundred persons.

[00:01:34]
David Boder: How is that?

[00:01:35]
Hadassah Marcus: My children still had six grandfathers and six grandmothers.

[00:01:38]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:01:39]
Hadassah Marcus: All alive.

[00:01:40]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:01:41]
Hadassah Marcus: There was little mortality with us.

[00:01:43]
David Boder: How can children have six grandfathers?

[00:01:45]
Hadassah Marcus: Four great grandmothers and four great grandfathers.

[00:01:49]
David Boder: Oh, Nu?

[00:01:51]
Hadassah Marcus: From both sides they were sll still alive.

[00:01:53]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:01:55]
Hadassah Marcus: 1942 when the edict came out [the doom was proclaimed] on the 22nd [of] the seventh month.

[00:02:02]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:02:03]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . a great panic gripped Warsaw.

[00:02:06]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:02:07]
Hadassah Marcus: And people began to look for places in industrial plants. By us they were called ‘shops’ [from the German Shuppen].

[00:02:13]
David Boder: In ’42? That late?

[00:02:15]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. Yes.

[00:02:16]
David Boder: Did you live in the Ghetto already before?

[00:02:18]
Hadassah Marcus: Before, in the Ghetto.

[00:02:19]
David Boder: And so let us begin this way. What happened when the Germans entered Warsaw? What happened then?

[00:02:23]
Hadassah Marcus: When the Germans entered there was a great panic. Right away we began to feel his strong hand. Right away he began strongly to exterminate us. And right away he began...at first with the great Jewith savants, and with our clergymen as well as with other men of learning. Right away he...all of our...the whole intelligentsia he took away from us. And later, when we had already lost the whole intelligentsia and all those who could show us a way [lead us], they started on us, the average people.

[00:03:01]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:02]
Hadassah Marcus: They began to take people into lagers. In the beginning we had words [regards] from the people.

[00:03:08]
David Boder: And so when did they take you into the Ghetto?

[00:03:10]
Hadassah Marcus: Into the Ghetto they took us in the year 1941.

[00:03:14]
David Boder: Yes? And you went into the Ghetto with the others?

[00:03:17]
Hadassah Marcus: Into the Ghetto with everything [everybody].

[00:03:18]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:19]
Hadassah Marcus: Because we were living in the region which was to become the Ghetto.

[00:03:23]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:24]
Hadassah Marcus: So we just remained there. People who...if they were living outside the Ghetto were greatly broken up.

[00:03:32]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:32]
Hadassah Marcus: They weren’t able by any means to find living quarters.

[00:03:35]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:35]
Hadassah Marcus: Because during all the time...during the entire war [the Jews of] the entire district of Poland...

[00:03:40]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:03:40]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . were pushed into Warsaw.

[00:03:42]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:42]
Hadassah Marcus: So that it was very crowded...

[00:03:44]
David Boder: Christians as well, or just Jews?

[00:03:45]
Hadassah Marcus: Only Jews.

[00:03:46]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:03:47]
Hadassah Marcus: Christians he left in peace entirely. He gave them all the rights that they demanded in order that the gentiles should be able to help, entirely in the open, with all the perpetrations that he wanted.

[00:04:00]
David Boder: The German?

[00:04:01]
Hadassah Marcus: The German.

[00:04:01]
David Boder: Nu? And so you were living in the Ghetto. On what street in Warsaw did you live?

[00:04:05]
Hadassah Marcus: On Nowolipki 66.

[00:04:06]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:04:06]
Hadassah Marcus: There I lived.

[00:04:07]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:04:08]
Hadassah Marcus: Everyone of us took in many of his relatives. We shared with everything, with what we were able to. But in the year 1942 on the 22nd of the seventh month, when the edict came out that the Jews should be resetlled, we didn’t know what he wants [us] to do. He hung out placards that we are being sent to Lublin. And everyone of us can take along fifteen kilos. The finest people, the strongest, the...the entire youth took along baggage and went there, but alas, we had no more word from them.

[00:04:44]
David Boder: Hm. That was still before the Ghetto was annihilated?

[00:04:47]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes, that was all still before.

[00:04:48]
David Boder: They hung placards that you should come to Lublin.

[00:04:50]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes, yes.

[00:04:51]
David Boder: Tell me, what was the occupation of your family in Warsaw?

[00:04:54]
Hadassah Marcus: We were diamond dealers.

[00:04:57]
David Boder: Oh. Where did you buy the diamonds? Where did you sell them?

[00:05:01]
Hadassah Marcus: One from another.

[00:05:02]
David Boder: Hm. In...in peace time you...

[00:05:04]
Hadassah Marcus: In peace time and during the war.

[00:05:06]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:05:06]
Hadassah Marcus: Because this had been for generations...dealers in silver and gold [and] diamonds.

[00:05:09]
David Boder: Do you understand diamonds?

[00:05:11]
Hadassah Marcus: I? No. I, myself, no.

[00:05:13]
David Boder: Nu. And so? What did you do with the merchandise that you had?

[00:05:19]
Hadassah Marcus: Nu, that...when the war started I had four factories of my own, and when the Germans entered.

[00:05:26]
David Boder: Factories?

[00:05:26]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:05:26]
David Boder: What sort of factories did you have?

[00:05:27]
Hadassah Marcus: Chemical. We manufactured argentum nitricum [silver nitrate].

[00:05:31]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:05:31]
Hadassah Marcus: That is needed for photographic [work], for lithography [words not clear].

[00:05:34]
David Boder: So you had another occupation besides diamonds.

[00:05:36]
Hadassah Marcus: Everything.

[00:05:37]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:05:37]
Hadassah Marcus: There was everything. I was a great enterprising power.

[00:05:41]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:05:42]
Hadassah Marcus: My husband was a...a...a...he had everything under his hand.

[00:05:47]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:05:48]
Hadassah Marcus: And the basic thing...our occupation was gold, silver, and diamonds. This was so from generation to generation.

[00:05:54]
David Boder: Hm. Yes? So what do you say was done, you did with your merchandise, with all that you had?

[00:06:01]
Hadassah Marcus: My merchandise...when there had come out the edicts that we should be resettled...

[00:06:08]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:06:08]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . we hid it.

[00:06:10]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:11]
Hadassah Marcus: But after a few months...someone had informed on us.

[00:06:14]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:15]
Hadassah Marcus: Because even then we were doing business. And they took my husband away. He sat [was imprisoned] for three months.

[00:06:20]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:20]
Hadassah Marcus: I was left alone then with the five children.

[00:06:23]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:06:24]
Hadassah Marcus: He was murderously beaten. One day he received seventy five strokes.

[00:06:28]
David Boder: Who?

[00:06:29]
Hadassah Marcus: The husband.

[00:06:30]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:06:30]
Hadassah Marcus: Only because they knew that he can hold out and that he has money.

[00:06:36]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:36]
Hadassah Marcus: He was merderously tortured, but [words not clear]...

[00:06:39]
David Boder: What did they want?

[00:06:40]
Hadassah Marcus: They didn’t want anything. They just tortured him.

[00:06:42]
David Boder: Yes, did they ask anything?

[00:06:44]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:06:44]
David Boder: Did they demand anything?

[00:06:48]
Hadassah Marcus: They demanded that we should give out to them the wealthy Jew [Jewish N’giddim] who were still around.

[00:06:54]
David Boder: What does N’giddim mean?

[00:06:55]
Hadassah Marcus: Where there are still the very wealthy...

[00:06:57]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:58]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . those who have money.

[00:06:58]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:06:58]
Hadassah Marcus: When he will betray them, then they will set him free.

[00:07:00]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:07:02]
Hadassah Marcus: But one was acting like one ought to act. And we succeeded in getting him out after three months of imprisonment.

[00:07:08]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:07:09]
Hadassah Marcus: We thought then that it was a piece of luck. But a few months later there began to erupt in the Ghetto strong blockades, as we called them.

[00:07:21]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:07:21]
Hadassah Marcus: Every day they took away ten...over ten thousand persons from Warsaw. They were sent away.

[00:07:27]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:07:29]
Hadassah Marcus: Where were they sent? That varied. From no one did we receive word any more. I lost my husband [in] the year [one] thousand nine hundred [forty] three...in the year ’42 in the eight month.

[00:07:44]
David Boder: Hm. In August.

[00:07:45]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:07:46]
David Boder: What does it mean?

[00:07:46]
Hadassah Marcus: Then I remained alone with all the children.

[00:07:49]
David Boder: What does it mean? Was he arrested, or was he...

[00:07:51]
Hadassah Marcus: He went out accidentally.

[00:07:53]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:07:55]
Hadassah Marcus: And there was going on a very strong blockade [raid].

[00:07:57]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:07:57]
Hadassah Marcus: All people were taken away.

[00:07:59]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:08:00]
Hadassah Marcus: At that time they took away the entire ‘shop’. At that time he was going to a ‘shop’.

[00:08:03]
David Boder: What? Oh. A german ‘shop’?

[00:08:04]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:08:05]
David Boder: He was working there?

[00:08:06]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:08:07]
Hadassah Marcus: And he was taken away, the entire ‘shop’, everybody. The entire ‘shop’ was liquidated at that time.

[00:08:11]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:08:13]
Hadassah Marcus: And I did not have any more...I was left with all the children alone...

[00:08:18]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:08:19]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . in very hard circumstances, because ten times a day such blockades were going on.

[00:08:28]
David Boder: Hm. During the blockades they did what?

[00:08:30]
Hadassah Marcus: During the blockades they shot, searched, and exterminated, in all the cellars, in all the offices.

[00:08:38]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:08:38]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . in all the places where one might be able...where it just looked that one might be hidden.

[00:08:45]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:08:45]
Hadassah Marcus: And he who was found was either shot on the spot, because he had hidden himself, or he was taken to the distribution depot and [from] there sent away to Treblinka. At that time Warsaw was going mostly to Treblinka.

[00:08:58]
David Boder: Treblinka is what, where? Near Katowice? Near Sosnowice?

[00:09:02]
Hadassah Marcus: No.

[00:09:03]
David Boder: Where is Treblinka?

[00:09:04]
Hadassah Marcus: Treblinka is not far from Warsaw. I don’t...

[00:09:06]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:09:06]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . know exactly.

[00:09:07]
David Boder: Yes, yes.

[00:09:08]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . where.

[00:09:08]
David Boder: Hm. Nu, go on.

[00:09:10]
Hadassah Marcus: During all that time all the transports went to Treblinka.

[00:09:14]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:09:15]
Hadassah Marcus: In the year 1943, the 18th, the first [month]...

[00:09:19]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:09:20]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . there was a great holocaust. They took all the shops away. Everything [was] liquidated.

[00:09:25]
David Boder: What does it mean, a holocaust?

[00:09:27]
Hadassah Marcus: That there was...nobody could save himself...

[00:09:30]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:09:31]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . but one shop. It was then on the Nowolipie Street. Shultz’s

[00:09:36]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:09:37]
Hadassah Marcus: That shop was left unharmed at that time. And the entire Ghetto was emptied out. And at that time, in my absence, on the 18th, first [month], they took all my children away.

[00:09:48]
David Boder: Just took them away?

[00:09:49]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:09:50]
David Boder: [00:09:50]
Hadassah Marcus: In my absence.

[00:09:51]
David Boder: [00:09:52]
Hadassah Marcus: I was not at home...home then [words not clear]...

[00:09:54]
David Boder: In your absence...

[00:09:55]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:09:56]
David Boder: . . . your children were taken away? How old were they?

[00:09:57]
Hadassah Marcus: The oldest child was ten and a half years old.

[00:10:00]
David Boder: Hm

[00:10:00]
Hadassah Marcus: The next one [was] seven years, and twins of four years.

[00:10:03]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:10:04]
Hadassah Marcus: One had died...

[00:10:06]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:10:06]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . a short time before, a handicapped[?].

[00:10:09]
David Boder: And there they permitted...

[00:10:11]
Hadassah Marcus: There...Yes. There people worked at furriery, at furs, at shoemaking, at various trades.

[00:10:18]
David Boder: Oh, it was a large shop.

[00:10:20]
Hadassah Marcus: A large shop. One of the largest shops.

[00:10:22]
David Boder: And did people live there like in lagers or in...or people lived at home?

[00:10:25]
Hadassah Marcus: Variously. In homes.

[00:10:27]
David Boder: And where did you live?

[00:10:28]
Hadassah Marcus: I was also living...at that time I still had an uncle...

[00:10:32]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:10:32]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . a brother, and a sister.

[00:10:34]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:10:34]
Hadassah Marcus: So we were [living] together.

[00:10:36]
David Boder: Hm. Nu?

[00:10:38]
Hadassah Marcus: In 1943 after the Ghetto purge...

[00:10:43]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:10:44]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . we perceived that the time was coming for Shultz’s terrain [factory] as well.

[00:10:49]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:10:50]
Hadassah Marcus: During the second Seder night [the second night of Passover] we went down into the bunker.

[00:10:53]
David Boder: During the second Seder?

[00:10:54]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:10:54]
David Boder: And where did you have a bunker?

[00:10:56]
Hadassah Marcus: The bunker was entirely under the ground, very deep underground.

[00:11:00]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:11:00]
Hadassah Marcus: Without windows, without air, and without anything.

[00:11:03]
David Boder: And who had made the bunker?

[00:11:05]
Hadassah Marcus: It was made by a few people...

[00:11:07]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:11:08]
Hadassah Marcus: Thirty-odd people were living in that bunker. [Words not clear. A few words might be missing due to a break in the wire. She apparently tells about camouflaging doors]...which were leading from the house. And they [pieces of furniture] were put back in the same place where they were before so that nobody in no way could find a trace, that something is to be found there.

[00:11:22]
David Boder: And so wait...wait a moment. The bunker was in a cellar or in a...

[00:11:26]
Hadassah Marcus: Underground.

[00:11:27]
David Boder: Underground.

[00:11:27]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:11:28]
David Boder: And how did one enter there? Through...

[00:11:29]
Hadassah Marcus: Through the...through rooms of the house.

[00:11:31]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:11:31]
Hadassah Marcus: And through there corridors were made.

[00:11:33]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:11:33]
Hadassah Marcus: Everything [was] underground.

[00:11:35]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:11:36]
Hadassah Marcus: And that is how we entered that cellar.

[00:11:38]
David Boder: Yes. Nu? Who was it that had built...built such things?

[00:11:42]
Hadassah Marcus: One’s own people, alone with our [own] hands.

[00:11:44]
David Boder: Nu? And where did one discard the earth, everything?

[00:11:48]
Hadassah Marcus: The earth was thrown out, because we had been preparing already [for] months in advance. We knew that a moment will arrive when they will make Warsaw completely Jew-clean [Juden-rein].

[00:11:58]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:11:59]
Hadassah Marcus: That which one could never imagine before, that such a thing could happen.

[00:12:02]
David Boder: Nu? And then?

[00:12:04]
Hadassah Marcus: On the 13th of April, on the 13th of the fourth [month]—this was after having been in a bunker a few weeks...

[00:12:10]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:12:11]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . we were discovered.

[00:12:13]
David Boder: How?

[00:12:14]
Hadassah Marcus: They let in to us...another bunker had been discovered and there was found someone who reported us [?]. He had no way out any more, and we had to start going out.

[00:12:24]
David Boder: How many people were you in the bunker?

[00:12:25]
Hadassah Marcus: Thirty-odd people we were then, one’s own [people].

[00:12:27]
David Boder: How did people sleep there? Eat?

[00:12:30]
Hadassah Marcus: Everything below..We had made makeshift beds.

[00:12:34]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:12:34]
Hadassah Marcus: As far as eating, we lived on whatever we could.

[00:12:37]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:12:38]
Hadassah Marcus: Because food did not have any place with us [did not enter one’s mind].

[00:12:41]
David Boder: And when one had to go? How did one...

[00:12:44]
Hadassah Marcus: Oh, everything [everybody] together, because we had no other possibilities. We couldn’t get to the surface.

[00:12:51]
David Boder: Hm. Nu

[00:12:53]
Hadassah Marcus: They took us out on a Friday at one o’clock.

[00:12:57]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:12:58]
Hadassah Marcus: Up to twelve o’clock of the same day the people who were discovered in bunkers were taken into the Ghetto—there were no more people there [ or: they did not appear human any more]—into the [house of the] Jewish Community Council.

[00:13:09]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:13:09]
Hadassah Marcus: And they gave everyone one shot, no more. That shot, wherever it hit...so that people were...from one shot can still live ‘quite well.’

[00:13:19]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:13:20]
Hadassah Marcus: One of those caught had to take all those people...

[00:13:24]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:13:25]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . who had received the shot [ not clear, possible a break in the wire]. And he who did that had to lie down last on top.

[00:13:36]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:13:36]
Hadassah Marcus: This was until twelve o’clock of the same Friday.

[00:13:39]
David Boder: Who told you that?

[00:13:41]
Hadassah Marcus: That was told to me by people who had...had been present.

[00:13:46]
David Boder: Did [words not clear]?

[00:13:46]
Hadassah Marcus: Such...Yes. Who had...There were people who had masqueraded as Germans. There was an apparatus [organization] for...people knew everything. All that was reported.

[00:13:57]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:14:00]
Hadassah Marcus: Fate wanted it that we should remain alive, and we were taken out an hour later. Because this edict [doom] lasted until twelve on the same day.

[00:14:09]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:14:11]
Hadassah Marcus: At one o’clock we were taken out and searched as big as we were. We couldn’t take anything along with us, and besides that, we didn’t want to, because we knew where we were going, that we were going to Treblinka.

[00:14:25]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:14:28]
Hadassah Marcus: Or else we thought that we were going to be burned by them like our previous people, But they led us to the distribution depot. There was the assembly place for all the people whom they had gathered together, and we were, on the same day, Friday afternoon, put into the RR-cars. In the wagon in which I was, were over a hundred people. The RR-car couldn’t take in any more than fifty-odd [persons].

[00:14:53]
David Boder: Men and women?

[00:14:54]
Hadassah Marcus: Men, women, and children. It is [was] without exception. Thirty-nine people were suffocated.

[00:15:00]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:15:01]
Hadassah Marcus: From the heat.

[00:15:01]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:15:03]
Hadassah Marcus: Because there were no windows. A very small window far up. Many people jumped out, not because they wanted to save themselves. They wanted to perish in the [open] air.

[00:15:18]
David Boder: One moment, please.

[00:15:19]
David Boder: This concludes Spool number 128, a report by Mrs. Hadassah Marcus. She is in a...and we continue on spool number 129. Henonville, fifty kilometers from Paris, in an Agudah Israel home, supported by the Agudah, and the educational part maintained by the ORT organization. We go over to Spool 129. Illinois Institute of Technology Wire Recording.

[00:16:03]
David Boder: France. September 13th, 1946. Henonville near Paris. A home for displaced Jews mainly maintained by...by a Kibbutz and supported by the Agudah Israel, and also having another organization, a Yeshiva from Lithuania. Mrs. Hadassah Marcus is continuing her report which had started on [Spool] 128.

[00:16:32]
David Boder: And so, Mrs. Marcus, they took you there to the distribution depot.

[00:16:35]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. On the same day, Friday, in the evening I was taken to the RR-cars. We were in the RR-cars over a hundred people where there could be only about fifty. Thirty-nine persons had suffocated, because we were completely without air. There was a small window. People were fighting to get out, to get out not for the sake of living, but at least to perish in the air.

[00:16:58]
David Boder: You mean to jump out?

[00:17:00]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:17:00]
David Boder: Nu, go on.

[00:17:01]
Hadassah Marcus: And in the...When dawn came we saw that we were being led not to Treblinka, but we were being led in the direction of Lublin, that means to Majdanek. We arrived in Lublin, and from there, guarded each fifth row by two soldiers with large dogs, with rifles ready, we were led to Majdanek, which is a few kilometers from Lublin. When we arrived in Majdanek we were the first transport of Jews, of Jewish women. Men were already there, Slovakian Jews.

[00:17:34]
David Boder: Who was there before?

[00:17:37]
Hadassah Marcus: The Germans. At that time this was a completely new lager.

[00:17:40]
David Boder: Oh, it was a new lager.

[00:17:42]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. We were among the first Jews in Majdanek.

[00:17:45]
David Boder: In ’43 it was?

[00:17:46]
Hadassah Marcus: In the year ’43 on the first of May we arrived in Majdanek.

[00:17:49]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:17:50]
Hadassah Marcus: We lived under very hazardous conditions. As Jews...They took away our shoes, and we had to stand all night on a field barefoot. Majdanek has a climate which has strong winds, unheard of, or great heats. Throughout the night a frost [snow?] of ten centimeters [ thick ] lay on the ground. They examined our feet, if we didn’t put a piece of paper underneath. Afterwards, in the morning, we had to run, not walk, to work, chased after by a young female SS man with a giant dog. Her name was Brigida.

[00:18:25]
David Boder: Brigida?

[00:18:26]
Hadassah Marcus: Birgida.

[00:18:26]
David Boder: She was an SS woman.

[00:18:28]
Hadassah Marcus: An SS woman.

[00:18:29]
David Boder: But you had said a female SS man [SS-manke].

[00:18:30]
Hadassah Marcus: A female SS.

[00:18:32]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:18:32]
Hadassah Marcus: She was...it is possible that we didn’t find in all that time another such woman as she was. Her badness exceeded all human understanding. Running barefoot...The Kommando [contingent of prisoners] numbered around fifteen hundred people.

[00:18:52]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:18:53]
Hadassah Marcus: Whether in rain or in snow at that time, we had to stand and work. She carried on a lot. When she noticed anything, she released a dog. We were bitten, our clothes torn off. And when one returned to the lager bitten, the next day he was taken to the crematory, because people who weren’t completely well, or if one had the smallest rash on himself, one didn’t have the right to live.

[00:19:23]
David Boder: Scabs—what they call it..

[00:19:25]
Hadassah Marcus: An itch, or a wind burn, or a blister from rubbing.

[00:19:29]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:19:30]
Hadassah Marcus: Immediately she had no right to live, and she was immediately taken to the crematory. We were given absolutely no medical help. Whoever gave us the least bit of help was punished.

[00:19:45]
David Boder: And what did you work at?

[00:19:47]
Hadassah Marcus: We worked then in the field.

[00:19:49]
David Boder: Hm

[00:19:49]
Hadassah Marcus: Later on we worked by bricks. We were helping, alas, to build a new crematory on that field which was in Auschwitz near the bath. At that time people were...they were burning, gassing the people in the bath where we bathed.

[00:20:04]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:20:04]
Hadassah Marcus: In another part. And they were burned in a pit.

[00:20:08]
David Boder: What do you mean, in a pit? In an open ditch?

[00:20:09]
Hadassah Marcus: In an open ditch.

[00:20:10]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:20:11]
Hadassah Marcus: We ourselves were present when we took out still unburned pieces, parts of people, and took them on the trucks and threw them in the water. The ashes [were] either thrown in the water or they were strewn in the gardens.

[00:20:27]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:20:28]
Hadassah Marcus: And so this crematory [the ditch?] was not enough for them, and we ourselves had to help carry bricks at night to build the crematory. Three months I was in Majdanek, After three months I was sent to Auschwitz.

[00:20:43]
David Boder: Why? What...

[00:20:44]
Hadassah Marcus: There were transports from Majdanek. We were told that we were being sent to factories to work.

[00:20:53]
David Boder: Where were you tattooed?

[00:20:54]
Hadassah Marcus: We were tattooed in Auschwitz.

[00:20:56]
David Boder: Hm. Nu, and so?

[00:20:58]
Hadassah Marcus: Only Auschwitz gave tattooes, no other lager.[?].

[00:21:01]
David Boder: Hm. Bergen-Belsen neither?

[00:21:03]
Hadassah Marcus: No.

[00:21:04]
David Boder: No. And so.

[00:21:05]
Hadassah Marcus: In Auschwitz I arrived...

[00:21:08]
David Boder: How many people were traveling with you to Auschwitz?

[00:21:10]
Hadassah Marcus: To Auschwitz we traveled in parties.

[00:21:12]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:21:13]
Hadassah Marcus: With my transport traveled over a thousand people.

[00:21:16]
David Boder: Only women, or men also?

[00:21:17]
Hadassah Marcus: Women and men.

[00:21:18]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:21:19]
Hadassah Marcus: The...A night before, before we went to Auschwitz...

[00:21:22]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:21:23]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . we had already been selected. We were at twelve at night...This was still in Majdanek.

[00:21:28]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:21:29]
Hadassah Marcus: We were already asleep. So they ordered [us] to dress quickly.

[00:21:33]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:21:34]
Hadassah Marcus: We didn’t know where we were being taken. The men of...of that field knew that now we were being led into the crematory. There was a case that one man had a wife among us, who still remained in Majdanek. He was a doctor, and he knew exactly where we were being led. So he poisoned himself.

[00:21:57]
David Boder: The doctor?

[00:21:58]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:21:58]
David Boder: A Jew?

[00:21:59]
Hadassah Marcus: A Jew. But the same night, as we were being led on the road to the crematory, there arrived someone riding a white horse, and...and he...and he gave some kind of an order, and we were led back again [Note on p. 48-(2743)].

[00:22:12]
David Boder: Where to? To...to where were you led back?

[00:22:15]
Hadassah Marcus: To...into the field.

[00:22:17]
David Boder: Into the field?

[00:22:17]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. While on the road.

[00:22:19]
David Boder: From Auschwitz?

[00:22:20]
Hadassah Marcus: In Majdanek.

[00:22:21]
David Boder: In Majdanek.

[00:22:22]
Hadassah Marcus: Because it had been the road to the crematory, but the one on the white horse had arrived...

[00:22:27]
David Boder: Who was he?

[00:22:27]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . in the midst of the road. An SS man, and with an order that we should be led back. When we returned we didn’t find that doctor any more, because he know that the wife had been led to the crematory. And he was found poisoned.

[00:22:40]
David Boder: So you were...you were then taken back to Majdanek.

[00:22:42]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:22:43]
David Boder: Nu? What did you...

[00:22:44]
Hadassah Marcus: But the next morning they led us to Auschwitz.

[00:22:46]
David Boder: Again you were led to Auschwitz?

[00:22:47]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. When we arrived in Auschwitz we were assured that we had arrived in a lucky moment, that there are no more crematories.

[00:22:55]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:22:55]
Hadassah Marcus: That means there are, but Jews are not being burned any more.

[00:22:57]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:22:58]
Hadassah Marcus: We calmed down a little, but immediately on arrival they made a selection. At that time I was still with a sister, with a very young sister. She we fifteen years old. I was put to the side, to go to the crematory. And...

[00:23:15]
David Boder: You had been told that they were not burning any more.

[00:23:17]
Hadassah Marcus: But so was the case. When we arrived it was so.

[00:23:20]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:23:21]
Hadassah Marcus: We were comforted with that, that they are not burning any more, but I myself was put to the side.

[00:23:25]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:23:26]
Hadassah Marcus: We sat a few hours and waited till we should be taken away, but an order came again that we should be taken into the lager together with the rest of the transport.

[00:23:38]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:23:39]
Hadassah Marcus: After that I worked for three months in Auschwitz, in water.

[00:23:43]
David Boder: When were you tattooed?

[00:23:45]
Hadassah Marcus: Immediately on arrival.

[00:23:46]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:23:47]
Hadassah Marcus: And so.

[00:23:48]
David Boder: Was your hair cut off?

[00:23:49]
Hadassah Marcus: I [?]...entirely cut off the hair. In Majdanek we had our hair.

[00:23:53]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:23:53]
Hadassah Marcus: In Auschwitz wherever a hair was found it was...

[00:23:57]
David Boder: Who did the cutting?

[00:23:58]
Hadassah Marcus: Women.

[00:23:59]
David Boder: Women.

[00:24:00]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:24:00]
David Boder: Were there any cases that men did it?

[00:24:04]
Hadassah Marcus: In my time there were no [such] cases, but in any case men were standing by.

[00:24:09]
David Boder: Men were standing by?

[00:24:10]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:24:10]
David Boder: They watched it?

[00:24:12]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:24:13]
David Boder: Who were the men?

[00:24:14]
Hadassah Marcus: Various ones.

[00:24:15]
David Boder: [00:24:16]
Hadassah Marcus: There were SS men...SS men. There were capos, and there were people who were working there in the bath.

[00:24:24]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:24:25]
Hadassah Marcus: Because in the bath men were working, men, too.

[00:24:27]
David Boder: Men [worked] in the bath.

[00:24:28]
Hadassah Marcus: Men and women.

[00:24:29]
David Boder: Yes. Nu?

[00:24:30]
Hadassah Marcus: After three months of work in the water—that means that in the morning we went in the water and stood up to the neck...

[00:24:37]
David Boder: What was the work in the water?

[00:24:40]
Hadassah Marcus: Gathered the leaves.

[00:24:41]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:24:41]
Hadassah Marcus: And gathered the...such long...

[00:24:44]
David Boder: The grass?

[00:24:44]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes. It was taken out on the field.

[00:24:47]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:24:48]
Hadassah Marcus: It was dried.

[00:24:48]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:24:49]
Hadassah Marcus: Afterwards it was gathered and...I don’t know what they used it for. [They were possible cutting peat or processing flax.]

[00:24:53]
David Boder: But they wanted to use it for something?

[00:24:56]
Hadassah Marcus: Possibly. This I don’t know.

[00:24:58]
David Boder: How many people were working in the water?

[00:25:01]
Hadassah Marcus: In my time, when I was working at this work, this Kommando numbered two hundred fifty people. Two hundred people were in the water at a time, and fifty people were working outside.

[00:25:12]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:25:12]
Hadassah Marcus: When there was no [work in the] water, we were carrying barrows, but barrows heaped up to capacity, that from seven till twelve we weren’t permitted to rest or to put down the barrow to load in the sand for us.

[00:25:25]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:25:25]
Hadassah Marcus: We had to carry it in the hand and go around, and ten Christians stood with shovels, and everyone threw in a shovel, so that, God forbid, we shouldn’t be able to rest, not at the loading and not at the unloading.

[00:25:38]
David Boder: Tell me about the water. How did one work in there? People went in with the clothes?

[00:25:42]
Hadassah Marcus: With the clothes we went in the water. Only the shoes were taken off.

[00:25:46]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:25:46]
Hadassah Marcus: If it happened that someone said that he isn’t feeling well, he cannot go into the water, [then] he couldn’t even take off the shoes. He was thrown in, the way he was standing and walking [just as he was], into the water.

[00:25:57]
David Boder: He was thrown into the water. Nu, what did one work? When one took out the grass...the grass, did one have to dive, or what?

[00:26:03]
Hadassah Marcus: We went...the water reached up to our neck.

[00:26:06]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:26:07]
Hadassah Marcus: And thus with the hands we gathered it and carried it to the shore.

[00:26:11]
David Boder: Hm.

[00:26:12]
Hadassah Marcus: . . . and went again, constantly farther...in summer...whatever could be found.

[00:26:16]
David Boder: All that happened already in Auschwitz.

[00:26:18]
Hadassah Marcus: Yes.

[00:26:19]
David Boder: Nu?

[00:26:20]
Hadassah Marcus: But in Auschwitz I had the opportunity, having been a year and a half in Auschwitz...

[00:26:25]
David Boder: Hm.
