[00:20:19]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:20:20]
Marko Moskovitz: Und wie lange kann das dauern? Wie lange...

[00:20:22]
David Boder: Dauern...drei Monate, es kann dauern sechs Monate, aber den finden sie gewöhnlich. Hm, hm, dieses Komitee ist hier in Paris. Sie fragen Herrn Bramson. Er wird sich mit denen in Verbindung setzen; und sie geben ihm den Namen und sie...

[00:20:44]
Marko Moskovitz: Den Namen des Onkels?

[00:20:45]
David Boder: . . . geben das in die News—in die Zeitungen und dann wird schon.

[00:20:47]
Marko Moskovitz: Ja.

[00:20:48]
David Boder: . . . dann wird schon jemand gefunden. Verstehen Sie?

[00:20:51]
Marko Moskovitz: Ja.

[00:20:52]
David Boder: Und sonst—wo denken Sie zu bleiben? Wohin wollen Sie gehen, wenn Sie haben gelernt ein Fach?

[00:20:57]
Marko Moskovitz: Vielleicht wenn man findet meinen Onkel in Amerika, vielleicht werd ich dort gehen.

[00:21:02]
David Boder: Und sonst?

[00:21:03]
Marko Moskovitz: Und sonst—hab nirgendwo hin zu gehen. Muss bleiben in Paris.

[00:21:12]
David Boder: Alright. Ich habe hier ein paar Bilder und ich will, dass Sie mir sagen, was ihre Meinung von die Bilder ist. Zum Beispiel: was ist das?

[00:21:24]
Marko Moskovitz: Das ist ein Bild.

[00:21:26]
David Boder: Ja, aber beschreiben Sie. Was ist es? Was denken Sie ist es?

[00:21:46]
Marko Moskovitz: Das ist eine Frau.

[00:21:48]
David Boder: Ja, hm?

[00:21:49]
Marko Moskovitz: Eine Arbeitsfrau.

[00:21:51]
David Boder: Ja.

[00:21:52]
Marko Moskovitz: Und ist sehr verklärt.

[00:21:55]
David Boder: Ist verklärt?

[00:21:55]
Marko Moskovitz: Ja.

[00:21:56]
David Boder: Was denken Sie, denkt sie?

[00:21:58]
Marko Moskovitz: Sie denkt an ihren Mann und an ihre Kinder.

[00:22:02]
David Boder: Hm, alright, was ist das?

[00:22:14]
Marko Moskovitz: Das war im Lager.

[00:22:16]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:22:17]
Marko Moskovitz: Ein Bruder zum Anderen hat gesagt: ‚Ah, ich bin jetzt krank, aber vielleicht wirst du nach Hause gehen, um zu sagen dem Vater, ich muss sterben.’ Also passiert in einem Lager.

[00:22:32]
David Boder: Was ist das? Moment, bitte—was ist dies?

[00:22:40]
Marko Moskovitz: Das ist zwei Mal Damen.

[00:22:41]
David Boder: Ja. Erzählen Sie mir, was kommt da vor?

[00:22:47]
Marko Moskovitz: Die sehen aus wie zwei Schwestern.

[00:22:50]
David Boder: Ja. Was hat passiert?

[00:22:55]
Marko Moskovitz: Sie haben vielleicht nach dem Krieg...Einem mit dem Anderen (zu leise—murmelt—unverständlich)

[00:23:02]
David Boder: Sprechen Sie lauter! Ja. Und was ist das?

[00:23:15]
Marko Moskovitz: Das ist ein Mensch.

[00:23:16]
David Boder: Ja. Und was?

[00:23:20]
Marko Moskovitz: Er sieht aus wie ein Muselmann.

[00:23:22]
David Boder: Ja? Sprechen Sie lauter. Wie sieht er aus?

[00:23:26]
Marko Moskovitz: Wie ein Muselmann.

[00:23:27]
David Boder: Ja? Was ist ein Muselmann?

[00:23:30]
Marko Moskovitz: Ein Muselmann ist ein Mensch Haut und Bein.

[00:23:34]
David Boder: Wer hat ihn genannt den Muselmann?

[00:23:35]
Marko Moskovitz: Was?

[00:23:36]
David Boder: Wer hat sie genannt Muselmann?

[00:23:38]
Marko Moskovitz: Die Deutschen.

[00:23:40]
David Boder: Und was haben sie getan mit dem Muselmann?

[00:23:41]
Marko Moskovitz: Sie haben gesagt: ‚Du bist ein Muselmann, du hast kein Recht zum Leben.’

[00:23:45]
David Boder: Und dann?

[00:23:46]
Marko Moskovitz: Und danach reden: „Steh auf, Mensch, Du darfst nicht leben. Geh nach Krematorium.’

[00:23:54]
David Boder: Ah hm. Und was ist das?

[00:24:00]
Marko Moskovitz: Und das ist zwei Frauen und ein Mann—arbeiten—im Feld arbeiten.

[00:24:06]
David Boder: Ja?

[00:24:13]
Marko Moskovitz: Und das - vielleicht sind sie in Amerika.

[00:24:18]
David Boder: Hm. Alright. Und was ist das?

[00:24:30]
Marko Moskovitz: Das ist ein Kind. Was der Doktor dem gelernt hat ist eine Fiedel. Und er kann es spielen, weil er gut war.

[00:24:40]
David Boder: Was war er?

[00:24:41]
Marko Moskovitz: Weil er gut war, kann er es spielen.

[00:24:44]
David Boder: Aha, nun?

[00:24:49]
David Boder: This concludes the interview with Mark Moskovski on July 30, 1946, a boy of, hm, Czechoslovakia, age 19.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Max Meyer Sprecher
entries.content:
[00:00:00] David Boder: Germany, September the 12th [23rd], 1946. Feldafing about 30 kilometers from Munich, a camp for displaced...a camp for displaced Jews covering about forty-five hundred people. Part of the camp is located [?] in a form of barracks of the Hitler Youth. I am having a room here in one...I am having a room here in one, and the floors are [here] what they call in German parquet, fine [inlaid] hardwood floors. The illumination,, although the tension of the current is weak, is in very fine armatures [fixtures.] There is central heating. There was an interruption...A large field, practically a city of barracks and barracks and barracks all over. All are occupied by displaced Jews, but I see a number of temporary buildings, private buildings. I am also told that several hundred families are billeted in German homes. That is of course a rather interesting, rare situation, and the Germans are being forced to find decent location for people with [DPs] families. These people are not fed by the camp. They have food ration cards and live on their money. What kind of money? — Well some [of them] managed to bring something [possibly post-armistice refugees from Poland, etc.] Some probably receive it from the States, and South America, and Africa. And the black market also helps. [00:00:00] David Boder: We are now going to interview Mr. Max Meyer Sprecher, 37 years old. He is at present...at present a student of medicine at Heidelberg University. He was a student before, and continues his medical student...[correction] studies now. He is going to speak to us in Yiddish...[Note: for some reason this interview was abruptly interrupted. The continuation is on spool 147.] [00:00:02] David Boder: This concludes the interview with [?], and we are going over to an interview again with Mr. Max Meyer Sprecher, with whom we started on Spool 146. Munich, September the 23rd...Munich, September the 23rd, 1946. We are not working here exactly under very ideal conditions. [00:00:28] David Boder: [?] And so Mr. Sprecher will you please tell me again where you were when the war started. Were you over in Germany? [00:00:33] Max Sprecher: I was then... [00:00:45] David Boder: Yes. Talk Yiddish. [00:00:47] Max Sprecher: I was then in Germany. I returned from the refugee camp in Beuthen on the German-Polish border. I was in ’38, the 28th of October, ’38, sent together with the Polish Jews from Germany to Poland. [00:01:08] David Boder: From what city were you sent? [00:01:10] Max Sprecher: From Berlin. Together with many thousand Polish Jews over the ‘green border’ to Poland. [‘green border’ apparently means the border line away from official points of entrance.] [00:01:17] David Boder: Had Germany then occupied Poland? [00:01:20] Max Sprecher: No, there was an ‘action’ specifically directed... [00:01:28] David Boder: We were interrupted again. These are quite trying conditions, to work in this camp; but we are beginning now again with Mr. Sprecher. [00:01:40] David Boder: So let us continue. And so beginning with the ‘green border’ continue... [00:01:44] Max Sprecher: The ‘green border’ is a field which is located between two countries. [00:01:51] David Boder: Yes. [00:01:52] Max Sprecher: There...it is not covered by any border guards. It is open, free. And so, since the Jews who were lead there did not want voluntarily to cross the border, the field, they were surrounded by German police with machine guns, and they were chased and compelled to cross the green field into Poland. For Germany we were Polish citizens. For Poland we were not Polish citizens. Therefore, we were interned in the Polish border city Bedzin, Zbolshin[?] in Polish, and remained there a very long time, almost three quarters of a year. [00:02:44] David Boder: Continue. And then you say... [00:02:46] Max Sprecher: In the course of time a possibility was found through an understanding with the German government, that a part of the people should be enabled to return and take with them the most necessary things, which they had left behind in Germany. Because the major part of the people had come simply...had brought with them only what they had...what they were wearing on their bodies, nothing else. A part returned in order to arrange their immigration into other lands. In this case I returned with the intention [the word is in Hebrew]. [00:03:25] David Boder: With what? [00:03:26] Max Sprecher: With the [translates]...with the purpose to continue the studies of medicine, and not in Germany, but in Switzerland. I have sent from the camp Bedzin my matriculation booklet to Basel with the hope to be accepted there by the university. But instead of going to Basel, to the university, I landed in a concentration camp. [00:03:51] David Boder: Well. In what lager did you land? [00:03:54] Max Sprecher: It was the 13th of [September]1939. On the 1st of September the war broke out with Poland. Between the 5th and the 10th we had to register in Berlin as enemy aliens. The Gestapo proclaimed specifically, against us personally, a number of security orders, and at dawn the 13th, between four and six o’clock in the morning, we were arrested and taken en masse to Sachsenhausen, Oranienburg near Berlin, fifty-five minutes by streetcar from Berlin. [00:04:36] David Boder: Is Sachsenhausen the same as Oranienburg? [00:04:39] Max Sprecher: Sach-...The lager
Sachsenhausen and lager...and concentration camp Oranienburg were at that time one and the same. At the founding of the lager, the lager was started in a small factory building next to the city Oranienburg. [00:04:57] David Boder: And Sachsenhausen is there nearby? [00:05:00] Max Sprecher: Then, a kilometer farther away...one and a half kilometers away is located the large lager
Sachsenhausen. [00:05:08] David Boder: Now describe the life in Sachsenhausen. [00:05:13] Max Sprecher: I cannot comply completely with this request, because soon after the arrival, and after the registration we were transferred to a strict quarantine. We were isolated from other lager... [00:05:29] David Boder: Yes, but tell me what happened to you there? [00:05:31] Max Sprecher: We were brought in there, seven hundred and fifty Polish Jews, into three blocks, at two hundred and fifty Jews in each block. [00:05:40] David Boder: Did not the Polish subjects have a diplomatic representative, who had undertaken to represent the Poles? [00:05:49] Max Sprecher: In Germany—nobody. Not the Swedish, not the Danish... [00:05:54] David Boder: [00:05:55] Max Sprecher: Nobody to represent us. Officially Sweden was assigned as the one to represent us. A few days before our arrest in Berlin, we have heard already about the actions against the Polish Jews in the various cities of the Germans provinces, Leipzig, Frankfurt. Therefore, we started running in droves to the Swedish counsul. Unfortunately, we were not given there any kind of answer, neither any kind of papers that we are standing under the protection of the Swedish government [pause]. [00:06:28] David Boder: And so, continue... [00:06:31] Max Sprecher: From the description referring to the earlier times...about the large lager...I unfortunately am unable...I am unfortunately unable to tell anything. [00:06:40] David Boder: No. I mean tell us about what happened to you there? Where were you? [00:06:44] Max Sprecher: We were delivered...the seven hundred and fifty Polish Jews... [00:06:48] David Boder: Men and women? [00:06:49] Max Sprecher: Only men. [00:06:50] David Boder: Yes. [00:06:51] Max Sprecher: In three blocks, two hundred and fifty people in each block. The youngest prisoners were, according to instructions, fifteen years old. In many cases the Polish Jews came with their youngest children, fourteen or fifteen years old. The oldest were seventy-five or older. [00:07:11] David Boder: And what was done with those who were younger? [00:07:14] Max Sprecher: The younger children were together with the parents [?] in the same block. None of us was doing any work. [00:07:22] David Boder: I have asked you whether there were children ten or twelve years of age? [00:07:26] Max Sprecher: No. Such children were not there. According to instructions only those had to register... [00:07:31] David Boder: Oh, they did not register? [00:07:33] Max Sprecher: They did not register...only those from fourteen years and older. [00:07:36] David Boder: Oh. [00:07:37] Max Sprecher: Not the younger children. [00:07:38] David Boder: Well. [00:07:39] Max Sprecher: At the beginning we were together in the block. We did not work. Because then the SS was doing the work, and also the indoor service of block elders, organized by them. Their work consisted in ‘exterminating’ us day in day out, and to eliminate [?] us. They succeeded in this work in a very short time... [00:08:03] David Boder: For instance? [00:08:04] Max Sprecher: A third of our block—similar conditions prevailed also in other blocks—have fallen right at the beginning. And... [00:08:19] David Boder: Tell it more specifically...What does it mean they had fallen? [00:08:22] Max Sprecher: We were given...they have chosen for us various torments, and punishments, which were to reduce our number. I shall describe a few of them. [00:08:33] David Boder: Indeed, go on. [00:08:35] Max Sprecher: It was called...it was called ‘belly recumbence’, lying on the stomach meant that we had to lie from four o’clock in the mor-...at daybreak, in the summer, September 1939 until five o’clock in the evening, on the belly without moving, the hands crossed on the back, the cap, the prisoner’s cap in hand. The hall was locked, the doors, the windows, the ventilation. And so at high...in the warm month of September 1939, there was no air to breathe. Older people ‘fell’ as a consequence of it, and one may say just like flies. [00:09:19] David Boder: Now tell me, who saw to it that people should lie that way? [00:09:23] Max Sprecher: The block elder, and his assistant the ‘room elder’ paraded all day from morning till evening before the block, along the rows of windows, and watched. They could ‘recognize’ us because according to instructions we had to hold the cap in the crossed hands on the back. If someone would move, so the cap would move. And in that they would recognize exactly that one or the other was moving. So he would mark down through the window from the outside which number, or which place was occupied by the prisoner who was moving, and he would come in and administer the punishment prescribed for it by the block-elder. The punishment consisted in calling the prisoner to the front, to the first row, and the block-elder, the room-elder, block-fuehrer in the uniform of the SS alternately belabored the poor prisoner with pieces of wood, pieces of iron until the man would break down. Often he right there ‘expired’his life. There were... [00:10:33] David Boder: Who were the block-elders? [00:10:36] Max Sprecher: The block-elders were in our Jewish blocks mostly criminals, previously punished [sentenced], who... [00:10:47] David Boder: Germans? [00:10:48] Max Sprecher: Germans, who for years have served were years ago sentenced to various lagers as criminals, and were later transferred to concentration camps. My block-elder bore the number 272 from Sachsenhausen. He was one of the oldest criminals, previously punished, in this lager. He was himself a boxer and ‘Ringer’, using all his strength to exterminate the Jews. [00:11:24] David Boder: What do you mean a boxer and a ‘Ringer’? [00:11:25] Max Sprecher: He was by profession outside, at liberty. Next to his vocation as...next to his vocation as B-Vauer he also was... [00:11:31] David Boder: Oh... [00:11:32] Max Sprecher: Next to his vocation as B-Vauer, or a professional criminal... [00:11:37] David Boder: Yes. [00:11:37] Max Sprecher: . . . he was also an amateur boxer and a ‘Ringer.’ [00:11:41] David Boder: A Ringer is what we call a wrestler in English, of course. All right. [00:11:46] Max Sprecher: This [his treatment] was already a softening up. His predecessor, by the name Zeres [could be a nickname derived from the Yiddish Zores trouble, misfortunes], a man who, for multiple murder, was sentenced to long imprisonment. He served his sentence for many years in various punitive camps. Finally... [00:12:06] David Boder: You mean prisons... [00:12:07] Max Sprecher: . . . prisons, and finally in the concentration camp Sachsenhausen. He...he has distinguished himself in his accomplishments. He has killed in the course of a very brief time a large number of my fellow prisoners in my block, Polish Jews, and then was discharged and set free. He was sent to his relatives in Berlin. Such was the opinion of the SS, that for the accomplishments that he has achieved in the course of such a short time during the month of September, he deserves his liberty, in spite [of the fact] that he was sentenced by a court to life long imprisonment. But the B-Vauers in Berlin thought differently about this [matter]. We had, through a contact... [00:12:54] David Boder: What does it mean, the B-Vauers? [00:12:55] Max Sprecher: B-Vauer means professional criminals. [Berufs-Verbrecher.] [00:12:57] David Boder: Aha. [00:12:58] Max Sprecher: . . . we had, through a contact... [00:13:00] David Boder: B-V means... [00:13:00] Max Sprecher: B-Vauer, means professional criminal [Berufsverbrecher]. [00:13:02] David Boder: Yes. [00:13:03] Max Sprecher: Through a contact with the Alexander Platz, that was the investigation [pretrial] prison of Berlin, we have reported that the famous B-Vauer Zeres was released from Feldafing [corrects himself] from Sachsenhausen and that he had in the course of one month killed tens of imprisoned Polish Jews...murdered. The B-Vauer tribunal of Berlin has sentenced... [00:13:32] David Boder: What do you mean, the B-Vauer tribunal? Was it a secret tribunal? [00:13:35] Max Sprecher: The tribunal of professional criminals has sentenced this man to death. They arranged a supposed celebration for the professional criminal Zeres, and during this celebration the verdict of the B-Vauer union was read, because you must know that the professional criminals of Berlin belong to unions, such organizations were organized... [00:14:05] David Boder: These were naturally secret organizations? [00:14:07] Max Sprecher: What? [00:14:08] David Boder: Secret organizations? [00:14:08] Max Sprecher: Secret organizations. [00:14:09] David Boder: Yes. [00:14:11] Max Sprecher: And... [00:14:11] David Boder: Underground organizations. [00:14:12] Max Sprecher: Yes. And so judged about this prison the world of professional criminals of Berlin, that the man deserves death, while the SS had judged that for his accomplishments he deserves [his] freedom [pause]. [00:14:26] David Boder: So what did the B-Vauers do with him? [00:14:28] Max Sprecher: They shot him to death during the celebration. [00:14:31] David Boder: Aha. [00:14:32] Max Sprecher: This information we have received from people who had arrived in our block from Alexander Platz. [00:14:38] David Boder: What was there at the Alexander Platz? [00:14:39] Max Sprecher: Alexander Platz was the investigatory [pretrial] prison of Berlin. [00:14:44] David Boder: Aha. [00:14:45] Max Sprecher: People who were to be distributed to various prisons, to various lagers, were assembled there. When there was assembled a certain number, they were sent in groups to the corresponding prisons or lagers. Now I shall continue describing our life in the...during the first days in the concentration camp. [00:15:07] David Boder: Right. [00:15:08] Max Sprecher: We had a series of punitive sports. One consisted in creeping, like a snake on the ground. Then there was leaping like a toad, like a frog. Do you understand me? [00:15:20] David Boder: Yes, of course. [00:15:21] Max Sprecher: Like a frog, like a toad, leaping, jumping, to half height of a human. The third consisted in rolling [word not clear] [00:15:30] David Boder: What is that? [00:15:31] Max Sprecher: Rolling, rolling. To roll [now it is clear] means, to turn like a tree [log] is being turned. That is how we had to ‘cower’. Now, there was something interesting in that ‘cowering’. It was fortunate for a Jew if he had a chance to die soon. But there were a lot of ‘falling’ people who suffered a day or two until they died. In order that these people could get a little bit more air, we usually placed them near the door, because through the cracks in the door these gravely ill people could get a little bit more air. [00:16:12] David Boder: Nu. [00:16:13] Max Sprecher: The pleasure of the SS and the block-elders consisted in coming in intervals from hour, and to make with us punitive sports in these overheated barracks. [00:16:27] David Boder: What does it mean in intervals from hour to hour? [This is a question for verification since his words were not clear] [00:16:29] Max Sprecher: I have told you that we were...in our section of the barracks the doors and windows were locked. Thus the air there was very bad. It was impossible to breathe. So it was very difficult for the block leaders, for the SS, to spend all day together with us in this heavy fowl air. So they stayed ordinarily outside. So they would come in from time to time during [?] the day, and made with us strenuous punitive sports. But as soon as they had spent with us a few minutes, it became hard for them to breathe in this heavy air, so they stopped, went out, and in an hour or two [then] the whole drill was ‘pigged’ over again [the whole procedure would start all over again]. [00:17:16] David Boder: So you were rolling indoors, inside... [00:17:19] Max Sprecher: In the block, two... [00:17:20] David Boder: But there was no room. [00:17:22] Max Sprecher: That was...that was the purpose of rolling, it was ordered that we were to roll in twos, in threes, that is one lies [corrects himself] rolls underneath on the ground, the second rolls over him, and the third rolls over the second. You can imagine that in this heavy air, and with these run-down people, they nearly crushed each other in the [process of rolling. There was no other way, because the block-elders together with the SS were compelling the unconscious people, unconscious from suffering, unconscious from the sticking air, and unconscious from the hard ‘sport’, which these exhausted [?] people were unable to stand. Now there is one thing about it. I have stated that we were placing first of all our sick, our gravely sick peoples near the door, so these people may have still a bit of air in their last hours of life. This by and by was noticed by the SS and the block-elders from outside, and they compelled [us]...so when they came in, they soon gave a command to roll, with the intent that we should roll above these gravely sick people, who were in part in coma [?] and so lead them into death. In the first [starting] row were lying a row of very young and well ‘sportly’ developed [physically strong] people. As soon as we heard the slightest motion in the vestibule, we instantly jumped back a half a meter. So when the command would come: ‘roll’, we would roll, but not over the sick but only one over the other, over those who were well. The aim of the SS [which] was that we ourselves should murder with our own bodies our gravely ill [?] brothers, did not materialize. [00:19:20] David Boder: Now, continue. What happened to you afterwards? [00:19:22] Max Sprecher: The other punishments, one could think it a light punishment, were [for instance] to lie simply on the stomach. The first day it was still tolerable. The second day many arose...many of us arose with torn skin and with blood on the chest. It is not as easy to bear for a few hours...to bear tightly pressed one against the other, from various...through the various pressures from people who were lying in front, behind and on the sides. The pressure, and the wounds were so acute, that after the first or second day we all had bleeding wounds. The hand was torn and it was bleeding like from a water main. At that there also occurred cases when particularly privileged [?] SS were looking for some special enjoyments. I shall describe one of them. There entered six inebriated SS. They had in their hands various pieces of wood, pieces of iron, and thick pieces of rubber hose. The title of the play was called that day ‘blood bath.’ A ‘blood bath’ consisted in the following: We had to line up in one row. Each SS man was given a row which he was to ‘belabor’. And he was beating over the face, over the eyes, over the nose, over the mouth until blood started flowing. When blood begins to flow a human grabs instinctively with his hand the bleeding wound, as if to stop the bleeding. In that moment would come the command: stand still. We were prohibited to move our hands, and the blood was flowing down to the ground. And in front of every person was formed a little puddle of blood. And so, since we were standing still, due to this standing the blood too stood still. So there came the command: ‘motion’, or, ‘lie down.’ Through the motion, and lying down with an open wound, the blood gushed, flowed again. When there was enough blood for each row, there came the command to lie down and to ‘roll’ in it with the face. Then we had to get up and all our faces were red from the blood. The SS was satisfied and the program for that day was completed. [Pause]. [00:22:06] David Boder: Now go ahead. What happened after this lager? [00:22:10] Max Sprecher: And so, we were submitted to a strong isolation. We were unable to learn from the fellow prisoners in the lager, of whom there were at that time ten thousand, what may happen to us, will happen. We were cut off from the outside [world], cut off from inside, delivered for life and death to a professional criminal as block-elder and to a women merchant, a room elder, as his helper. [00:22:43] David Boder: What is a women merchant? [00:22:44] Max Sprecher: A women peddler is a man from the underworld who occupies himself professionally with the sale of women, and... [00:22:54] David Boder: Oh, a women merchant. [00:22:55] Max Sprecher: . . . and with women. And a manager, or proprietor of houses of shame, which deal in women. Our number grew smaller from day to day, and we did not know when it will end. We are at present before Rosh Hashana. So I want to recollect that we were delivered to the concentration camp in 1939 on the eve of Rosh Hashana. So at the evening of Yom Kippur, the SS acertained from calendars which they have found on Jewish prisoners, which were brought in, that it is a great holiday for the Jews. And then they invented a special procedure: The hall, the barrack in the block 38 of Sachsenhausen, the isolation block, was closed shut for the whole day, and no bit of air was let in. In the evening the Jews... [00:23:57] David Boder: What was it Yom Kippur or Rosh Hashana? [00:23:58] Max Sprecher: The eve of Yom Kippur. [00:24:00] David Boder: Yes. When the time of transport [evacuation] came for the special commando, they refused to join the transport because two groups of the transport details to whome it was promised that they will be taken to other places to work, were shipped to the famous [?] gas chamber in Auschwitz and there they were gas-killed. Since they knew what was threatening them, they took their grenades, in their hands, and fighting, four hundred Jews fell with arms in their hands, members of the special commando in Auschwitz. I in part assisted in this thing [project] which was for all of us a satisfaction [to know] that if we shall have to die, we will know that as far as it was possible for us, we have obstructed the work of extermination which they perpetrated on us in the lager. In addition a substantial part of the work consisted in sabotage of the work, of the productive work which we had...had to do, be it construction work, be it...destruction and breaking of valuable tools...and that is how we endeavored through the work of sabotage [he becomes oratorical and fails to find the proper words] a part of the satisfaction...a part of the meaning [purpose] for us and the sake of other people. [01:05:17] David Boder: Now then go ahead. What happened to you then? Return to your personal [experiences]. [01:05:22] Max Sprecher: The 8th of January we went to transport. The transport proceeded in part on foot. We came from there, and part of the road was already encircles by the Russian army. Rather hastily we were crowded into RR-cars, into open RR-cars, freight RR-cars, and we were taken to Dachau. [Pause]. [01:05:57] David Boder: And where were you liberated? [01:05:59] Max Sprecher: I was liberated in Tuzing [?] [01:06:03] David Boder: How did you get from Dachau to Tuzing? [01:06:06] Max Sprecher: We were then...from Dachau we marched on to Bolshlager [?] near Muehldorf. There they were building a large subterranean bunker, a concrete bunker. At it were occupied...we all worked there. At the approach of the American army, the work was interrupted, and it was decided to send all us Jewish prisoners to the Tirol. We did not know at that time the significance of the Tirol. We only learned after liberation that it was decided that since there the SS fought [held out] the longest we were there to be in some way either outright killed, or pressed into service as auxiliary soliders in the desperate fight of the SS. [01:07:00] David Boder: Now where were you liberated? [01:07:02] Max Sprecher: We were liberated near Tuzing [?], and a train which was designated for the Tirol, but due to the destruction of the railroad tracks by the American Army...we were unable to get through, and so by accident we remained alive. [01:07:20] David Boder: And what are you doing now? [01:07:23] Max Sprecher: After liberation I attempted in this lager together with a few other [?] people to devote myself to practical work. Our work consisted in installing a network of shops, trade shops for carpenters, for electricians, for metal workers, for tailors, which... [01:07:58] David Boder: In what lager was that? [01:07:59] Max Sprecher: I did not work in lagers...[?] [01:08:01] David Boder: But wait a moment, how did you get here? [01:08:04] Max Sprecher: We were then brought here by train from Tuzing. [01:08:09] David Boder: and...to Feldafing. [01:08:09] Max Sprecher: To Feldafing. [01:08:10] David Boder: To Feldafing. [01:08:10] Max Sprecher: And,only after a few days, we started our practical work. Partly we were involved in social [community] work before we got into the [KZ] camp, and the first thing we considered appropriate after getting out of the [KZ] camp, to do some community work for the Jews. And the most important work consisted in leading again these declassed, broken-up people toward productive, normal work. And that consists... [01:08:37] David Boder: Did... [01:08:37] Max Sprecher: In leading the Jews into the shops. [01:08:39] David Boder: Does the ORT have any shops here? [01:08:41] Max Sprecher: At that time there was no... [01:08:43] David Boder: But now? [01:08:44] Max Sprecher: At that time there was no ORT, today there is a ORT. The shops which have been built here were not built by ORT. They were built by a small group of people, who have concentrated around the Jewish workmen’s committee. [01:08:59] David Boder: All right. But now you don’t live in Feldafing. [01:09:02] Max Sprecher: I have left Feldafing in September ’45 for Heidelberg. There I have studied, now for two semesters, medicine. I am...I have started my studies still before in [I have come to] Germany and am continuing now. I am precisely now just after my physicum examinations [these cover the first half of the medical curriculum] after the interuption. A part of my physicum examinations I passed eight years ago in Berlin and the remaining part I passed last week in Heidelberg. [01:09:39] David Boder: How do the professors behave? How many Jewish students are there now, who were such before they were confined to concentration camps? [01:09:46] Max Sprecher: We are there twenty students. Of them eighteen were in concentration camps. Two have returned from Russia. [01:09:55] David Boder: Is there a quotta for Jews in Heidelberg? [01:09:58] Max Sprecher: There is no quota for Jews, but there is a quota for foreigners. [01:10:03] David Boder: Yes. [01:10:03] Max Sprecher: And this quota for foreigners is not being filled by people from among the DPs. It is being filled in part with people who came here from various countries, especially from the Baltic countries, and the predominant number of students at the universities are from these previous inhabitants of the Baltic states who are concentrated here in very large numbers. [01:10:31] David Boder: Yes. And how do the other students, the German students behave toward the Jewish students? [01:10:40] Max Sprecher: The attitude may be in general characterized as courteous but...but not frank. Because we...because it is a fact that those students who are studying now, in a large part had the opportunity to conclude their prepatory training [Gymnasium] or to be educated in German universities due to special contacts, or special services in the activities of the National Socialist Party. Even if it is not possible to prove it against one or another, it does not mean that he did not belong [to the Nazi party], it simply has not been proved to date that he did belong. And we have developed a fifth sense [obviously sixth sense] in the lager. And that sense is called instinct. [01:11:27] David Boder: Hm. [01:11:28] Max Sprecher: And our instinct does not deceive us. [01:11:43] David Boder: Well...maybe you are just suspicious. Have you not become suspicious in the lager? [01:11:47] Max Sprecher: It is...we are strongly suspicious. And our suspicion is only a ‘regulator’ not a falsifier of our instinct. There are among them officers of the German Army, there are among them many people who feel themselves nowdays insecure in Lithuania. There are gradually returning Jews who recognize [them because of] their previous activities. There are returning other inhabitants of Lithuania, who have not compromised [involved] themselves with the Germans, and out of fear of these Jews, and of those inhabitants of the Baltic States who are now returning home, they hold it appropriate [prudent, safe] to abandon their countries and to come here. [01:12:38] David Boder: Tell me this, who pays for you at the University. [01:12:46] Max Sprecher: For the past semester UNRRA has paid. We...I am speaking now about conditions in Heidelberg. For this semester UNRRA has not paid. [01:12:57] David Boder: Yes. [01:12:57] Max Sprecher: We utilized the things which we are getting allotted from the [DP] camp. [01:13:02] David Boder: Hm. [01:13:03] Max Sprecher: We converted them into money, and paid with our own money. [01:13:07] David Boder: How much is the tuition? [01:13:09] Max Sprecher: The tuition amounts for us medical students from 220 to 250 marks a semester. [Note: This fact needs some illumination. UNRRA as an official agency would have to pay for 250 marks about $25.00 in American currency, while a carton of American cigarettes could bring on the black market at that time at least one thousand marks. —D.P.B.] [01:13:15] David Boder: And how was that realized from allotted supplies from the lager? For instance... [01:13:19] Max Sprecher: There is a way, not a nice one, but we had to tread on it. The things which we were getting we had to convert into money through people who occupy themselves professionally with swindle, trading, and black marketing, so we should be able to pay the semester’s tuition. Otherwise, we were informed, we were threatened with loss, of the semester. And while others may be able to afford to lose semesters, we with the many years [lost] in the lager, who have gotten old not studying—we cannot afford such luxury. [01:13:19] David Boder: Now then in how many years will you be a doctor? [01:13:53] Max Sprecher: That is a question... [01:13:54] David Boder: No, I mean if everything should proceed normally. [01:13:56] Max Sprecher: We have...I am speaking about myself. I still have before me a study period of four semesters, counting the [length] of the study of medicine, eleven semesters, I am now entering the seventh semester. [01:14:07] David Boder: When are you making your ‘half-doctor’? [01:14:09] Max Sprecher: My ‘half-doctor’ I have already made. I have started it [the examinations] eight years ago in Berlin, and finished them a week ago in Heidelberg. [01:14:18] David Boder: They recognized everything [all your credits]? [01:14:19] Max Sprecher: They recognized all that I had covered...what [the exams] I have passed eight years ago, and the rest I have passed now. [01:14:28] David Boder: Are there any Jewish professors at the university? [01:14:31] Max Sprecher: At the university Heidelberg there are no...there are no Jewish professors. There are two Aryan professors who have Jewish wives. At the other universities, for instance Munich, there is a small number of Jewish professors. [01:14:49] David Boder: And the rector of the university is the same who was [there] during the Nazis. [01:14:54] Max Sprecher: No. The director, the rector of the university was confirmed by the military government. The first rector, rector Bauer is the husband of a Jewish wife. He was the first rector of the Heidelberg university... [01:15:14] David Boder: After the... [01:15:15] Max Sprecher: After the liberation, after the Americans have marched in. Now there is different one, Baron von Kampenhausen a Jewish [corrects himself] a German philologue... [01:15:26] David Boder: Also, this concludes the interview with Mr. Max Meyer Sprecher, a medical student at the age thirty-seven at the University of Heidelberg, where he is concluding his studies which have been interrupted some eight years ago. This is Camp Feldafing. He doesn’t live here any more but has his attachments, belongs apparently to some organizations in this camp. September the 23rd, 1946, Germany, Feldafing, near Munich. Illinois Institute of Technology wire recording. [01:15:59] David Boder: I thank you very much, Mr. Sprecher, I wish you all the success in your work, and in your studies.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Nechama Epstein-Kozlowski
entries.content:
[00:00:02]
DAVID BODER: Spool 95. 21, between Como and Milano, on August 31st, 1946. This is Mrs. Nechamah Epstein, 23 [years old], a nice looking..a neat looking woman already in the sixth or so month of pregnancy—very cheerful, very proud of it. And she lives here with her husband in a co-operative camp, a co-operative group, in a castle near Como which is being maintained by the Hachshara under the auspices of the American Joint Distribution Committee and, apparently, UNRRA.

[00:00:52]
DAVID BODER: And so, Mrs. Epstein.

[00:00:54]
KOZLOWSKI: [00:00:55]
DAVID BODER: here, in this direction. You understand?

[00:01:01]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:01:01]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Approximately, get it? Talk in a manner that you notice at times that the [indicator] light goes on. That means that you are talking loud enough. You understand?

[00:01:13]
KOZLOWSKI: Aha. When the light goes on...

[00:01:16]
DAVID BODER: Like now. You see. And so, Mrs. Epstein, would you tell me please where you were when the war began and what happened to you then?

[00:01:30]
KOZLOWSKI: I can begin?

[00:01:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:01:32]
KOZLOWSKI: It has started for me with the Warsaw Ghetto.

[00:01:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes. And so where were you when the war began?

[00:01:39]
KOZLOWSKI: In Warsaw, in the Ghetto.

[00:01:41]
DAVID BODER: When the war began?

[00:01:42]
KOZLOWSKI: When it started? No, no, there was no Ghetto yet in Warsaw.

[00:01:46]
DAVID BODER: You were in Warsaw?

[00:01:48]
KOZLOWSKI: In Warsaw.

[00:01:48]
DAVID BODER: With whom did you live? Who were your family?

[00:01:50]
KOZLOWSKI: Family? With a father, with a mother, with four brothers, with three sisters.

[00:01:55]
DAVID BODER: Four brothers and three sisters.

[00:01:56]
KOZLOWSKI: Three sisters and father and mother, two brothers-in-law, two sisters-in-law, the brothers’ children, the sisters’ children...

[00:02:02]
DAVID BODER: But, yes...

[00:02:03]
KOZLOWSKI: I have remained all alone.

[00:02:06]
DAVID BODER: What? And where are all the others?

[00:02:08]
KOZLOWSKI: I will tell you where they went to.

[00:02:09]
DAVID BODER: Yes, but you know about them?

[00:02:11]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes. I know exactly.

[00:02:12]
DAVID BODER: They are...

[00:02:13]
KOZLOWSKI: Two brothers I saw being shot before my eyes.

[00:02:16]
DAVID BODER: Hm. And?

[00:02:18]
KOZLOWSKI: And the brother’s child with my mommie and another small brother went with me to Treblinka.

[00:02:24]
DAVID BODER: Aha. You were in Treblinka.

[00:02:26]
KOZLOWSKI: And I jumped out of the train.

[00:02:28]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:02:28]
KOZLOWSKI: Not having been to Treblinka...if I had been to Treblinka I would not have lived.

[00:02:32]
DAVID BODER: All right.

[00:02:33]
KOZLOWSKI: My small brother...

[00:02:33]
DAVID BODER: And so let us begin at the beginning. You were in Warsaw. Tell me about [it] when the Germans entered. That is seven years ago [?].

[00:02:40]
KOZLOWSKI: The Germans entered...

[00:02:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:02:43]
KOZLOWSKI: There were in Warsaw..yet before the Germans entered there had arrived very many Jews. There had been bombings.

[00:02:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:02:49]
KOZLOWSKI: People were killed under the ruins. Very many were lost.

[00:02:53]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:02:54]
KOZLOWSKI: And there was a severe hunger.

[00:02:56]
DAVID BODER: Where...?

[00:02:56]
KOZLOWSKI: Still before the arrival of the Germans.

[00:02:57]
DAVID BODER: Aha. Nu?

[00:02:58]
KOZLOWSKI: People had....We were not sure of the minute. There were severe air-raids [for] four weeks’ time. There had fallen very many people, children, everything. It was not possible to walk in the streets. Then, when there was the armistice...

[00:03:12]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:03:13]
KOZLOWSKI: ...the Germans entered. It was Saturday morning. The moment they entered they said they will distribute bread for the people.

[00:03:20]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:03:20]
KOZLOWSKI: And I myself had gone out. There reigned a great hunger among us. My brother’s child was two years old then. It was without a mother. The mother had died.

[00:03:28]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:03:30]
KOZLOWSKI: And I myself went out to the square. I saw the Germans are arriving. I also wanted to get a piece of bread for the children. So at that instant there a Christian was standing, and he said that I am a Jew. So I was immediately chased away.

[00:03:41]
DAVID BODER: A Pole?

[00:03:42]
KOZLOWSKI: A Pole. [Repeats in Polish] A Pole. So I was immediately chased away. So I went farther. There arrived peasants with potatoes.

[00:03:48]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:03:48]
KOZLOWSKI: So I went...For five Zlotys one could buy there potatoes. I went over to buy potatoes. I already had the potatoes in the sack. I was very happy.

[00:03:57]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:03:57]
KOZLOWSKI: So again someone arrived and said this is a Jew. So the Germans came over and grabbed me, and he grabbed me. He spilled the potatoes, gave [me] a few kicks and a few slaps, and threw [me] aside.

[00:04:10]
DAVID BODER: How old were you then?

[00:04:12]
KOZLOWSKI: I was then about [?] seventeen years old.

[00:04:14]
DAVID BODER: Aha. What did your father do for a living?

[00:04:20]
KOZLOWSKI: The father was a tailor.

[00:04:21]
DAVID BODER: All right. He was a tailor. All right. Did he earn enough for such a large family?

[00:04:24]
KOZLOWSKI: No, he did not earn [enough]. The children also helped. There were four grown-up children.

[00:04:28]
DAVID BODER: The children also worked?

[00:04:29]
KOZLOWSKI: We had [enough] to eat, but no great luxuries.

[00:04:32]
DAVID BODER: Aha. Nu? Where did you live in Warsaw?

[00:04:35]
KOZLOWSKI: I lived on Nowolipka 18.

[00:04:36]
DAVID BODER: On Nowolipka.

[00:04:37]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:04:37]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Nu, and so...well, you came home. Did you bring anything to eat? [Words not clear.]

[00:04:45]
KOZLOWSKI: I brought home nothing, because I was not given anything. Afterwards in Warsaw was it very bad. For a time we lived peacefully. Later the Ghettos began. Then began the hunger death.

[00:05:02]
DAVID BODER: Nu, and so would you tell me what happened until the Ghetto.

[00:05:07]
KOZLOWSKI: Until the Ghetto?

[00:05:07]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:08]
KOZLOWSKI: I can tell you everything. Into here [the mocrophone]?

[00:05:09]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:12]
KOZLOWSKI: When the Ghettoes began, among us began a great fight of hunger.

[00:05:18]
DAVID BODER: Of what?

[00:05:18]
KOZLOWSKI: Of hunger.

[00:05:19]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:05:20]
KOZLOWSKI: We began selling everything, the jewelry.

[00:05:24]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:05:24]
KOZLOWSKI: We finished at the...at the last, at the featherbed [eiderdown].

[00:05:28]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:29]
KOZLOWSKI: And with that...

[00:05:30]
DAVID BODER: Who bought it?

[00:05:31]
KOZLOWSKI: People who were smuggling. They had. They were earning. Christians bought it.

[00:05:37]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:05:38]
KOZLOWSKI: And then we could already see that it was very bad. We had nothing to sell any more. Eight people were living on a kilo of beets [enunciation not clear] a day.

[00:05:49]
DAVID BODER: A kilo of what?

[00:05:49]
KOZLOWSKI: Beets.

[00:05:50]
DAVID BODER: What is that?

[00:05:50]
KOZLOWSKI: Red beets.

[00:05:51]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:51]
KOZLOWSKI: Eight people lived [on it] a day.

[00:05:54]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:54]
KOZLOWSKI: With water. And every day, day by day, there remained less strength. We did not have anymore strength to walk. My brother’s four year old child did not have anything to eat. He was begging for a small baked potato. There was none to give him.

[00:06:07]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:06:07]
KOZLOWSKI: And this child was crying terribly. Why is that? Other children have [something] to eat and this child does not.

[00:06:13]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:06:15]
KOZLOWSKI: And thus it lasted a year’s time. Until....The first burned offering in my home was my father who, talking and walking, said he is fading from hunger, and died. My father was sixty years old.

[00:06:33]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:06:34]
KOZLOWSKI: When my father died, there began among us a still greater hunger. A kilo of bread cost twenty Zlotys.

[00:06:40]
DAVID BODER: That was not in the Ghetto yet.

[00:06:42]
KOZLOWSKI: It was already in the Ghetto.

[00:06:43]
DAVID BODER: Oh, wait a moment. You did not tell me when you went over into the Ghetto.

[00:06:47]
KOZLOWSKI: Into the Ghetto. The Ghetto began...I don’t remember the date exactly.

[00:06:52]
DAVID BODER: [00:07:04]
KOZLOWSKI: I do not remember the exact date.

[00:07:06]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:06]
KOZLOWSKI: The date I do not remember exactly. The Ghetto began, I believe, in the year ’41.

[00:07:11]
DAVID BODER: Yes, nu?

[00:07:13]
KOZLOWSKI: And...

[00:07:13]
DAVID BODER: When did you go over into the Ghetto? Or did you live there where...

[00:07:17]
KOZLOWSKI: No.

[00:07:17]
DAVID BODER: ...the Ghetto was made?

[00:07:17]
KOZLOWSKI: Then I went over to the Tapierzynska 10, moved over there.

[00:07:22]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:07:23]
KOZLOWSKI: There was already...there was too much rent. We could not afford it. We moved to smaller quarters.

[00:07:29]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:07:29]
KOZLOWSKI: We lived on Tapierzynska 10. There in that house died hundreds of people and children from hunger.

[00:07:36]
DAVID BODER: Did Tapierzynsk 10 belong to the Ghetto?

[00:07:38]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes, yes. The Ghetto consisted of many streets.

[00:07:41]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:41]
KOZLOWSKI: Tapierzynska 10 was inside the Ghetto.

[00:07:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:43]
KOZLOWSKI: So I was on Tapierzynska 10. There I lived without....Every day there were other dead, small children, bigger children, older people. All died of a hunger death.

[00:07:56]
DAVID BODER: What was done with the dead?

[00:07:59]
KOZLOWSKI: The dead were taken...if one fell on the street.

[00:08:02]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:08:02]
KOZLOWSKI: ... a paper was taken. He was covered. A stone was put on top, and thus he lay until....There was not enough time to collect the dead.

[00:08:10]
DAVID BODER: Why the stone?

[00:08:11]
KOZLOWSKI: There were many dead. For the paper not to fly away.

[00:08:13]
DAVID BODER: Oh, a small stone.

[00:08:15]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:08:16]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:08:16]
KOZLOWSKI: And than people drove around with small carts. There were no [funeral] coaches any more, nothing. People drove around with small carts, collected the dead, loaded them up, took them to the cemetery, and buried them — women, men, children, everybody in one grave.

[00:08:29]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:08:31]
KOZLOWSKI: Later....I will tell you short and sharp [to the point]. Later...I suffered very great hunger already after my father’s death. I had remained with my mother, with a brother...two brothers I had still, a big one and a small one. A sister of mine was living on Nowolipka 78 with a husband of whom I know nothing, what has become of them, because I left and she remained. I was deported together with the mommie and with the child, with a small brother.

[00:08:59]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:09:00]
Nechama Epstein-Kozlowski: And we...at first we were....It had broken out, the first [in Polish: wysiedlenie] deportation [used a Polish word] that was in the year ’42...

[00:09:06]
DAVID BODER: The first what?

[00:09:07]
KOZLOWSKI: The first deportation.

[00:09:08]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:09:09]
KOZLOWSKI: That was in the year ’42.

[00:09:10]
DAVID BODER: Wysielenie [deportation in Polish], you said?

[00:09:11]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes, wysiedlenie.

[00:09:12]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:09:13]
KOZLOWSKI: It was the first deportation. It happened in the year ’42. In the morning...I do not remember...It was winter.

[00:09:20]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:09:20]
KOZLOWSKI: I do not remember the exact month. In the beginning of winter. There came down a whole...a few thousand Germans had come down, with weapons, with machine guns, with cannons and they began to....They made a blockade. They surrounded from one end of the street to the other end of the street.

[00:09:36]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:09:36]
KOZLOWSKI: They began to chase the people out of the houses.

[00:09:40]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:09:40]
KOZLOWSKI: And they began....It was terrible. Many ran into the gates. They saw small children. They grabbed them by the legs and knocked them against the walls [enunciation not clear].

[00:09:47]
DAVID BODER: The Germans?

[00:09:48]
KOZLOWSKI: The Germans. The SS men. Grabed...

[00:09:50]
DAVID BODER: Knocked against what?

[00:09:51]
KOZLOWSKI: Against the walls.

[00:09:52]
DAVID BODER: Oh, the walls. Yes?

[00:09:53]
KOZLOWSKI: Against the walls. Then they took...They saw...The mothers saw what is being done to their children. They threw themselves out of windows.

[00:10:00]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:10:00]
KOZLOWSKI: Then we were....They went into a hospital, a Jewish hospital. There was a hospital on the corner of Niska. And they began taking out all the sick that were there. So the sick...

[00:10:08]
DAVID BODER: Did you see it yourself?

[00:10:10]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes. I was going there from the Tapierzynska. I was being led to the Unschlag [distribution depot].

[00:10:14]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:10:15]
KOZLOWSKI: So they....The sick began jumping out the windows. So they ran on the roofs with machine guns and shot down at the sick. And all were shot. And we were led away to the distribution depot. It was on the corner of Niska and Dzika. There I was the whole night. That night was a terrible one.

[00:10:31]
DAVID BODER: On the square?

[00:10:33]
KOZLOWSKI: No, inside. It was called the Umschlagplatz.

[00:10:35]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:10:35]
KOZLOWSKI: There...

[00:10:35]
DAVID BODER: What sort of a building was it?

[00:10:38]
KOZLOWSKI: It was a former school.

[00:10:40]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:10:41]
KOZLOWSKI: A school was there at one time.

[00:10:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:10:42]
KOZLOWSKI: And when the hospital....There was a Czysta [Street] Hospital in Warsaw [?] It was transferred. Here was the hospital...

[00:10:49]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:10:49]
KOZLOWSKI: ...across the street.

[00:10:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:10:50]
KOZLOWSKI: And afterwards there was a school [synagogue?]. Then a place [depot]. Was made there, and the Jews of the Ghetto were all concentrated there. They were led in there, and there they were a night, two nights. They led a railroad siding to the street, and in trains [they were] transported to Treblinka.

[00:11:06]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:11:06]
KOZLOWSKI: The night was very terrible one.

[00:11:08]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:09]
KOZLOWSKI: At night Germans came in, threw han grenades [a short defect in the wire; possibly a few words missing]. At the people...

[00:11:14]
DAVID BODER: Where did they throw the grenades?

[00:11:15]
KOZLOWSKI: Into...into the school [synagogue?].

[00:11:17]
DAVID BODER: Why?

[00:11:18]
KOZLOWSKI: Because Jews were there. There came in bandits, Germans, and threw in hand grenades. There were loud screams. We had no place to go out. One lay on top of the other. We had to...eh...relieve ourselves there on the spot.

[00:11:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:32]
KOZLOWSKI: It was a frightful moment [experience] to live through that night.

[00:11:35]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:11:35]
KOZLOWSKI: And there came in...all of a sudden a German comes in. He goes over to a fifteen year old boy and says to him if he wants to live he must eat a candle.

[00:11:44]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:11:44]
KOZLOWSKI: A candle. A candle.

[00:11:45]
DAVID BODER: Oh. Nu?

[00:11:46]
KOZLOWSKI: And the boy began to cry how can he do it. So he takes out his revolver and says, ‘If you do not eat it up I will shoot you.’

[00:11:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:52]
KOZLOWSKI: And the boy began eating, and he vomited, but he did eat it up.

[00:11:56]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:11:56]
KOZLOWSKI: And he left.

[00:11:57]
DAVID BODER: Who brought it in?

[00:11:59]
KOZLOWSKI: It was brought in by the German.

[00:12:00]
DAVID BODER: By the German?

[00:11:59]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:12:01]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:12:01]
KOZLOWSKI: And he told him to eat the candle. And he could not, but he had to. He was afraid. He wanted to live.

[00:12:05]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:12:06]
KOZLOWSKI: He ate up the candle. The night had passed, very frightful, with much deadly fear. In the morning they began to chase us out. ‘Alle aus.’ We should go out.

[00:12:15]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:12:15]
KOZLOWSKI: We went out. Already RR-cars had been prepared. All were chased into RR-cars.

[00:12:19]
DAVID BODER: that synagogue was near the station.

[00:12:22]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes..not to the station. Railroad tracks had been laid on the street.

[00:12:25]
DAVID BODER: On the street railroad tracks?

[00:12:26]
KOZLOWSKI: On the street railroad tracks had been laid.

[00:12:28]
DAVID BODER: To the station?

[00:12:29]
KOZLOWSKI: No it was not the station. It was about two kilometers away from the station.

[00:12:32]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:12:33]
KOZLOWSKI: And they began to arrange in rows of five mothers with children, men, everybody together. And whoever could not...there were about thirty feet to walk out of there...

[00:12:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:12:44]
KOZLOWSKI: Whoever could not walk straight, he was immediately shot on the spot.

[00:12:48]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:12:48]
KOZLOWSKI: He said to walk in rows of five. We got into the RR-cars. Two hundred persons were packed into one RR-car. Riding in these wagons everyone saw death before the eyes at any instance. We lay one on top of the other. One pinched pieces from another. We were tearing pieces.

[00:13:06]
DAVID BODER: Why?

[00:13:06]
KOZLOWSKI: Because everybody wanted to catch...to save oneself. Everybody wanted to catch air. One lay suffocating on top of another.

[00:13:11]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:13:12]
KOZLOWSKI: We could do nothing to help ourselves. And then real death began.

[00:13:18]
DAVID BODER: In the RR-cars?

[00:13:19]
KOZLOWSKI: In the RR-cars. After we had traveled for four hours, it became terribly hot. But so fast did the train travel that there was nothing [to do]...faster then an express.

[00:13:29]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:13:30]
KOZLOWSKI: We began thinking, the youths, what should we do. The mothers were telling their children they should save themselves, they should jump. Maybe in spite of all they will remain alive.

[00:13:38]
DAVID BODER: Were the doors open?

[00:13:40]
KOZLOWSKI: Closed, everything. There was a small window with bars.

[00:13:42]
DAVID BODER: Nu, how could one jump?

[00:13:44]
KOZLOWSKI: Well, I will tell you how it was.

[00:13:46]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:13:46]
KOZLOWSKI: Many had along with them files, knives, hammers. Many had along with them [such things].

[00:13:52]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:13:52]
KOZLOWSKI: And we were in that RR-car a whole night. There had begun a great thirst. It became terribly hot. Everybody undressed nude.

[00:14:00]
DAVID BODER: Men and women?

[00:14:02]
KOZLOWSKI: Men..no. What does completely naked mean? We undressed..in the shirts we went around.

[00:14:06]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:14:07]
KOZLOWSKI: Men, women, children.

[00:14:08]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:14:09]
KOZLOWSKI: There were small children who began to cry terribly, ‘Water!’

[00:14:12]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:14:13]
KOZLOWSKI: So we started banging on the doors. The Germans should give water.

[00:14:16]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:14:17]
KOZLOWSKI: We were screaming. So they began to shoot inside, from all four sides.

[00:14:20]
DAVID BODER: On the stations?

[00:14:21]
KOZLOWSKI: Not on the sta—...while traveling. They were sitting on the roofs.

[00:14:23]
DAVID BODER: While traveling?

[00:14:24]
KOZLOWSKI: Germans were sitting on the roofs.

[00:14:25]
DAVID BODER: Oh.

[00:14:26]
KOZLOWSKI: On the roofs by the...where one steps down, on the steps, German were sitting.

[00:14:31]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:14:31]
KOZLOWSKI: And they began to shoot inside. When they began to shoot inside, very many pople fell [were killed]. I was sitting and looking how one gets [hit by] a bullet, another one gets [hit by] a bullet. I, too, expected to get hit in a moment.

[00:14:45]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:14:45]
KOZLOWSKI: And I saved myself by hiding under the dead. I lay down underneath the dead. The dead lay on top of me. The blood of the killed was flowing over me.

[00:14:55]
DAVID BODER: The what?

[00:14:56]
KOZLOWSKI: Blood.

[00:14:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:14:56]
KOZLOWSKI: I was completely bespattered with blood.

[00:14:58]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:14:59]
KOZLOWSKI: There lay a little girl of four years. She was calling to me, ‘Give me a little bit of water. Save me.’ And I could do nothing. Mothers were giving the children urine to drink. You know what urine is?

[00:15:09]
DAVID BODER: Is it really true?

[00:15:10]
KOZLOWSKI: I saw it. I did it myself, but I could not drink it. I could not stand it any more. The lips were burned from thirst.

[00:15:18]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:15:19]
KOZLOWSKI: I thought this is it, I am going to die.

[00:15:20]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:15:20]
KOZLOWSKI: So I saw that the mother is doing it, and the child said, ‘Mama, but it is bitter. I cannot drink it.’

[00:15:25]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:15:26]
KOZLOWSKI: So she said, ‘Drink, drink.’ And the child did not want to drink it, because it was bitter. And I myself imitated it, but I was not able to drink it, and I did not drink it. But what then? There were girders inside the RR-cars.

[00:15:36]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:15:37]
KOZLOWSKI: Girder, iron girders.

[00:15:39]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:15:39]
KOZLOWSKI: From the heat, perspiration [precipitation] was pouring from the girders. This we..one lifted the other one up. It was high up, and we licked [the moisture] off the grinders.

[00:15:49]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:15:50]
KOZLOWSKI: We traveled this way the whole night, and we were approaching ever closer to the real death. And so my mommie began to cry very much.

[00:15:59]
DAVID BODER: You were licking the perspiration from the cold...

[00:16:03]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes, from the cold girders.

[00:16:04]
DAVID BODER: Yes, from the...

[00:16:05]
KOZLOWSKI: There was nothing to drink.

[00:16:05]
DAVID BODER: From the rods, from the iron rods of the bars?

[00:16:09]
KOZLOWSKI: It was very stifling. There was that little window, a tiny one, so we wanted to open it. Every time we opened it, they would shoot in, not minding that...

[00:16:17]
DAVID BODER: What month was it in?

[00:16:18]
KOZLOWSKI: It was...I do not remember exactly. I remember it was winter.

[00:16:20]
DAVID BODER: Winter.

[00:16:21]
KOZLOWSKI: Winter, yes.

[00:16:22]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:16:22]
KOZLOWSKI: And when we wanted to open it...Not minding that they were shooting, we did open it. There were small children, and they were all suffocating.

[00:16:30]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:16:30]
KOZLOWSKI: We could not stand it any more.

[00:16:31]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:16:32]
KOZLOWSKI: And thus I rode all night. Early in the morning — it was about two in the morning, maybe three, just before dawn — my mommie began crying very much. I was with my small brother eithteen years old.

[00:16:44]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:16:45]
KOZLOWSKI: So the mommie began to cry very much. She begged us to save ourselves. The boys took a saw and cut out...it was locked with a chain from the other side, a whole....

[00:16:53]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:16:54]
KOZLOWSKI: And we took the bars off the windows.

[00:16:57]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:16:58]
KOZLOWSKI: And we started to jump. No. What does to jump mean? One pushed out the other one.

[00:17:02]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:17:03]
KOZLOWSKI: And while jumping.

[00:17:03]
DAVID BODER: Aha. Did the Germans let them?

[00:17:04]
KOZLOWSKI: They did not let them. They immediately started shooting on the spot. Many were shot. Out of a hundred people there could remain ten.

[00:17:10]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:17:10]
KOZLOWSKI: My little brother jumped out five minutes before me, and he was shot. When I jumped out I fell into a ditch.

[00:17:17]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:17:18]
KOZLOWSKI: And I remained lying completely unconscious. And the RR-car...the train passed.

[00:17:22]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:17:22]
KOZLOWSKI: I came to. It was at night, around three in the morning, so I...

[00:17:28]
DAVID BODER: And your mother herself did not jump.

[00:17:30]
KOZLOWSKI: No. The mother could not. With the small child she could not jump. And a woman of sixty, she could not jump.

[00:17:35]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:17:36]
KOZLOWSKI: And I...

[00:17:36]
DAVID BODER: How big was the hole through which you had jumped?

[00:17:39]
KOZLOWSKI: It was perhaps...

[00:17:41]
DAVID BODER: No, no [words not clear].

[00:17:41]
KOZLOWSKI: High up...

[00:17:42]
DAVID BODER: Oh, the hole that was there was enlarged?

[00:17:45]
KOZLOWSKI: Right next to the roof. Yes, it was right next to the roof.

[00:17:47]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:17:48]
KOZLOWSKI: We jumped out, and I remained completely unconscious. I came to. I got back my thoughts, so I went to look for my brother. I knew that he had jumped at the same time I did.

[00:18:00]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:18:01]
KOZLOWSKI: In the meantime there arrived some sort of a Polish militia man...

[00:18:03]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:04]
KOZLOWSKI: ...who walks at the stations at night...

[00:18:05]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:06]
KOZLOWSKI: ...and told me that I should quickly run away from here, because the Gestapo is all around here. I will be shot here. I should run away. He told me that I had jumped near Radzin and Lukow. There was the road leading to5Radzin, a road to Lukow.

[00:18:18]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:19]
KOZLOWSKI: So he told me to go to the Miedzyrzec Ghetto. There is a ghetto with Jews.

[00:18:23]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:23]
KOZLOWSKI: In Warsaw they had already begun....He said, ‘There it is not good. The Jews are being deported.’ I should go to Miedzyrzec. I began to walk on foot toward Miedzyrzec.

[00:18:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:31]
KOZLOWSKI: To Miedzyrzec. When I jumped out I met a little girl. She had also jumped. She had her entire leg completely torn open. While jumping she had caught on a piece of iron, and she tore open her leg.

[00:18:44]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:45]
KOZLOWSKI: And the two of us started to walk. Yes, after getting up I went to look for my brother. I had gone about ten feet. He lay shot. He had a bullet here in the heart [?].

[00:18:55]
DAVID BODER: In the heart [?]?

[00:18:56]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes, here in the heart [?] I could not move away from him, but that Christian said that I should go away quickly. [Pause.] The struggle for life was stronger than anything. I left my brother on the road. I do not know what happened to his bones. And I went on. I had walked with that little girl for about three hours. Dark it was. Through woods, through fields we crawled, crawled, crawled. [The word crawled is repeated by an echo of the large room of the castle where the interview took place, and is clearly heard on the wire.] Suddenly Polish police arrived. He asked us where we are going. He wanted to arrest us. He wanted to had us over to the German authorities. We started to cry bitterly. That child cried bitterly. She begged [that] they should let us go on. It was at night. I do not know what happened — they said...

[00:19:40]
DAVID BODER: That little girl was a stranger?

[00:19:42]
KOZLOWSKI: A strange little girl. I don’t know at all that little girl.

[00:19:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes. How old was she?

[00:19:45]
KOZLOWSKI: She was about fourteen years old.

[00:19:46]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:19:47]
KOZLOWSKI: And the little girl with the bleeding leg...for terror she did not feel the pain.

[00:19:52]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:19:53]
KOZLOWSKI: After having walked thus for perhaps ten kilometers, the two of us remained sitting where the road leads [?] into a forest. And we could not walk any more. The child said that she cannot walk any more. The leg hurts her. We don’t know what will be. In the meantime I had heard gentiles talking, that Germans prowl on this road looking for Jews. And I saw it is bad. With the child I cannot walk. So I took the child. I did not know what to do. I carried her perhaps...perhaps, who knows, a kilometer or two. I myself did not have any strength. I was barefoot. My shoes had remained in the RR-car, because I had undressed. I did not have the time to put anything on. I was completely naked and barefoot. And that child remained in the field. And I went away. I could not help any more at all. The child had fallen, and I could not do anything to help any more. I went away. [A pause.]

[00:20:47]
DAVID BODER: Go on.

[00:20:50]
KOZLOWSKI: After I had walked thus for about twenty kilometers, I came to...

[00:20:56]
DAVID BODER: Go on.

[00:20:58]
KOZLOWSKI: I had walked thus for about twenty kilometers. I do not know myself how many kilometers I had covered. I came to the Miedzyrzec Ghetto [Meseritz is German for Miedzyrzec].

[00:21:06]
DAVID BODER: Miedyrzec. [Both pronounce it Medrich. Not to be confused with Meseritz in Poznan.]

[00:21:07]
KOZLOWSKI: Miedzyrzec.

[00:21:08]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:21:08]
KOZLOWSKI: Arriving in Miedyrzec, I went in [to the Ghetto]. It was a day after a large deportation. So I went in.

[00:21:16]
DAVID BODER: It was [in German] a deportation?

[00:21:17]
KOZLOWSKI: A deportation.

[00:21:18]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:21:19]
KOZLOWSKI: Entering the Ghetto, it became faint before my eyes. It was at night. I did not have anywhere to go. When arriving there, I regretted very much that I had jumped off the train, because at every step, wherever I went, shot people were lying. Broken windows, all stores looted. Terrible things happened there.

[00:21:39]
DAVID BODER: What was the name of that town?

[00:21:41]
KOZLOWSKI: Miedzyrzec [pronounced Mezrich].

[00:21:42]
DAVID BODER: Miedzyrzec.

[00:21:42]
KOZLOWSKI: The Miedzyrzec Ghetto.

[00:21:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Nu?

[00:21:44]
KOZLOWSKI: In that Ghetto I lived eight months...

[00:21:48]
DAVID BODER: Did you...

[00:21:49]
KOZLOWSKI: ...in deathly fear.

[00:21:50]
DAVID BODER: ...register with the..

[00:21:51]
KOZLOWSKI: There was a Jewish community council. I registered with the Jewish Community Council, and I sat. It was not worth it. Every four weeks there were new deportations. From the small towns all around and around Jews were brought in there. And there was a sort of an assembly depot for Jews. And from there all the Jews were being sent to Treblinka. There I lived through three terrible deportations. During the first deportation I hid in an open attic and lay there for four weeks. I lived just on raw beets.

[00:22:22]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:22:22]
KOZLOWSKI: I did not have anything to drink. The first snow fell then, so I made a hole in the roof and pulled in with the hand a little snow. And this I licked. And this I lived on.

[00:22:33]
DAVID BODER: Were you there alone?

[00:22:35]
KOZLOWSKI: No. We were about...about...there were about twenty people there. There was a father with a mother with child. There were some other...

[00:22:42]
DAVID BODER: In the attic.

[00:22:43]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes, in the attic.

[00:22:48]
DAVID BODER: Nu, and so you were there on the roof [attic] in the Ghetto. With how many people?

[00:22:55]
KOZLOWSKI: There were about twenty people.

[00:22:56]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:22:57]
KOZLOWSKI: We had nothing to eat. Thus we lived four weeks. We found raw peas [which] we ate. I had pared the beets, and afterwards I gathered the rinds of the beets, because I had nothing more to eat. And thus I nourished myself for four weeks, till there had passes a [in Polish] deportation...[in German;] a deportation. It lasted four weeks, that deportation. After the deportation we came down from the attic. At that time a lot of Jews had also been shot. Coming down from the attic, it was a terrible thing to see. We had to...we were taken to work removing the dead.

[00:23:29]
DAVID BODER: Who were the SS. Germans and who else? [This is a reference to the Polish and Ukranian element in the SS.]

[00:23:33]
KOZLOWSKI: Germans.

[00:23:33]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:23:34]
KOZLOWSKI: Only Germans. Just Germans.

[00:23:35]
DAVID BODER: Nu, go on.

[00:23:37]
KOZLOWSKI: There were a few Ukranians, too, but not many.

[00:23:40]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:23:40]
KOZLOWSKI: Ukranians.

[00:23:41]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:23:41]
KOZLOWSKI: From the Ukraine. They were serving in the German army.

[00:23:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:23:45]
KOZLOWSKI: And I went down. We all went down. It was worse yet than in the attic. We saw numerous dead. All the streets were splashed with blood. In every ditch Jewish blood had been poured. We went down. We had nothing to eat. We started looking for something to eat so we...

[00:24:04]
DAVID BODER: Was there no Council, no Community Council...

[00:24:08]
KOZLOWSKI: At that time tha chairman had been taken away. The chairman had been shot. He was taken out first. He was the first.

[00:24:14]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:24:14]
KOZLOWSKI: A very fine man. He was taken out the first with the wife, with the child. They were told to turn around, and they were shot. There were Jewish police, too.

[00:24:23]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:24:23]
KOZLOWSKI: Jewish policeman. So they were shot little by little. During each deportation ten, twenty were taken and also transported into the RR-cars. And they were shot, sent away. Those who escaped were shot.

[00:24:36]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:24:37]
KOZLOWSKI: In any case, they were all killed. So there was nobody to turn do. Everybody was hidden in the cellar. Everybody was afraid to go out. Many were lying [in hiding] there still a few weeks after the deportation. They did not know that it is already ‘free’ that one can be [is let alone] already. When we came down it was sort of peaceful for about two months. For two months time we lived on that which the Jewish Council gave to those who were strangers [Jews who were again assembled from other towns waiting for deportation].

[00:25:03]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:25:04]
KOZLOWSKI: They gave them every day a kilo of potatoes and a piece of bread. The food was not important [?], because it was...every day we lived in great fear. People walking in the streets were shot at.

[00:25:15]
DAVID BODER: Did you have relatives there? Did you know anyone?

[00:25:17]
KOZLOWSKI: Nobody. I was all alone. [Excited] Without relatives, without anybody.

[00:25:21]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:25:22]
KOZLOWSKI: Mine had all gone away. I had remained all alone. I had to support myself. By what did I support myself? I carried water.

[00:25:31]
DAVID BODER: For whom?

[00:25:32]
KOZLOWSKI: For the Jews who lived there I carried water. And for that I received a few groschen. And that is how I supported myself.

[00:25:40]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:25:40]
KOZLOWSKI: I lived in such a...a large hall. There was once a circus.

[00:25:46]
DAVID BODER: A circus.

[00:25:47]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes. There lived all the deportees.

[00:25:50]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:25:51]
KOZLOWSKI: Short and sharp [to the point], it dragged on till winter, till [in Polish] the Birth of Christ.

[00:25:57]
DAVID BODER: That is when? [In Russian] Christmas?

[00:25:59]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:25:59]
DAVID BODER: The 24th of December. Nu?

[00:26:01]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes. Then there was a frightful night to live through. There came down drunken Gestapo [men] from Radzyn.

[00:26:07]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:26:09]
KOZLOWSKI: And...in the middle of the night we were asleep in a room. There were perhaps, who knows, thirty people altogether in that house where we were, in one room. And they entered. I was sleeping there with two little girls. These children had also escaped from the Radzin Ghetto. Two girls, little ones. One was about eight years old, and one about six years. I was sleeping with them in the room. There were other girls. In our room there were about fifteen persons. In the middle of the night we hear...there lived a woodcutter [?], so we thought that someone is chopping wood. We jump up. We hear shooting. They began shooting. We lay in great deathly fear. And they were knocking on our door. And I did not know why they could not enter through the door. I the morning I got up. I opened the door. A shot person fell into...into my room, itno the house where we were lying. When we came in [into the other rooms] there lay shot all who were living in those rooms. Two children with a father who were sleeping in bed, everything was shot. A man lay with his stomach completely torn open, his guts outside on the ground. And later Jewish police came in. The Germans had left, and we had to clean up the blood and all that. There was lying the bedding and the shot. All that we had to clean up. There were also two men who had been in a lager. At that time there were lager.. It was in Oswoboj.

[00:27:33]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:27:34]
KOZLOWSKI: And those two boys...

[00:27:35]
DAVID BODER: It was where?

[00:27:35]
KOZLOWSKI: Oswoboj near Chelm. They had escaped from there, from that lager. They had been thirty people. So they were taken out one nice clear day, and they were led to...graves had been dug beforehand, and they were all led...

[00:27:47]
DAVID BODER: Who had dug those graves?

[00:27:49]
KOZLOWSKI: These people themselves had dug these graves.

[00:27:51]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:27:52]
KOZLOWSKI: And they were led down there to the graves, and they were all going to be shot. A cannon [machine gun?] was erected, and they were going to shoot them all. So these two young men had escaped. They succeeded [there follows about 40 seconds of silence on the wire]....They made a commotion and escaped.

[00:28:06]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:28:06]
KOZLOWSKI: They arrived in the Miedzyrzec Ghetto. Then that night when the Germans came it was on New Year’s Eve...when the Germans came. So one received four bullets in the neck. And one received six bullets. And the one who received six bullets was in agony for about four hours. He tried to choke his other friend. He had gone completely out of his mind.

[00:28:26]
DAVID BODER: Hm

[00:28:27]
KOZLOWSKI: And he died. The underwear that they wore became completely red from the blood. In another bed lay a third friend who remained alive by hiding under the bed. The second one who had remained alive, who had received the four bullets, was in agony for two weeks. He had pus, and there was no doctor. Pus, [repeats in Polish] pus.

[00:28:48]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:28:48]
KOZLOWSKI: ...in the neck.

[00:28:49]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:28:49]
KOZLOWSKI: And I myself bandaged him.

[00:28:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:28:52]
KOZLOWSKI: The bullets were inside.

[00:28:55]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:28:56]
KOZLOWSKI: He had pus in the neck, and he lay so long till there appeared white snakes [worms] on the neck. Snakes had appeared.

[00:29:01]
DAVID BODER: Worms.

[00:29:02]
KOZLOWSKI: Worms which smelled bad. And he was pleading for death, to be shot. And so I and some other girl were there, a friend of mine. We covered the mouth and the nose so as not to smell. We took off the bandage and took off the snakes. Then it became a little easier for him. The same day, in the afternoon, he died. He died. I was there for a time in the Ghetto, and I lived through another deportation. There was a large synagogue. There all the Jews were assembled. In the synagogue it was terrible. They simply came in...if they heard a cry, they shot in. The threw grenades. They beat. They truck. They did not give anything to drink. We had to relieve ourselves on the same place where we slept. I was there a whole night. I saw it was bad. I did not want to go to death. I went on fighting against it. I went over to a window. It was on the first floor. We took two towels, I and another girl. We lowered the towels from the windows, and we crawled down and escaped down into a cellar, and there we again lived through the second [other] deportation.

[00:30:16]
DAVID BODER: From the second floor?

[00:30:17]
KOZLOWSKI: From the first floor.

[00:30:18]
DAVID BODER: Aha, from the first...

[00:30:19]
KOZLOWSKI: Lowered ourselves down...

[00:30:19]
DAVID BODER: That is really the second [floor], one flight upstairs [the story above the ground floor is considered in Europe as the first floor].

[00:30:21]
KOZLOWSKI: Yes.

[00:30:22]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:30:22]
KOZLOWSKI: The second [floor].

[00:30:23]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:30:23]
KOZLOWSKI: And we lowered ourselves down and hid in a cellar. It did not last four weeks any more. It only lasted three days, and then we went out again. Again we lived [there] a few months. During the last deportation I was not able to hide any more. I was led away into a transport. It was a beautiful summer day. It was very beautiful. It was May Day, May.

[00:30:46]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:30:47]
KOZLOWSKI: We were led away in the year ’43 in May. We were loaded on RR-cars. We were led through the streets exactly like we had been driven to Treblinka.
