DAVID BODER: To bring you over?

[01:04:53]
NELLY BONDY: To bring my...to bring me over. Well, the next day she came to fetch me and just the morning of this day—it was in the afternoon when she came to fetch me—but in the morning the Russians had arrived there.

[01:05:02]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:05:03]
NELLY BONDY: And now there was a Russian guard...Russian...

[01:05:05]
DAVID BODER: Guard on this side?

[01:05:05]
NELLY BONDY: . . . guard on this side of the bridge. He told me that I needed a Russian authorization. I was...and I said...ah...I didn’t take...pay any heed to him. I said I was ordered, was sick and I had an American authorization [?].

[01:05:17]
DAVID BODER: What language did he talk?

[01:05:18]
NELLY BONDY: Russian. Well, he...I made myself understood, the French.

[01:05:21]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:05:23]
NELLY BONDY: Well, I got over and they put me off to a hospital there immediately; and three or four days there was a French prisoner who was making lists for French people and...ah...she took my name down and a few days later I was sent to Leipzig and...sent back to France.

[01:05:39]
DAVID BODER: Ja...tell me about your husband.

[01:05:46]
NELLY BONDY: My husband was a Czech subject. He had been...he had engaged himself as a volunteer at the beginning of the war. One we—...one week after the...

[01:05:56]
DAVID BODER: Did you marry him [in] Vienna?

[01:05:57]
NELLY BONDY: Well, yes. He was living in Paris since ’26, but he came to Vienna for the...for the marriage—just for the wedding ceremony.

[01:06:04]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:06:05]
NELLY BONDY: Then we left Vienna.

[01:06:05]
DAVID BODER: You knew him before?

[01:06:07]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. I had known him when I had been in Paris previously in ’35.

[01:06:11]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:06:14]
NELLY BONDY: We...when he had been...he had to be called to the colors in...ah...January ’40; and he had been discharged from the army in September ’40. Then we went back to Paris.

[01:06:30]
DAVID BODER: Why was he discharged?

[01:06:32]
NELLY BONDY: Well, the war was over.

[01:06:33]
DAVID BODER: The armistice? The...

[01:06:34]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. The armistice.

[01:06:34]
DAVID BODER: Ja...this arranged armistice.

[01:06:35]
NELLY BONDY: Yes, that’s right.

[01:06:37]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:06:38]
NELLY BONDY: In...ah...April, ’41, our third child was born and four weeks later he was...

[01:06:46]
DAVID BODER: Which child was born, the fourth one?

[01:06:47]
NELLY BONDY: Our youngest child. He was...

[01:06:48]
DAVID BODER: That’s the third or the fourth?

[01:06:49]
NELLY BONDY: Third. Yes, we had a little boy.

[01:06:51]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:06:52]
NELLY BONDY: Four weeks later he was arrested and he never returned to Paris. He had...he was kept in a camp near Orleans which was before [?]; and he was sent...ah...depor—...he was deported to an unknown destination thirteen months later. That was in June of ’42. I never had any news from him, but when I came to Auschwitz myself—I was working in the so-called Politische Abteilung, that was the administration of the camp, and I found his file card and I found that [he] had been...[pause]

[01:07:27]
DAVID BODER: When you were at Auschwitz, you say?

[01:07:29]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. When I was in Auschwitz I worked in the so-called Politsche Abteilung, that was part of the administration of the camp, I found out by his file card that he had been, three months after his arrival, killed by a guard, in ’42.

[01:07:44]
DAVID BODER: Did they say why or what, or...?

[01:07:46]
NELLY BONDY: Nothing.

[01:07:49]
DAVID BODER: Eh...now tell me. You were in Auschwitz in the office?

[01:07:54]
NELLY BONDY: Yes.

[01:07:55]
DAVID BODER: Did you know then at all these gassing and...ah...so on procedures?

[01:08:00]
NELLY BONDY: Yes, I did.

[01:08:00]
DAVID BODER: What did you know about it?

[01:08:02]
NELLY BONDY: Well, officially everything was kept secret.

[01:08:05]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[01:08:06]
NELLY BONDY: But of course, we knew because...ah...before selections were made we got the lists.

[01:08:12]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:08:13]
NELLY BONDY: And we made out the lists. We were taking out a file card on everybody and marking his death even before he was dead.

[01:08:20]
DAVID BODER: Oh, that...ah...and what did they call it officially there?

[01:08:25]
NELLY BONDY: Pardon?

[01:08:26]
DAVID BODER: What did the Germans call such a procedure? So what will they...they would say to make out a list and take out a card. Wofur? Wozu?

[01:08:35]
NELLY BONDY: Well, we never were...ah...su—...supposed to ask any questions. They told us...

[01:08:39]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:08:39]
NELLY BONDY: . . . do that and do that and we had to do it. Everybody knew why, but...ah...they weren’t given any reason.

[01:08:43]
DAVID BODER: And what would you...so when you found your husband’s card what did it say?

[01:08:47]
NELLY BONDY: Well, he was already dead.

[01:08:49]
DAVID BODER: What did it say?

[01:08:50]
NELLY BONDY: It was said that he had died on that and that date.

[01:08:54]
DAVID BODER: Hm...

[01:08:54]
NELLY BONDY: But...as we knew that there was a big selection on this day...

[01:08:59]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:08:59]
NELLY BONDY: . . . so we...we knew about that.

[01:09:00]
DAVID BODER: Um-hum...

[01:09:01]
NELLY BONDY: By the by, they burned all these cards...ah...you see.

[01:09:04]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:09:05]
NELLY BONDY: They...they burned the cards when...after a certain fire. My husband’s file card was still there in...ah...in July ’43; but it was no more there in October ’43.

[01:09:16]
DAVID BODER: They would pick out the cards and...

[01:09:17]
NELLY BONDY: They would take out the cards by and by and burn them...officially they were sent to Birkenau, but...

[01:09:23]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:09:23]
NELLY BONDY: . . . they were burned.

[01:09:25]
DAVID BODER: Were you somewhere near those crematories in Auschwitz?

[01:09:29]
NELLY BONDY: Well, we had one quite near our office; but it didn’t work anymore when I came there. It had been working there before, and it...ah...the chimney was taken away during my time.

[01:09:38]
DAVID BODER: Why?

[01:09:40]
NELLY BONDY: I don’t know exactly, but I suppose they wanted to leave as few traces as possible.

[01:09:45]
DAVID BODER: Aha...

[01:09:47]
NELLY BONDY: The...these killings by gas were supposed to stop altogether since...ah...October or November ’44. I couldn’t tell you exactly if they really did, but...ah...lots of these chimneys were taken away at that time, even the chimneys in Birkenau.

[01:10:05]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, there is one thing that is so...ah...ah...cloudy and maybe you worked...having worked in an office you know...eh. What do they say about the Gypsies—the Zigeuner?

[01:10:20]
NELLY BONDY: Well, the Gypsies...ah...were considered the...the worst...ah...inhabitants after the Jews.

[01:10:29]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:10:30]
NELLY BONDY: You see, there were certain...certain...hierarchive [hierarchy].

[01:10:33]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Gra—...gradua—...gradation.

[01:10:35]
NELLY BONDY: “Graduation.” Yes. Well, the lowest...the lowest case were the Jews. Then came the Gypsies.

[01:10:40]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:10:40]
NELLY BONDY: Then came the...the Poles or so...well, all people who were not German. Then came the so-called antisocial or asocial German inmates.

[01:10:52]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:10:53]
NELLY BONDY: And the political prisoners.

[01:10:54]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Well, so what about the Gypsies?

[01:10:57]
NELLY BONDY: Well, the Gypsies were not treated much better than the Jews. There was a so-called...ah...family camp for Gypsies; but the Gypsies were killed by gas...ah...exactly as Jews.

[01:11:07]
DAVID BODER: Eh...they permitted the Gypsies to live together—the men and the women?

[01:11:11]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. Men and women and children lived together in one big camp in Birkenau. But the camp dissolved and they sent away the part of young men and young Gypsies to other camps for...I suppose they’d se—...they sent them to work in a...in a war factories.

[01:11:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[01:11:28]
NELLY BONDY: Ammunition factories or so.

[01:11:30]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[01:11:31]
NELLY BONDY: And the others were killed.

[01:11:32]
DAVID BODER: The others were killed...

[01:11:33]
NELLY BONDY: Yes.

[01:11:34]
DAVID BODER: There was no Zigeunerlager in...ah...Auschwitz?

[01:11:36]
NELLY BONDY: Yes, a Zigeunerlager.

[01:11:37]
DAVID BODER: There was in Auschwitz a Zigeunerlager?

[01:11:38]
NELLY BONDY: In...ah...in Birkenau.

[01:11:40]
DAVID BODER: In Birkenau there was a Zigeunerlager?

[01:11:41]
NELLY BONDY: Yes.

[01:11:43]
DAVID BODER: So that’s what you know about them. Where did they get all those Gy—...Gypsies?

[01:11:46]
NELLY BONDY: Well, they picked them up exactly as they captured Jews...the Jews.

[01:11:50]
DAVID BODER: And were there that many? Well, did they get them from Austria, from...

[01:11:53]
NELLY BONDY: From Austria, yes. From Germany. From all over the...the...the German-occupied Europe.

[01:11:59]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:11:59]
NELLY BONDY: There were Romanian and Italian and Hungarian and Slovakian and all kinds of nationalities.

[01:12:04]
DAVID BODER: Hm...how old are your children now, Miss...Mrs. Bondy?

[01:12:07]
NELLY BONDY: Well, I have a daughter who’s nine, and two boys, of seven and five years.

[01:12:11]
DAVID BODER: And where are they now?

[01:12:12]
NELLY BONDY: They are in the center of France...ah...where they have stayed ever since I was deported.

[01:12:17]
DAVID BODER: Aha...eh...do you go visit them, or what?

[01:12:20]
NELLY BONDY: I go to see them sometime, but it’s rather far from Paris. I...I wish to take them back to Paris but till this day I didn’t...get my flat back. We had a big flat before...

[01:12:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:12:32]
NELLY BONDY: And...ah...it’s occupied now and I couldn’t get it back.

[01:12:36]
DAVID BODER: How...

[01:12:36]
NELLY BONDY: I have been back for more than a year and I...I can’t get in.

[01:12:39]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, why...who lives there?

[01:12:42]
NELLY BONDY: There is a man who was once a prisoner in Germany.

[01:12:46]
DAVID BODER: Yes...

[01:12:46]
NELLY BONDY: He came back in ’42 and fought the Free [?] and he has a military requisition.

[01:12:51]
DAVID BODER: Ah...

[01:12:52]
NELLY BONDY: And...ah...even though this requisition have...ah...no more sense now the war being over...

[01:12:58]
DAVID BODER: No more value.

[01:12:59]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. I can’t get him out.

[01:13:01]
DAVID BODER: And...eh...that is why you can’t bring your children over?

[01:13:04]
NELLY BONDY: That’s why I can’t bring my children back with me to Paris; and they need it very badly because they’re in a...quite a small place where there is no good school. My daughter is nine years [?]. She ought to speak a second language by now...by now; and...ah...no kind of education and nothing at all. I’m very worried about her.

[01:13:21]
DAVID BODER: Eh...tell me...ah...you are here with the...with the Joint Distribution Committee?

[01:13:27]
NELLY BONDY: Yes, I work with...

[01:13:28]
DAVID BODER: How did you find them; to work for them?

[01:13:32]
NELLY BONDY: I knew a lady who was working for the Joint and I had met her once in...in these critical days in ’42 when we...everybody was trembling to be arrested. She just came to see me. She was a friend of my governess.

[01:13:46]
DAVID BODER: Hm...

[01:13:47]
NELLY BONDY: And she was working here, and when I came back to my governess I got in touch with her, and she...eh...she got me here.

[01:13:52]
DAVID BODER: Your governess was never deported?

[01:13:54]
NELLY BONDY: No, she slipped through.

[01:13:56]
DAVID BODER: She lived through.

[01:13:57]
NELLY BONDY: But was very...she was awfully kind as well as [?]...it was very lucky for me because she took care of the children, really as if they had been hers.

[01:14:05]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Tell me, Mrs. Bondy, you were...since you were near the...ah...Nazi now and then in the office, what were they talking? Did they believe they will win the war and all that?

[01:14:17]
NELLY BONDY: I don’t think they did. Finally they did not. They were supposed to make us believe that they would win the war, and I remember after the...the Americans had come to Paris that...ah...

[01:14:30]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:14:31]
NELLY BONDY: . . . they told us that the Germans had...ah...had...ah...blown up half of the city. And he even told me the different quarters which had been blown up. He talk—...he talked about the Republique...the Quarter of the Republique, the Quarter of the Opera.

[01:14:44]
DAVID BODER: Where did they talk about it, in Auschwitz?

[01:14:46]
NELLY BONDY: In Auschwitz. He told me that all these quarters in Paris had been blown up by the Germans before they left.

[01:14:50]
DAVID BODER: Aha...

[01:14:51]
NELLY BONDY: So we...

[01:14:51]
DAVID BODER: So in Auschwitz they knew already that the Germans had left Paris?

[01:14:53]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. It was in...in August or September, ’44.

[01:14:56]
DAVID BODER: And that they were talking freely; so you knew what was going on.

[01:14:59]
NELLY BONDY: Well, we knew. You see, we...we knew what was going on. Some of the girls were working with high officers who had broadcastings in their rooms so sometime they manage to hear.

[01:15:07]
DAVID BODER: Eh...to...radio sets in there?

[01:15:09]
NELLY BONDY: Yes.

[01:15:09]
DAVID BODER: Ja...some of them managed to hear it.

[01:15:11]
NELLY BONDY: Managed to hear. Yes. They were never supposed to listen because it was...ah...

[01:15:15]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:15:15]
NELLY BONDY: . . . prohibited.

[01:15:15]
DAVID BODER: High treason?

[01:15:17]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. Everything was verboten.

[01:15:20]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, in general...did the women fare who had to work with the Nazis? How did they behave...behave towards women?

[01:15:29]
NELLY BONDY: Well, they didn’t behave very well, I’m sorry to say. That’s to say, they made an exception for us who were working with them. They behaved fairly well. Of course, if they had an occasion they got drunk even if we were there or not. That was a different kind of thing; but on a general scale they treated us...ah...like machines, like automatons, you see.

[01:15:51]
DAVID BODER: Ja...

[01:15:52]
NELLY BONDY: “Do this and do that,” and...

[01:15:53]
DAVID BODER: What did they call you?

[01:15:55]
NELLY BONDY: They called us with our names.

[01:15:55]
DAVID BODER: Did they call you “Clara” [?] ?

[01:15:56]
NELLY BONDY: No, they called me “Bondy.”

[01:15:58]
DAVID BODER: Bondy. By the...by the last name.

[01:16:01]
NELLY BONDY: Yes. Some of the girls they called by their first names.

[01:16:04]
DAVID BODER: Aha...well, Mrs. Bondy, it was awfully good of you.

[01:16:09]
NELLY BONDY: Well, I...

[01:16:10]
DAVID BODER: I think it was worthwhile to trouble here with electricity. I will have a bill for a broken lamp.

[01:16:16]
NELLY BONDY: Oh, I’m sorry!

[01:16:17]
DAVID BODER: But that was...[laughing] well, that’s all right. We will charge it to research; and it was awfully good of you. I’m glad I have met you.

[01:16:24]
NELLY BONDY: Oh, that’s OK.

[01:16:25]
DAVID BODER: Thank you very much. See that you get me somebody else.

[01:16:28]
NELLY BONDY: That’s all right [?]. Somebody else? From Auschwitz I haven’t got ...

[01:16:31]
DAVID BODER: Well, Auschwitz or some other place.

[01:16:33]
NELLY BONDY: All right [?] .

[01:16:35]
DAVID BODER: Eh, this concludes...Spool...61...taken at the...headquarters of the Joint Distribution Committee on August 22nd, 1946, in Paris. A Illinois Institute of Technology wire recording.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Pinkhus Rosenfeld
entries.content:
[00:00:00] David Boder: This is Spool 9-130B, Mr. Pinkhus Rosenfeld, interviewed at Hénonville, France—Hénonville near Paris. November 7th, 1950, Boder. [00:01:00] David Boder: Paris, September 13, 1946. Hénonville, a suburb of Paris, in a home of Jewish displaced people. The interviewee is Mr. Pinkhus Rosenfeld who lives himself in Paris but has children here in the...in the Kibbutz. [00:01:23] David Boder: And so, Mr. Rosenfeld, tell me your full name and where you were born. [00:01:32] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Pinkhus Rosenfeld, born in Lodz. [00:01:35] David Boder: How old are you, Mr. Rosenfeld? [00:01:36] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: On the second [day] of the first [month, January], 1903. [00:01:39] David Boder: Then you are now forty-three years old, isn’t that so? [00:01:41] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Yes. [00:01:42] David Boder: And so tell me, you are living in Paris now? [00:01:46] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I have been living in Paris now for three weeks. [00:01:49] David Boder: Aha, and what are you doing there? [00:01:52] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: What...I am looking for possibilities of going to Palestine where I have my own home... [00:01:58] David Boder: Yes. [00:01:58] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . and also a house that my father has there. [00:02:00] David Boder: Yes? [00:02:01] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And, alas, I cannot go there. I am [words not clear]. I am navanat... [00:02:07] David Boder: Hm. [00:02:08] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . all the time. [00:02:09] David Boder: And...and what beziehung [connection] do you have here with this kibbutz in Hénonville? [00:02:15] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: What does beziehung mean? [00:02:16] David Boder: I mean, I see you here, you are here. [00:02:19] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I have here two children who were also with me all the time. [00:02:22] David Boder: Aha. [00:02:23] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I am not able to maintain them in Paris. I cannot afford to live in Paris, so that... [00:02:29] David Boder: Hm. [00:02:30] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . I have placed them in the kibbutz, and they have a very happy life. [00:02:31] David Boder: And your wife is where? [00:02:34] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: My wife, alas, perished in Auschwitz. [00:02:37] David Boder: Hm. So who looks after the children here? [00:02:40] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: They themselves. [00:02:42] David Boder: What? [00:02:42] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Themselves. They are... [00:02:43] David Boder: How old are they? [00:02:43] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . grown up children. [00:02:44] David Boder: Oh. [00:02:44] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Nineteen and twenty-one years. [00:02:45] David Boder: What are they, boys, girls? [00:02:47] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Two boys. Two... [00:02:48] David Boder: Two... [00:02:49] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I had girls. They perished in the Warsaw Ghetto. [00:02:52] David Boder: In the Warsaw Ghetto. [00:02:53] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Yes. [Words not clear.] [00:02:55] David Boder: And so, Mr. Rosenfeld, will you please tell me where you were when the war started and the main events that happened to you? Take your time. You can talk as much as you want. Go on. [00:03:10] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: the war started, I was in Lodz. [00:03:14] David Boder: Hm. [00:03:17] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And then it happened. On the night of the 5th and 6th of September... [00:03:23] David Boder: Yes? [00:03:24] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . we were running. [00:03:27] David Boder: Why were people running? [00:03:28] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Because we had heard that the German is arriving, and the fear immediately brought great panic [?] so that at once we were running. We did not know where, what, or when. We did not take under consideration that the German army with its mechanization, with all its technique, that it will run faster than we, but the fear moved us to run. Thus, we are running until today. It is already seven years. Today is exactly seven years since the war started, and we are still running. [00:03:56] David Boder: And so, Mr. Rosenfeld, give it to me one thing at a time, in details. Where did you go from Lodz? What was your occupation in Lodz? [00:04:03] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: In Lodz I was a textile manufacturer. We had our own factory in Zdunska Wola. [00:04:08] David Boder: Aha. Tell me...[you had] a textile business. Did you know the Sigmunds [mispronounced Sigman] in Lodz, from Chicago? They had a big textile factory. [Pause.] Sigmund [Sigman]. [00:04:19] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Sigmund in the texti-...no. [00:04:21] David Boder: No, and so, nu, you had what sort of business, a factory? [00:04:26] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: We had a factory. [00:04:27] David Boder: Who is the we? [00:04:28] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Rosenfeld and Patovski was [the name of] the firm. [00:04:31] David Boder: Aha. [00:04:32] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And we had the factory... [00:04:34] David Boder: Is it not the Patovski of whom one is in New York? [00:04:39] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I would not know. [00:04:41] David Boder: You would not know. And so, go on. [Pause.] Now, where did you run? What did you take along? [00:04:48] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: We took along a little money in the pocket. The rest we left, everything unguarded, and we ran. Finally we saw on the road that the Germans have come ahead of us. [00:05:01] David Boder: Nu? [00:05:03] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And we began to reflect that our running was totally useless, so we turned around and we came back to Lodz. [00:05:13] David Boder: Back to Lodz? [00:05:13] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Back to Lodz. [00:05:15] David Boder: Yes, nu? [00:05:17] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Nu, naturally in Lodz we were already met at certain points by the Germans, and the local folk-Germans [Poles who claimed German ancestry]... [00:05:26] David Boder: Hm. [00:05:26] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . the so-called Poles, and we were at once cleaned up. They took away everything we had, the little money. Now we were already completely without anything. [00:05:37] David Boder: Hm. [00:05:40] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Afterwards happened the story that Lodz was incorporated by the German into the Reich. [00:05:46] David Boder: Oh. [00:05:48] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And there began to happen all the calamaties, with dragging for labor and with going to work, and the summons to the Gestapo, so that my father, as an elderly man, decided that he will leave Lodz. Because I am only...my only desire is to be able to go to Eretz Yisroeil, and there I will already live through my years. [00:47:03] David Boder: Why don’t you eat meat all week? [00:47:05] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: That is very simple, because there is none. [00:47:09] David Boder: One has no means? [00:47:11] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: One has no financial means. There are none. In the German lager there is still an UNRRA. There still is... [00:47:15] David Boder: You say that you are getting rent in Palestine. Can’t they send the money from there? Pardon me for asking that. [00:47:22] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: You have a perfect right and you are completely in order. I must explain to you this, that the English made a law... [00:47:28] David Boder: Oh. [00:47:29] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: . . . that all those who are there...that means, the property of enemy aliens, of people who are not there, all that reverted under the [control of] English government. [00:47:38] David Boder: But it is deposited. It is being kept for you. [00:47:39] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Everything is being kept there and deposited. [00:47:43] David Boder: What sort of enemy alien are you? [00:47:45] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I do not know. That is how it was. It seems that Jews are enemies, because all that was...in the end it is not just for enemy aliens. Later it was done because all the heirs were not there, because there are huge estates to which there are no claimants, so the government took it all away [over]. [00:48:01] David Boder: In Palestine? [00:48:02] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: In Palestine, yes. Up to now I was in Germany in a lager [DP] camp and had no chance whatsoever to communicate. It was very hard. They did not...all languages were... [00:48:09] David Boder: Were you there in the [DP] camp with the children? [00:48:10] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I was, yes. [00:48:11] David Boder: In which one? [00:48:12] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: In Landsberg. A whole year. [00:48:14] David Boder: Yes. After the liberation. [00:48:16] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: After the liberation. Where we were maintained by the UNRRA. [00:48:19] David Boder: Yes? [00:48:19] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I could not send mail to Eretz Yisroeil. I must mention that this is also an unheard of wrong. [00:48:25] David Boder: Yes? [00:48:26] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Letters can be sent in English, in French, in Russian, and in Polish, but Yiddish letters cannot be written [sent]. And so I had... [00:48:33] David Boder: [00:48:34] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: To Palestine. [00:48:35] David Boder: From the American zone? [00:48:37] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: From the American zone. [This seems incorrect. Refers possibly to telegrams.] [00:48:38] David Boder: The Americans have no Jewish censors? [00:48:40] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: That’s how it is. And so I am affirming it as a fact. [00:48:44] David Boder: Yes? Nu? [00:48:45] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: That one cannot write in Yiddish. [00:48:47] David Boder: And this is still until today? [00:48:48] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: This is still until today. I left...until three weks ago one could not write in Yiddish [?]. [00:48:53] David Boder: From Landsberg. [00:48:53] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: From Landsberg. Just these four languages. English, French and German and Polish. [00:49:01] David Boder: Polish. Nu? [00:49:04] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Nu, I began to correspond. [00:49:07] David Boder: With Palestine. [00:49:08] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: With Palestine. So that I am...so that... [00:49:10] David Boder: Did you enter France legally? [00:49:12] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I entered France legally. [Words not clear.] [00:49:16] David Boder: Yes. Nu? [00:49:18] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: But, unfortunately, I am sorry that I came too late. If I had come earlier I would have been able to enter with the Aliyah B. Today I hear people are going to Cyprus, but I must say that my... [00:49:29] David Boder: The Aliyah B is the underground Aliyah. [00:49:31] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Yes. The under...the so-called illegal Aliyah. [00:49:34] David Boder: Yes. Nu? [00:49:37] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: So that I myself, I cannot decide whether to go to Cyprus. The children do not want to stay here. They say even to Cyprus they want to go. And so, in any case, I want to return to your question. [00:49:48] David Boder: Cyprus or no Cyprus, they want to go. [00:49:50] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Yes. [00:49:51] David Boder: Yes? [00:49:51] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: In any case...because to suffer hunger here—it makes no difference to them. Let it be Cyprus as long as it is near Eretz Yisroeil. They think there they will be closer. In any case I want to return to your question. You asked that if having there such an estate which before the war brought in around seven hundred pounds per year, why I should suffer hunger here. [00:50:07] David Boder: Yes. [00:50:07] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I am explaining to you that it is for the reason that it was frozen, my estate, and that is why I have no means. And I am not let in either, so that I am now in a completely desperate situation. [00:50:20] David Boder: And so, you see then that everyone has a different story. [00:50:24] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Naturally. Everyone has different troubles, and everyone has a different story. [00:50:33] David Boder: And what do you now in Paris? Do you talk with the English? Do you try to do something? [00:50:39] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: There are many people arriving from Eretz Yisroeil. I think that if someone will be able...I plead that perhaps my account may be opened. I want to do it through a notary, that I am here with two children, that something should be given to me to live on from my estate. [00:50:39] David Boder: [00:50:54] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And I do not have an answer yet. And then, it is only three weeks since I have come to Paris. [00:51:00] David Boder: Hm. And you are staying in Paris and the children are staying here? [00:51:02] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: And the children are here. [00:51:02] David Boder: What is the name of the Kibbutz here? [00:51:06] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Hénonville. [00:51:07] David Boder: No, no, no, I mean the Kibbutz. [00:51:11] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: What the name is? [00:51:12] David Boder: The Kibbutz has a name. [00:51:13] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Neizach Yisroeil. [00:51:15] David Boder: Hm, the Neizach Yisroeil. And have you always been a Hassid? [00:51:19] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I always have been a Hassid. I come from Hassidic parents, and I remain a Hassidic Jew, and will go on bringing up my children as Hassidic Jewish children. [00:51:28] David Boder: And so, Mr. Rosenfeld, I thank you very much. You have given me a very good report, and I am convinced it will do something for us all. [00:51:42] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: But I want to ask you again... [00:51:44] David Boder: Hm. [00:51:44] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: I want to ask you to talk to the Jewish commonwealth [Klal Yisroeil], that they should all see...we are tormented here greatly. And we are suffering. We have no housing and we have no food. We have nothing. The situation has not improved much over the German times, but this, especially, I must... [00:52:01] David Boder: Come, come... [00:52:03] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Nu, naturally we are not under SS men. [00:52:05] David Boder: You do not tremble for your life. [00:52:07] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: We do not tremble for our lives, but we do not have the proper nourishment. We are undernourished. You have to know that five, six, seven years we were undernourished. Today we should be fed a little better, and we do not have it. Moreover, I am a man who has such a fortune in Eretz Yisroeil. I am sure I do not have to be a burden to anyone. Why must I have to suffer here? [00:52:29] David Boder: Nu, you will pay it back someday [that is, what you receive from charity]. You will give it back. You don’t have to worry over it. [00:52:37] Pinkhus Rosenfeld: Nu, but in the meantime... [00:52:41] David Boder: Hm. And so, one has to view things from all sides. Maybe this little story will contribute a bit of truth to the whole situation. And so... [00:52:55] David Boder: Hénonville, September the 13th, 1946, near Paris.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Rita Benmayor
entries.content:
[00:00:00]
DAVID BODER: This is Spool 27 of the collection of Illinois Institute of Technology, taken in Paris on August the 5th, on 9 Rue Guy Patin, a home for adult displaced people, especially Jews. The interviewee is, eh, Miss Rita Benmayor, eh, age twenty, from Jewish Greek, from Saloniki? From Saloniki. Eh, she carries on her left arm a tattoo number, 38758, underneath a little triangle, indicating her Jewish descent.

[00:00:52]
DAVID BODER: Now tell me, Mrs., eh, Miss, eh, Benmayor, eh, where were you born, who is your family, and how many were in your family, and what were your parents doing?

[00:01:08]
RITA BENMAYOR: I was born in Greece, and in ’43, in ’43 the Germans came to Greece, they took the whole family.

[00:01:20]
DAVID BODER: Yes—how many people were in your family?

[00:01:23]
RITA BENMAYOR: My family, was five people.

[00:01:25]
DAVID BODER: Five people, who were they, you say?

[00:01:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: My father, mother and two brothers and I.

[00:01:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes, now—where are now your father and your mother?

[00:01:34]
RITA BENMAYOR: My father, my mother were deported, and the whole family was in the crematorium, was in the crematorium, all died.

[00:01:42]
DAVID BODER: Eh, your two brothers, too?

[00:01:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: My two brothers, too.

[00:01:46]
DAVID BODER: And?

[00:01:47]
RITA BENMAYOR: I am left alone from the whole family.

[00:01:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes, so—say, when the Germans came in ’42 [sic], how old was your father?

[00:01:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: My father was forty years old.

[00:01:58]
DAVID BODER: And your mother?

[00:01:59]
RITA BENMAYOR: My mother was thirty-eight years.

[00:02:01]
DAVID BODER: And the two brothers?

[00:02:03]
RITA BENMAYOR: Two brothers, one twenty-five and one eighteen years old.

[00:02:06]
DAVID BODER: Were you—and how, how old were you?

[00:02:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: I was sixteen years.

[00:02:12]
DAVID BODER: Your were sixteen—now, and were your brothers married?

[00:02:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: The one was married and the other was not married.

[00:02:19]
DAVID BODER: . . . was not married—and where is, eh, the wife of the married brother?

[00:02:24]
RITA BENMAYOR: The wife of the married brother was also in the crematorium, she had small children and was in the crematorium.

[00:02:30]
DAVID BODER: She had—oh, she had a little child?

[00:02:33]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, she had many little child[ren]...

[00:02:34]
DAVID BODER: How many?

[00:02:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: Four.

[00:02:36]
DAVID BODER: She had four little children?

[00:02:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: She was four...

[00:02:39]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:02:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: Four.

[00:02:41]
DAVID BODER: Now, tell me, eh, your whole story, where did your brother, your married brother, with his wife—did he live with you, or did he live by himself?

[00:02:52]
RITA BENMAYOR: He lived with yours.

[00:02:54]
DAVID BODER: What, he lived for himself—tell me—lived for himself?

[00:02:57]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:02:58]
DAVID BODER: So tell me, you lived in Saloniki?

[00:03:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:03:03]
David Boder: Yes, speak louder, and please speak into this direction [?]. Well now, so then: the Germans came to Saloniki, what did they order there and what did they do there?

[00:03:13]
RITA BENMAYOR: When the Germans came Saloniki, that was good [?] you...

[00:03:17]
DAVID BODER: Aha...

[00:03:17]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . and then in ’43—’42...

[00:03:20]
DAVID BODER: Aha, yes...

[00:03:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . and then in ’43 the Gestapo came and took all Jews.

[00:03:24]
DAVID BODER: They took all Jews—where did they take them?

[00:03:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: It was two o’clock at night, came to the house, and took the whole family.

[00:03:33]
DAVID BODER: And where did one take you?

[00:03:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, brought [us] to Auschwitz.

[00:03:37]
DAVID BODER: Well now, right from the house, where did they take you, to the, eh, station?

[00:03:43]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . to the station of Saloniki.

[00:03:46]
DAVID BODER: Well, say, one came at two o’clock at night—and where did one take you, directly from the house...

[00:03:53]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . from home...

[00:03:54]
DAVID BODER: . . . from home...

[00:03:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . from home took the whole family and—

[00:03:57]
DAVID BODER: . . . and has...

[00:03:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . and was in the station in a railway car...and [there] were seventy-two people in the car...

[00:04:04]
DAVID BODER: Yes, what was that, a passenger car, or a, eh...a, eh...goods...a eh—freight car...

[00:04:11]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, eh, car...

[00:04:12]
DAVID BODER: . . . a freight car—were there benches to sit on in the car?

[00:04:17]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, [one] sat down...

[00:04:17]
DAVID BODER: One sat on the floor...

[00:04:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . sat, yes...

[00:04:20]
DAVID BODER: Was there, eh, a toilet- was there a commode?

[00:04:23]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, there was a bucket...

[00:04:25]
DAVID BODER: There was a bucket there...

[00:04:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . a bucket...

[00:04:28]
DAVID BODER: And were men and women together in the car?

[00:04:31]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, [there] were seventy-two people, men and women, little children, all together.

[00:04:35]
DAVID BODER: . . . and little—yes. Now, and what was said, where would you be taken?

[00:04:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: said, all go to Poland, and all Jews [would be] together.

[00:04:44]
DAVID BODER: All Jews together...

[00:04:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: But [we] did not know what was done...

[00:04:47]
DAVID BODER: You did not know.

[00:04:48]
RITA BENMAYOR: We did not know.

[00:04:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes—so...and so you rode, how long did you ride?

[00:04:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . eh...

[00:04:54]
DAVID BODER: . . . from Saloniki on the train, how long did you ride?

[00:04:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: Eight days...

[00:04:59]
DAVID BODER: You were eight days...

[00:04:59]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . [after] eight days, we came to Auschwitz, were in Auschwitz.

[00:05:02]
DAVID BODER: . . . came to Auschwitz—what happened there in Auschwitz?

[00:05:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . we were in Auschwitz, the Germans came, saw—the men...

[00:05:12]
DAVID BODER: . . . separated...

[00:05:13]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . separated, and the women separated...

[00:05:15]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:15]
RITA BENMAYOR: The men were taken by an automobile, soon to the crematorium. Those were the old people...

[00:05:21]
DAVID BODER: Oh, those were the old people...

[00:05:22]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . the old people soon [went] to the crematorium...and the young people were in [a] lager.

[00:05:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes—and what did they do with you?

[00:05:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: I was young, I was sixteen years, and [they] took me and all together...

[00:05:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . to work in lager, in a lager.

[00:05:38]
DAVID BODER: Yes. And, eh...

[00:05:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . my...

[00:05:40]
DAVID BODER: You came to Auschwitz together with your father and your mother?

[00:05:43]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, my...

[00:05:45]
DAVID BODER: And your fa—...yes?

[00:05:46]
RITA BENMAYOR: my mother in [the] car, go into a car—why, they were old—and my father also in the car, soon [to be] brought to the crematorium...

[00:05:55]
DAVID BODER: Good, you say, your father was forty years, that is not old.

[00:05:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes. But [it] was done so...

[00:06:02]
DAVID BODER: Yes. They did that—and your brothers, eh, and your two brothers?

[00:06:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: The one brother I did not know all...and the other one was also in another camp.

[00:06:12]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:06:12]
RITA BENMAYOR: And goes free...

[00:06:14]
DAVID BODER: Oh, and he became free, liberated?

[00:06:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . became liberated.

[00:06:17]
DAVID BODER: And where is he now?

[00:06:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: Now he is in Palestine.

[00:06:20]
DAVID BODER: In Palestine?

[00:06:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:06:21]
DAVID BODER: How did he get there?

[00:06:22]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . .

[00:06:25]
DAVID BODER: Without permit. Please speak into here...

[00:06:29]
RITA BENMAYOR: Without permit...

[00:06:30]
DAVID BODER: . . . just went there and got in?

[00:06:33]
RITA BENMAYOR: When [he] was freed, he was in Greece, searched for the family. He knew the whole family...

[00:06:40]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:06:40]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . nobody—and he [went to] Palestine.

[00:06:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and he is—did he write you from Palestine?

[00:06:47]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, he did...back, he, er, yes.

[00:06:50]
DAVID BODER: Did he write you?

[00:06:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:06:52]
DAVID BODER: You know that he is there?

[00:06:53]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:06:53]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and, er...now, and so you stayed in the camp, what did they do to you in the camp?

[00:07:01]
RITA BENMAYOR: Me?

[00:07:02]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: When I was in the camp, the Germans took [me] and had all my hair c—...

[00:07:07]
DAVID BODER: They cut all your hair off.

[00:07:09]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . cut.

[00:07:10]
DAVID BODER: She now has a wonderful head of hair, that she says that her hair will—was cut off entirely.

[00:07:16]
DAVID BODER: Now, they cut your hair off, and then?

[00:07:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: Cut the hair, took all clothes.

[00:07:25]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: Gave me male clothes.

[00:07:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes, male clothing?

[00:07:28]
RITA BENMAYOR: Male clothing, yes.

[00:07:28]
DAVID BODER: Yes, a men’s outfit—pants, too?

[00:07:29]
RITA BENMAYOR: Men’s outfit, pants and jacket.

[00:07:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:31]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then I was [at] work on the road.

[00:07:33]
DAVID BODER: Work on the road?

[00:07:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: On the road.

[00:07:35]
DAVID BODER: And when did they tattoo you—when was the tattoo made?

[00:07:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: The first day when [we] came into the camp...

[00:07:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:07:43]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . that was two prisoners, who did the whole...

[00:07:47]
DAVID BODER: Yes, that did...

[00:07:48]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . made the number.

[00:07:48]
DAVID BODER: . . . made the number.

[00:07:49]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . was two men...

[00:07:49]
DAVID BODER: . . . and then, when they gave you the number, then you knew already that you would stay alive, that you...

[00:07:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: No.

[00:07:55]
DAVID BODER: Why not?

[00:07:56]
RITA BENMAYOR: Why, we got the number, but we were gaunt, all month, like—every month there was a selection.

[00:08:03]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:08:04]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . who was gaunt, who was in bad condition, all went to the crematorium, that had...

[00:08:09]
DAVID BODER: . . . that was in Auschwitz?

[00:08:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:08:10]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and, eh, why did you keep yourself healthy?

[00:08:13]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, I ate all dirt, we stole each other the bread, we did that.

[00:08:20]
DAVID BODER: What does that mean we have eaten dirt, we ate dirt?

[00:08:22]
RITA BENMAYOR: The dirt of the potato ...

[00:08:25]
DAVID BODER: The dirt from the potato you ate?

[00:08:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . the potato—I ate.

[00:08:28]
DAVID BODER: . . . and that kept you a little stronger?

[00:08:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:08:31]
DAVID BODER: And, eh, you say, further you say you took the bread away from each other?

[00:08:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, eh...

[00:08:37]
DAVID BODER: Keep on talking [please]...Yes.

[00:08:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:08:39]
DAVID BODER: Now, and what did you work? In Auschwitz?

[00:08:41]
RITA BENMAYOR: The first month, three month[s], I worked at the road, through road, eh, did stones...

[00:08:48]
DAVID BODER: You worked on stones...

[00:08:49]
RITA BENMAYOR: Stones...

[00:08:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes—now?

[00:08:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then I was in the shoe detail, I repaired shoes, I was [in] the shoe detail...

[00:08:56]
DAVID BODER: Eh, you were in the she detail?

[00:08:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: Shoe detail...

[00:08:59]
DAVID BODER: Did you learn to repair shoes?

[00:09:00]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . repair shoes.

[00:09:02]
DAVID BODER: Eh, eh, whose shoes were they?

[00:09:05]
RITA BENMAYOR: From the SS.

[00:09:07]
DAVID BODER: Oh, those were SS shoes?

[00:09:09]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . SS shoes.

[00:09:10]
DAVID BODER: Eh—have you—what did you work with, with eh, with [a] hammer, or with the machine?

[00:09:17]
RITA BENMAYOR: With arms.

[00:09:18]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:09:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: With arms.

[00:09:19]
DAVID BODER: You worked with your hands?

[00:09:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: With your hands.

[00:09:21]
DAVID BODER: And, eh, did you really learn to repair shoes?

[00:09:25]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:09:26]
DAVID BODER: Can you still do it?

[00:09:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:09:27]
DAVID BODER: You could be a shoemaker?

[00:09:28]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:09:28]
DAVID BODER: Yes, now, and...

[00:09:31]
RITA BENMAYOR: I was one year in the shoe detail.

[00:09:33]
DAVID BODER: You were a whole year in the shoe detail.

[00:09:34]
RITA BENMAYOR: A whole year in the shoe detail.

[00:09:35]
DAVID BODER: A whole year in the shoe detail.

[00:09:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:09:37]
DAVID BODER: And then, what happened then?

[00:09:40]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then, when we—when the Russians came [to] Auschwitz, we were transported to another camp...

[00:09:46]
DAVID BODER: Aha, when the Russians came to Auschwitz...

[00:09:48]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . we were transported...

[00:09:49]
DAVID BODER: You were transported to another...

[00:09:49]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . to another camp, we were in Ravensbrück.

[00:09:52]
DAVID BODER: Ravensbrück, where is that?

[00:09:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: In Germany.

[00:09:55]
DAVID BODER: That is in Germany, now tell me, how many days did your drive from Auschwitz to Ravensbrück?

[00:10:00]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, five days we went, on foot...

[00:10:05]
DAVID BODER: You went by foot for five days?

[00:10:07]
RITA BENMAYOR: Five days...

[00:10:08]
DAVID BODER: Er, eh, who, how many people walked the way?

[00:10:11]
RITA BENMAYOR: Three peop—, three hundred people.

[00:10:14]
DAVID BODER: Three hundred people, men and women?

[00:10:15]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, only women.

[00:10:16]
DAVID BODER: Only women, and who guarded you?

[00:10:20]
RITA BENMAYOR: The, eh, the guards of the SS.

[00:10:22]
DAVID BODER: The SS, were they good to you?

[00:10:24]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, who could not walk much, was quickly....

[00:10:29]
DAVID BODER: What, shot?

[00:10:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . shot.

[00:10:31]
DAVID BODER: Oh, did you see that yourself?

[00:10:33]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:10:34]
DAVID BODER: Yes, what did the...

[00:10:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: Many.

[00:10:36]
DAVID BODER: What did they do, shot them with a revolver?

[00:10:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, shot them...they shot...[?]

[00:10:41]
DAVID BODER: Ah the, the shotgun?

[00:10:42]
RITA BENMAYOR: The shotgun, yes.

[00:10:43]
DAVID BODER: Took them and shot them right there.

[00:10:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:10:45]
DAVID BODER: . . . and...

[00:10:46]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . who could walk, would walk, who could not walk, did not eat, did...

[00:10:51]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:10:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . only one [piece of] bread for four days...

[00:10:53]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:10:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . has eaten every two days, eaten the bread...

[00:10:57]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:10:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . could, could not walk, was quickly shot.

[00:11:01]
DAVID BODER: Now, and so you came from Auschwitz to where?

[00:11:05]
RITA BENMAYOR: To Ravensbrück.

[00:11:06]
DAVID BODER: You came to Ravensbrück, what did they do there?

[00:11:09]
RITA BENMAYOR: There we, eh, worked on the road again.

[00:11:13]
DAVID BODER: What, you worked on the road?

[00:11:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: Carrying stones.

[00:11:16]
DAVID BODER: Carry stones, and what, they built a road?

[00:11:18]
RITA BENMAYOR: R—, eh, yes.

[00:11:19]
DAVID BODER: Yes, now, and then?

[00:11:22]
RITA BENMAYOR: We worked there for four months, and then we were, eh...at Stucko[?] that was...

[00:11:30]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:11:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . worked in the block.

[00:11:31]
DAVID BODER: worked in the block, how many people were in the block?

[00:11:34]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . in the block were a hundred and fifty people.

[00:11:37]
DAVID BODER: One hundred and fifty people, how did you sleep in the block?

[00:11:40]
RITA BENMAYOR: ...in the...

[00:11:42]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:11:42]
RITA BENMAYOR: In the bed.

[00:11:43]
DAVID BODER: were beds, or...?

[00:11:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: were five people sleeping in one bed.

[00:11:46]
DAVID BODER: Five people in one bed?

[00:11:47]
RITA BENMAYOR: Five people in one little bed.

[00:11:48]
DAVID BODER: Eh, so, have you, eh, have you, was it clean, was it clean?

[00:11:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: Clean, yes...

[00:11:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:11:56]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, it was clean.

[00:11:59]
DAVID BODER: You were able to wash and so on—did you have lice, fleas, lice?

[00:12:03]
RITA BENMAYOR: Lice, many.

[00:12:05]
DAVID BODER: Oh, you had many lice?

[00:12:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: We had many lice.

[00:12:07]
DAVID BODER: And what did you do to get rid of the lice?

[00:12:12]
RITA BENMAYOR: we did so in...

[00:12:14]
DAVID BODER: What, scratched yourself?

[00:12:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:12:16]
DAVID BODER: Eh...? She said they scratched themselves.

[00:12:21]
DAVID BODER: Now, so, eh, and then, how long were they there in that camp, what is the name of the second camp?

[00:12:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: Is Ravensbrück.

[00:12:29]
DAVID BODER: That is called Ravesblick [Boder does not seem to know the camp]...and, eh, how long were you in Ravensbrück?

[00:12:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: Four months.

[00:12:36]
DAVID BODER: Four months. And what happened then?

[00:12:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: Was always there...

[00:12:40]
DAVID BODER: Yes, but after the four months, what happened there?

[00:12:43]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then we were transported again, why [because] the Russians came to Ravensbrück, [we] were transported to another camp, Retzow.

[00:12:50]
DAVID BODER: To, you were transported to Retzow...

[00:12:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: Retzow.

[00:12:53]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and what did...

[00:12:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: We had to carry stones again, worked at the roadside...

[00:12:59]
DAVID BODER: What, did you always build roads?

[00:13:01]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, always there.

[00:13:02]
DAVID BODER: . . . always built roads, now, and so you worked in Retzow, how long were you in Retzow?

[00:13:09]
RITA BENMAYOR: Three months.

[00:13:10]
DAVID BODER: Three months—you were you treated there, how did they, eh, treat you? Were they good to you or kind?

[00:13:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: In Raven—, in Retzow, it was not good, there was nothing to eat, we had soup once and a little piece of bread to eat.

[00:13:28]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:13:29]
RITA BENMAYOR: Many people died of hunger.

[00:13:31]
DAVID BODER: People—now tell me, died of hunger, how does one, of hunger, what, how does that [?] happen?

[00:13:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: Early we had coffee...

[00:13:41]
DAVID BODER: And?

[00:13:41]
RITA BENMAYOR: At midday half a liter of soup...

[00:13:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:13:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: And in the evening a little piece of bread to eat.

[00:13:47]
DAVID BODER: Now, and you say, people died of hunger, how did it happen to them? Did they get sick, did they became gaunt, what...?

[00:13:53]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, emaciated...

[00:13:55]
DAVID BODER: Emaciated...

[00:13:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . cannot walk, the SS has, eh,...

[00:13:58]
DAVID BODER: Eh, with the whip...?

[00:14:00]
RITA BENMAYOR: With the whip, and long...

[00:14:01]
DAVID BODER: She makes a gesture.

[00:14:02]
DAVID BODER: They whipped them, now, and?

[00:14:05]
RITA BENMAYOR: And [they] died.

[00:14:06]
DAVID BODER: And they died. Oh, tell me, what did you call a Mussulman, do you know what that is?

[00:14:12]
RITA BENMAYOR: Mussulman, yes.

[00:14:13]
DAVID BODER: Yes, what is that?

[00:14:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: The—did not eat, was Mussulman, and the SS, they took the Mussulman, straight to the crematorium.

[00:14:22]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:14:37]
DAVID BODER: So, Mussulman was a...[?] person—and what did the SS, do with the Mussulman, you said?

[00:14:45]
RITA BENMAYOR: Straight to the crematorium.

[00:14:47]
DAVID BODER: And, now, eh, and so, how long were you in Retzow?

[00:14:52]
RITA BENMAYOR: Three months.

[00:14:53]
DAVID BODER: And then, from there you went where?

[00:14:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then we were again transported to, eh, Malchow. One day and the two days—we had the Russians coming. We had, eh,...

[00:15:03]
DAVID BODER: You were freed?

[00:15:04]
RITA BENMAYOR: Freed...

[00:15:05]
DAVID BODER: Now, so, the Russians, eh, that was in Malchow?

[00:15:08]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . Malchow.

[00:15:09]
DAVID BODER: Now tell me, when the Russians freed you, what happened then?

[00:15:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: We had a...

[00:15:15]
DAVID BODER: Where did the SS go when the Russians came?

[00:15:18]
RITA BENMAYOR: We got up early, and we...stayed with the SS. And then we all five together went in [?] we stayed, the five, for a whole hour there, and then the SS [was] gone....We stayed without Russians, without Germans.

[00:15:38]
DAVID BODER: And...

[00:15:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . we were all alone, the people...

[00:15:40]
DAVID BODER: And what did you do, were there...?

[00:15:42]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . the prisoners. We walked on the street, just like that, the prisoners alone, and the whole day we were without guard...

[00:15:49]
DAVID BODER: Without guards.

[00:15:50]
RITA BENMAYOR: Without Germans, without guards.

[00:15:52]
DAVID BODER: You were, on the road...

[00:15:52]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . to...

[00:15:53]
DAVID BODER: . . . or did you go in to the Germans, what did the Germans do?

[00:15:56]
RITA BENMAYOR: Nothing, the Germans [were] all gone.

[00:15:59]
DAVID BODER: The...the, the civilians, too? [He uses the term “private individuals.”]

[00:16:01]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:16:02]
DAVID BODER: Now, did...

[00:16:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . the civilians, too, they t—...took a suitcase, and...

[00:16:06]
DAVID BODER: Well?

[00:16:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: All gone.

[00:16:07]
DAVID BODER: Gone.

[00:16:08]
RITA BENMAYOR: We did not see, we just...

[00:16:09]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:16:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: So [they were] gone.

[00:16:10]
DAVID BODER: Did the houses remain open, did you take a look inside?

[00:16:13]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:16:13]
DAVID BODER: In the houses?

[00:16:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:16:15]
DAVID BODER: Did you go in?

[00:16:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:16:16]
DAVID BODER: Did you take anything, food, did you find food?

[00:16:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, we went into the houses, we took food, we took clothes...

[00:16:24]
DAVID BODER: Clothes?

[00:16:25]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then we quickly left.

[00:16:26]
DAVID BODER: And...

[00:16:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: We were without Russians, without Germans, for two days...

[00:16:30]
DAVID BODER: Hm...

[00:16:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: And after three days we saw tanks...

[00:16:33]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:16:34]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . we saw...

[00:16:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:16:35]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . the Russians coming. And quickly, eh...

[00:16:38]
DAVID BODER: Yes. And?

[00:16:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . an officer came there, [asked] who is prisoners, who was in the camp, we quickly [went] with [the], eh, officer, and then we [went] to another camp with the Russians...

[00:16:46]
DAVID BODER: . . . went with the Russians?

[00:16:47]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes. Went back to the other....

[00:16:48]
DAVID BODER: . . . went back to the camp with the Russians. Did you get to eat?

[00:16:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: And the Russians gave us much to eat, we fixed ourselves up, we had soap to wash...

[00:16:57]
DAVID BODER: Aha...

[00:16:58]
RITA BENMAYOR: They were good [to us].

[00:16:58]
DAVID BODER: Aha. Yes. And then you went back where?

[00:17:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: Then we went back to [the] American [side]...

[00:17:05]
DAVID BODER: Where?

[00:17:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, we walked a lot, one, one, three weeks [we] walked on foot, we wanted [to get to the] American [side]...

[00:17:13]
DAVID BODER: Oh, you ran away from the Russians?

[00:17:15]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, we ran away from the Russians, we wanted to go with the Americans.

[00:17:19]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and so, where did you...?

[00:17:20]
RITA BENMAYOR: We should walk for three weeks, we, we, we did not know...

[00:17:23]
DAVID BODER: How many people walked?

[00:17:25]
RITA BENMAYOR: We were twenty-five people.

[00:17:27]
DAVID BODER: Men and women?

[00:17:29]
RITA BENMAYOR: Men and women.

[00:17:30]
DAVID BODER: And where did you go, through Germany?

[00:17:32]
RITA BENMAYOR: Back in Germany to [the] American [side]...

[00:17:34]
DAVID BODER: To the American side?

[00:17:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:17:36]
DAVID BODER: And how long did that take for you to get to the American side?

[00:17:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: Three weeks.

[00:17:40]
DAVID BODER: Speak louder, three weeks?

[00:17:41]
RITA BENMAYOR: Three weeks.

[00:17:42]
DAVID BODER: Didn’t anybody stop you, did nobody ask you where you are going?

[00:17:46]
RITA BENMAYOR: No, we had an address where the American [side] was...

[00:17:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:17:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: And so we walked...

[00:17:51]
DAVID BODER: Where was that?

[00:17:52]
RITA BENMAYOR: That was in Germany.

[00:17:54]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:17:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: Where it was—the side of the Russians.

[00:17:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:17:57]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . we took an address from an Americ— from a Russian officer who said how long to the American side, if [we] wanted to go, [we] could walk for three weeks...

[00:18:05]
DAVID BODER: ...could walk for three weeks...

[00:18:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: We walked for three weeks we came to the American [side]...

[00:18:08]
DAVID BODER: And what did you eat on the way?

[00:18:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: We went to the houses of the Germans, we stole food.

[00:18:15]
DAVID BODER: Did the Germans themselves not give you to eat?

[00:18:18]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, it—what—No.

[00:18:20]
DAVID BODER: Did not want to take...?

[00:18:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . did not, we stole.

[00:18:23]
DAVID BODER: ...stole food?

[00:18:24]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:18:25]
DAVID BODER: What did you steal?

[00:18:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: Bread, butter, sugar, eh, we stole...

[00:18:31]
DAVID BODER: From where did you steal that?

[00:18:32]
RITA BENMAYOR: And very—, and, from the houses of the Germans.

[00:18:34]
DAVID BODER: Where the—where the Germans were gone, where they were not at home?

[00:18:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, yes.

[00:18:37]
DAVID BODER: Didn’t you meet Americans, didn’t you meet...

[00:18:40]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then after three weeks, we had—we came to the American side, and quickly the American [Red] Cross gave us to eat, gave us much...

[00:18:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes, but [during] the three weeks that you walked, were you on the Russian side?

[00:18:53]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:18:54]
DAVID BODER: And the Russians let you go?

[00:18:56]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:18:56]
DAVID BODER: Aha. And then you came through to the Russian side, and came over to the Americans, and there the Red Cross...

[00:19:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:19:02]
DAVID BODER: And they helped you?

[00:19:03]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:19:05]
DAVID BODER: Now, why did you come to Paris?

[00:19:09]
RITA BENMAYOR: I did not, I did not want to go to Greece, why, I had no family...

[00:19:14]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:19:15]
RITA BENMAYOR: And I [would be] all alone in...

[00:19:17]
DAVID BODER: Yes—now?

[00:19:19]
RITA BENMAYOR: In Greece...

[00:19:20]
DAVID BODER: Yes. And so?

[00:19:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: I went to Greece, see my house without my mother, without father, I cannot see that...I have quickly, eh, had, I have had two friends, French...

[00:19:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:19:33]
Rita Benmayor: Who told me: do you want to come to Paris? I said yes....[so] I came to Paris.

[00:19:38]
DAVID BODER: Who were the two French?

[00:19:40]
RITA BENMAYOR: Two French.

[00:19:41]
DAVID BODER: Man, eh, men or women?

[00:19:43]
RITA BENMAYOR: Women.

[00:19:43]
DAVID BODER: French women?

[00:19:45]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:19:45]
DAVID BODER: And they had walked with you?

[00:19:47]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, yes.

[00:19:48]
DAVID BODER: Aha, and so you came to Paris, did the French let you in?

[00:19:52]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:19:53]
DAVID BODER: Eh, speak up [please]...the French let you in?

[00:19:55]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:19:56]
DAVID BODER: And when did you get on a train, that you could ride?

[00:19:59]
RITA BENMAYOR: Came with a train, yes.

[00:20:01]
DAVID BODER: Who, from where have [you,] from the American side?

[00:20:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . from the American side.

[00:20:03]
DAVID BODER: Then you got on a train, to drive off—how many people together?

[00:20:08]
RITA BENMAYOR: It was a hundred and fifty people.

[00:20:11]
DAVID BODER: A special train?

[00:20:12]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:20:13]
DAVID BODER: With refugees?

[00:20:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: With refugees.

[00:20:15]
DAVID BODER: And did one give you food and so on?

[00:20:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes, the Americans gave us a lot to eat.

[00:20:19]
DAVID BODER: And then you came to Paris?

[00:20:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: To Paris.

[00:20:22]
DAVID BODER: And who did you go to here, who did you meet?

[00:20:25]
RITA BENMAYOR: I met nobody, I had two Greeks, two Greek friends, we had a big, eh. Greek cross coming...

[00:20:34]
DAVID BODER: . . . a Red Cross?

[00:20:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . Red Cross came...

[00:20:37]
DAVID BODER: From Greece?

[00:20:37]
RITA BENMAYOR: From Greece.

[00:20:38]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and?

[00:20:39]
RITA BENMAYOR: And [they] gave me a dress, a coat, and to eat...

[00:20:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:20:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: And then the Jewish organization gave me shelter.

[00:20:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes, a—yes, and now you live here?

[00:20:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: And I live here.

[00:20:52]
DAVID BODER: Now, and, eh, what are you doing now—what are you doing here now [Ina?]—what, where do you want to go, what do you want to do?

[00:21:00]
RITA BENMAYOR: I go to America.

[00:21:01]
DAVID BODER: Oh, you are going to America?

[00:21:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: I have an uncle...

[00:21:05]
DAVID BODER: Who found the relative for you, or did you search?

[00:21:07]
RITA BENMAYOR: I found a soldier...

[00:21:10]
DAVID BODER: A...

[00:21:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: . . . a Greek soldier, American...

[00:21:12]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:21:13]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes. I told him. Maybe he can [find] my uncle. I gave him my addre—...eh, the address I did not know, I gave him the name of my uncle, he found [him].

[00:21:23]
DAVID BODER: The soldier...

[00:21:24]
RITA BENMAYOR: Just with the name...the soldier.

[00:21:26]
DAVID BODER: Now, who is your uncle?

[00:21:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: And the soldier quickly sent [a letter] to my uncle, and my uncle sent me a letter.

[00:21:31]
DAVID BODER: A, eh, a letter?

[00:21:32]
RITA BENMAYOR: A letter.

[00:21:32]
DAVID BODER: Did one send an affidavit?

[00:21:33]
RITA BENMAYOR: An affidavit, he sent me all papers.

[00:21:36]
DAVID BODER: So, why don’t you go to America?

[00:21:38]
RITA BENMAYOR: Because the quota for Greeks is closed, I cannot go.

[00:21:42]
DAVID BODER: And so you are waiting here now, what do you do here?

[00:21:45]
RITA BENMAYOR: Now I wait, until the quota is open.

[00:21:48]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:21:49]
RITA BENMAYOR: I go to America to my uncle.

[00:21:51]
DAVID BODER: Aha—and you are all alone here?

[00:21:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: All alone.

[00:21:55]
DAVID BODER: And your brother is where?

[00:21:56]
RITA BENMAYOR: My brother is in Palestine.

[00:21:59]
DAVID BODER: Palestine? Now, and now tell me, you live in the same room with Mrs., eh, Bottom...

[00:22:04]
RITA BENMAYOR: Bottom...

[00:22:04]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and why were you in such a hurry this morning, to [go to] work, what did you work?

[00:22:11]
RITA BENMAYOR: I go to work—every, eh,...[?] vacation...

[00:22:14]
DAVID BODER: Mmh.

[00:22:14]
RITA BENMAYOR: All...

[00:22:16]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:22:16]
RITA BENMAYOR: All [?] I cannot [get] work. After mo—, after month of September, we go to work.

[00:22:24]
DAVID BODER: What can you work?

[00:22:26]
RITA BENMAYOR: I can sew a little.

[00:22:26]
DAVID BODER: You can sew, don’t you want to make shoes again?

[00:22:30]
RITA BENMAYOR: No.

[00:22:30]
DAVID BODER: Why not?

[00:22:31]
RITA BENMAYOR: That was in the lager.

[00:22:31]
DAVID BODER: And you don’t want [that] anymore?

[00:22:33]
RITA BENMAYOR: No.

[00:22:34]
DAVID BODER: But you can still do it?

[00:22:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: I can.

[00:22:39]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:22:44]
DAVID BODER: And, eh, are you learning a new vocation here, or you can sew?

[00:22:49]
RITA BENMAYOR: Well, I can sew.

[00:22:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes, eh—how long did you go to school in Gree— in Saloniki—did you go to school?

[00:22:57]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:22:57]
DAVID BODER: How many years did you go to school?

[00:22:59]
RITA BENMAYOR: At sixteen I was in [a] Greek school...

[00:23:02]
DAVID BODER: Yes—eh—tell me, eh, they say, that there were songs in Auschwitz that the girls would sing—can you remember which, which poems that were made there in Auschwitz?

[00:23:15]
RITA BENMAYOR: No.

[00:23:16]
DAVID BODER: No songs either? You don’t know camp—, camp songs...what?

[00:23:21]
RITA BENMAYOR: No.

[00:23:21]
DAVID BODER: You don’t know any camp songs. And, eh, where is your uncle in America?

[00:23:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: In Hartford.

[00:23:29]
DAVID BODER: In Hartford, Connecticut? What does he do there [plenty]? [apparently said to someone else] What kind of job, what does he do there?

[00:23:36]
RITA BENMAYOR: The one, I have two uncles, the one works in the factory, I don’t know what...

[00:23:41]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Yes, and the other one?

[00:23:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: The other one, I don’t know, I can’t...

[00:23:46]
DAVID BODER: You don’t know what he is working? Now, eh...but you think you will, eh, in, eh, in a year or so, get an affidavit?

[00:23:57]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:23:58]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and until then you will stay in Paris?

[00:24:01]
RITA BENMAYOR: I have been in Paris for one year already.

[00:24:04]
DAVID BODER: And you will wait until...

[00:24:05]
RITA BENMAYOR: I wait until the quota for Greeks is open...

[00:24:07]
DAVID BODER: Were you told when it could be open?

[00:24:11]
RITA BENMAYOR: I, eh, the—the American Consulate, does not know either...

[00:24:14]
DAVID BODER: Does not know either—now, something will probably be done. Look that you can learn something here. If not, in the town—learn a nice vocation?

[00:24:27]
RITA BENMAYOR: I would like to learn.

[00:24:29]
DAVID BODER: Yes, you want to—now?

[00:24:31]
RITA BENMAYOR: Everybody—all, hm...

[00:24:33]
DAVID BODER: All are on vacation?

[00:24:34]
RITA BENMAYOR: must, in the month of September...

[00:24:36]
DAVID BODER: In the month of September you will start. Now, I thank you very much, Miss Benmayor.

[00:24:39]
DAVID BODER: Do you speak Spanish?

[00:24:44]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:24:45]
DAVID BODER: And, eh...What other languages can you speak?

[00:24:51]
RITA BENMAYOR: Italian...

[00:24:52]
DAVID BODER: Where did you learn Italian?

[00:24:54]
RITA BENMAYOR: At the scuola.

[00:24:55]
DAVID BODER: At school...And, eh...do you speak French now?

[00:25:00]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:25:00]
DAVID BODER: Can you read French?

[00:25:02]
RITA BENMAYOR: A little.

[00:25:04]
DAVID BODER: Well, it would be great, in the end, [?] this book, then.

[00:25:06]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:25:08]
DAVID BODER: Well, thank you very much, madam.

[00:25:10]
RITA BENMAYOR: Yes.

[00:25:11]
DAVID BODER: This concludes...this concludes the spool of the Illinois Institute of Technology, Spool 27, taken from Rita Benmayor, age twenty, tattoo 38758, and the triangle. Eh, she is a husky looking young woman, and eh, has her affidavit from America, but the quota is not yet open. The spool is, eh, of, eh, about twenty-six minutes length.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Samuel Isakovitch
entries.content:
[00:00:16]
DAVID BODER: This is Spool number 7, taken from a young man, Samuel Isakovitch, from the Roumanian side of a little town which borders with Czechoslovakia.

[00:00:30]
DAVID BODER: What is your name?

[00:00:32]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: [00:00:34]
DAVID BODER: And so, what is your name?

[00:00:37]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Isakovitch, Samuel. [He speaks Yiddish with a great admixture of ‘lager German.’]

[00:00:39]
DAVID BODER: Samuel?

[00:00:40]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Isakovitch.

[00:00:40]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:00:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Isakovitch, Samuel.

[00:00:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes? And how old are you, Isakovitch?

[00:00:46]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I am eighteen years old.

[00:00:48]
DAVID BODER: Eighteen years old? Are you younger than...

[00:00:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Than Moskovitch?

[00:00:51]
DAVID BODER: Moskovitch.

[00:00:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:00:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes, but you are much bigger than he.

[00:00:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:00:55]
DAVID BODER: You are bigger. How tall are you?

[00:00:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One seventy. [170 centimeters, about 68 inches.]

[00:00:59]
DAVID BODER: And how much do you weigh?

[00:01:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I weigh sixty-nine kilo. [About 151 pounds.]

[00:01:03]
DAVID BODER: Sixty-nine kilo. Sit down a little closer and tell me, where were you born?

[00:01:10]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Born in Marmaros-Sighet.

[00:01:12]
DAVID BODER: In what country?

[00:01:14]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In Roumania.

[00:01:15]
DAVID BODER: Hm. What was your father’s occupation?

[00:01:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A field-worker [farm worker].

[00:01:23]
DAVID BODER: A field...

[00:01:24]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Earth-worker.

[00:01:25]
DAVID BODER: What was he? What did he do?

[00:01:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the fields...

[00:01:29]
DAVID BODER: Did he own his fields?

[00:01:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: His own...he worked on his own fields.

[00:01:32]
DAVID BODER: He was a ‘farmer’?

[00:01:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, he was.

[00:01:34]
DAVID BODER: And what did he plant?

[00:01:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Trees, wheat...

[00:01:39]
DAVID BODER: Wheat. Yes?

[00:01:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...wheat and food stuffs...bread...

[00:01:43]
DAVID BODER: Bread.

[00:01:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...everything.

[00:01:43]
DAVID BODER: Did you have any cows?

[00:01:45]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Cows, yes, and horses.

[00:01:46]
DAVID BODER: How many cows did you have?

[00:01:48]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We had six cows.

[00:01:49]
DAVID BODER: Six cows, and how many horses?

[00:01:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Three horses...

[00:01:53]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:01:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and two-hundred sheep.

[00:01:56]
DAVID BODER: Two-hundred sheep?

[00:01:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Sheep, yes.

[00:01:58]
DAVID BODER: And what did you do with the sheep?

[00:01:59]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Most of them perished.

[00:02:01]
DAVID BODER: But...

[00:02:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...when we were taken away to camp...lager...and that is when they perished.

[00:02:06]
DAVID BODER: You weren’t allowed to liquidate your...to sell your belongings, or so?

[00:02:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No, no. Everything remained. We were taken away from the house and everything was taken away. Everything remained there with the house.

[00:02:20]
DAVID BODER: Hm. Now let us start from the beginning. When did the Germans come to your town?

[00:02:25]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: To our town they came in...in...they came in the year forty-one.

[00:02:30]
DAVID BODER: In what [year]?

[00:02:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the year forty-one, the 5th [?] of September.

[00:02:33]
DAVID BODER: And before, what country was it?

[00:02:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Roumania.

[00:02:36]
DAVID BODER: Before it was Roumania?

[00:02:38]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:02:38]
DAVID BODER: And the Germans came in forty-one?

[00:02:40]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In forty-one.

[00:02:41]
DAVID BODER: Nu, how were they before...were the Roumanians good to you before? Were the Roumanians good to you?

[00:02:46]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It was only a little different.

[00:02:54]
DAVID BODER: They let you live.

[00:02:55]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:02:55]
DAVID BODER: Oh, and when did the Germans arrive? Tell me what happened on the day when the Germans arrived?

[00:03:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They marched in...there were...when they came...first an order was given to wear a yellow patch, a yellow star.

[00:03:10]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:03:10]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and then, it was not allowed to walk out on the street, only mornings, from eight till eleven o’clock...

[00:03:17]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:03:18]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and in the afternoon, from four till six...

[00:03:21]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:03:21]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...we were allowed on the street, and only with a yellow star. Then we were taken into the ghetto...

[00:03:28]
DAVID BODER: Hm...

[00:03:29]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and from the ghetto we were taken, in the year forty-two, to a lager in Posen.

[00:03:34]
DAVID BODER: Now wait, don’t go so fast. You say that you had land...

[00:03:38]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:03:39]
DAVID BODER: ...and that you had all that...when was it when you were... not allowed to come out, did they allow to work the fields?

[00:03:47]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It was thus. When the ghetto began, we weren’t allowed to leave the ghetto any more...everything remained there [behind].

[00:03:52]
DAVID BODER: And who took it over?

[00:03:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Nobody.

[00:03:54]
DAVID BODER: What do you mean? Who fed the cows? Who fed the...

[00:03:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Everything remained there. Everybody was removed [?].

[00:04:01]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:04:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and everything remained. What happened afterwards is not known, and...

[00:04:08]
DAVID BODER: So you were sent to a ghetto. How long were you in the ghetto.

[00:04:11]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One month.

[00:04:12]
DAVID BODER: How did you live in the ghetto, the whole family together?

[00:04:16]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The whole family. We were...the family was together and everyone older than sixteen worked at the railroad...

[00:04:25]
DAVID BODER: Where?

[00:04:26]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: At the railroad, by coal.

[00:04:27]
DAVID BODER: By coal.

[00:04:28]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:04:29]
DAVID BODER: Now, what was the ghetto? Were there houses? What was it?

[00:04:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Houses, yes.

[00:04:34]
DAVID BODER: Whose houses were they?

[00:04:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Jewish houses.

[00:04:38]
DAVID BODER: Before they had belonged to Jews also?

[00:04:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:04:40]
DAVID BODER: And so, nu, and what kind of things did you take along?

[00:04:45]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Everyone took thirty-eight kilo, so many pounds of food and so many

[00:05:09]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:05:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and looked in the shoes who...

[00:05:11]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:05:11]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...had money.

[00:05:11]
DAVID BODER: Didn’t one have jewelry, rings...

[00:05:14]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We buried everything. in the ground and...it disappeared. And who went home, [after the war] maybe somebody found something still, and others maybe didn’t find anything.

[00:05:24]
DAVID BODER: Hm. So you buried your valuables in the ground and you don’t know where to find them?

[00:05:30]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One can’t know.

[00:05:32]
DAVID BODER: Would you know where they were buried if you went back and looked for it?

[00:05:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Do I know? Can I know? My parents...I was only thirteen ...the parents were [still] at home...

[00:05:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:05:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...[we were] not taken away together... [some words not clear]...

[00:05:44]
DAVID BODER: Oh! You were not taken away together?

[00:05:46]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No.

[00:05:46]
DAVID BODER: But did you meet them in the ghetto?

[00:05:48]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the ghetto, yes.

[00:05:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes. What...all right, so you were in the ghetto. How long were you in the ghetto.

[00:05:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I was there one month.

[00:05:55]
DAVID BODER: And then what happened?

[00:05:56]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Then we were taken away to the lager.

[00:05:58]
DAVID BODER: Which lager?

[00:05:59]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Posen.

[00:06:00]
DAVID BODER: To Posen. The whole family?

[00:06:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The whole family.

[00:06:03]
DAVID BODER: Your mother and father together with the children?

[00:06:05]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We were all transported together and there we were separated...nobody knows where to...we entered from the RR-car ...we got off the RR-cars, the youngsters were immediately taken away...it was called out, ‘The youngsters step forward,’ and the others... [?]

[00:06:19]
DAVID BODER: Who? The youngsters?

[00:06:20]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:06:21]
DAVID BODER: What does it mean, ‘the youngsters’? The youth...

[00:06:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The young people, those from...

[00:06:23]
DAVID BODER: ...or the men?

[00:06:23]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...eighteen...the men from eighteen years...

[00:06:26]
DAVID BODER: Oh.

[00:06:26]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...to thirty-five. It was said, ‘Step forward,’ and we stepped forward, the fourteen-year olds, too. We stepped forward, and about the others we don’t know where they went.

[00:06:35]
DAVID BODER: What does it mean, you don’t know where they went?

[00:06:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They left and were not seen any more.

[00:06:39]
DAVID BODER: And...and your father and your mother?

[00:06:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It is not known what happened to them either.

[00:06:44]
DAVID BODER: When were you separated from your parents?

[00:06:46]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the year forty-two.

[00:06:47]
DAVID BODER: There at the train?

[00:06:49]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, at the station [?]. Yes.

[00:06:50]
DAVID BODER: Hm. And then where were you taken?

[00:06:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I was taken to work...to the factory...at a construction detail.

[00:06:59]
DAVID BODER: What kind of detail?

[00:07:00]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Construction detail. Construction. A factory was being built.

[00:07:04]
DAVID BODER: Oh. You were building a factory?

[00:07:05]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:07:06]
DAVID BODER: Were you...what was your...

[00:07:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Mason [Enunciation not clear.]

[00:07:10]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:07:10]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A mason.

[00:07:11]
DAVID BODER: What is that?

[00:07:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A mason, nu. Building work.

[00:07:15]
DAVID BODER: A mason.

[00:07:15]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A mason, yes.

[00:07:16]
DAVID BODER: Hm. Nu, where did you live, where did you eat, sleep?

[00:07:20]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the lager.

[00:07:21]
DAVID BODER: In the lager.

[00:07:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: [00:07:22]
DAVID BODER: The lager was what?

[00:07:24]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It was a lager — a German concentration camp.

[00:07:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:07:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: With prisoners...as a prisoner.

[00:07:29]
DAVID BODER: Were there men...men and women in the lager?

[00:07:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No women. Only men.

[00:07:33]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:07:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Only men.

[00:07:34]
DAVID BODER: Only men.

[00:07:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:07:36]
DAVID BODER: And what was there...tell me, when did you get up and what did you do there?

[00:07:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: There we—we got up at a quarter to five in the morning, we went out to appell, we stood...

[00:07:47]
DAVID BODER: What do you call an ‘appell’?

[00:07:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the morning we were counted.

[00:07:52]
DAVID BODER: Counted. Where the names called out or...

[00:07:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No, it was arranged...every block had its people. As many people the block had...then they were lined up. There came the lager-fuehrer, the block obersturm-fuehrer, and counted how many people there are in the block. Then if it was correct, good. And if not—then he looked so long, till he was found.

[00:08:13]
DAVID BODER: And if he wasn’t found?

[00:08:14]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Then another ten were taken and shot.

[00:08:17]
DAVID BODER: Why? If somebody ran away?

[00:08:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: If somebody escaped, another ten were taken and shot.

[00:08:23]
DAVID BODER: Where? Right there?

[00:08:25]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Not right there. They were taken out. They were taken behind the lager and immediately shot.

[00:08:30]
DAVID BODER: Was it their fault that...

[00:08:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: But...

[00:08:31]
DAVID BODER: ...another one escaped [?]?

[00:08:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They said thus, “Who...in case anybody escapes, other ten comrades will be shot.’

[00:08:39]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:08:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: So that nobody should escape.

[00:08:40]
DAVID BODER: Did anybody escape?

[00:08:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Some[?].

[00:08:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:08:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Who could escape.

[00:08:46]
DAVID BODER: Who was able, ran away?

[00:08:47]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Who could escaped.

[00:08:49]
DAVID BODER: Didn’t he know that ten of his comrades will be shot?

[00:08:52]
