SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: He knew; but he wanted his life...wanted his life...first of all...

[00:08:58]
DAVID BODER: Did they really shoot ten people every time?

[00:09:00]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Always.

[00:09:02]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:09:03]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They shot always. They shot always, whenever somebody escaped. And then when one escaped he was [considered] committing sabotage; and for sabotage one was hanged.

[00:09:17]
DAVID BODER: What kind of sabotage?

[00:09:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Sabotage...was...when something by the construction—by the construction detail...if one broke anything or anything... if one didn’t put on the five hundred bricks a day, then this was also considered sabotage. He was also hanged like the others. The electricians or machinists...we worked at machines...

[00:09:39]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:09:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...they were also hanged like the others if they didn’t work the way they should have.

[00:09:48]
DAVID BODER: Who was it who said that they didn’t work?

[00:09:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The...the master, the foreman, the Oberschar-fuehrer...

[00:09:56]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:09:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...the block leader [a few words not clear]...

[00:10:00]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:10:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: [00:10:02]
DAVID BODER: Nu, and so, in the morning you had what, the appell?

[00:10:05]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, in the morning...then at six o’clock we began working.

[00:10:11]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:10:11]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We worked till the evening. We worked till dinner time, [the mid-day meal]. For dinner we had half an hour and then again...

[00:10:18]
DAVID BODER: What were you given to eat for dinner?

[00:10:19]
Samuel Isakovitch: At dinner time nothing. In the morning we were given bread and a little piece of margarine and coffee...[Footnote: It was assumed that the prisoners would save part of their bread ration for dinner and even for supper. But in most cases they either ate the whole ration in the morning or traded it away for cigarettes or other objects or favors.]

[00:10:27]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:10:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and in the evening a liter of soup.

[00:10:29]
DAVID BODER: And for dinner [mid-day] you weren’t given anything to eat?

[00:10:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No.

[00:10:32]
DAVID BODER: So? Nu, you only rested at mid-day time?

[00:10:37]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, we rested for half an hour. And then we started to work again.

[00:10:41]
DAVID BODER: And how late did you work?

[00:10:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We worked till six o’clock in the evening and then we marched in. And again we stood on the appell square till ten o’clock at night.

[00:10:49]
DAVID BODER: Why so long?

[00:10:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Why? They had time. They had time...they wanted...till the lager-fuehrer came; till the block-fuehrer came. Then the music didn’t play well.

[00:11:02]
DAVID BODER: What kind of music did you have in the lager?

[00:11:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: While marching out and marching in there had to be music.

[00:11:07]
DAVID BODER: Why?

[00:11:08]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: To march better.

[00:11:09]
DAVID BODER: Yes. So, who played the music?

[00:11:11]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Our men.

[00:11:12]
DAVID BODER: Where did you get the instruments?

[00:11:14]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We already got them from Auschwitz.

[00:11:16]
DAVID BODER: What do you mean ‘from Auschwitz’? They have sent...

[00:11:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:11:19]
DAVID BODER: ...instruments from Auschwitz...

[00:11:20]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, and then we too went away to Auschwitz...

[00:11:24]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:11:24]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And then we too left for Ausch-...

[00:11:26]
DAVID BODER: Now wait, we are not through with this camp. So, in the evening what? Music played when you returned?

[00:11:32]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:11:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes? And then?

[00:11:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And then...

[00:11:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and then we went in...stood for appell...

[00:11:38]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:11:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Finished with the appell, we entered the ‘block’ and received the soup...

[00:11:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and then, at nine o’clock, feet-washing and lay down to sleep.

[00:11:50]
DAVID BODER: Feet-washing. Were you given water and soap for that purpose?

[00:11:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One received soap and water.

[00:11:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:11:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:11:58]
DAVID BODER: And the soup. Did everyone have a plate for himself?

[00:12:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes...as we stood in line, when one finished eating, the other got it. He took from the other one the...the plate and then...he ate.

[00:12:10]
DAVID BODER: So everyone did not have a plate of his own?

[00:12:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No. To a ‘block’ there were maybe forty plates...

[00:12:17]
DAVID BODER: Yes, so?

[00:12:17]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and from these forty, the other two, three hundred ate.

[00:12:21]
DAVID BODER: Did they wash the plates?

[00:12:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Who...who would do it? Nothing was washed. Everyone in line wanted to eat quickly...one had to hurry.

[00:12:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Nu, tell me this. And then, in the evening, did they allow you to talk to one another?

[00:12:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One could...it was permitted...by the time we had washed our feet, we already had to go to sleep. There was ‘foot control’...

[00:12:51]
DAVID BODER: What...what was the ‘foot control’?

[00:12:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The feet were looked over [as to]whether they were clean.

[00:12:56]
DAVID BODER: Why did they bother so much about the feet and not about ‘the rest’?

[00:12:59]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Everything was looked over, but in the evening, the feet were checked whether they are clean...whether they don’t stink.

[00:13:06]
DAVID BODER: Oh! And how did you sleep? What did you sleep on?

[00:13:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We slept on a plank bed, on boards.

[00:13:15]
DAVID BODER: Ah. And how close was one to another?

[00:13:18]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We were together...pushed together...one centimeter one from another...everybody together; squeezed together like herrings.

[00:13:25]
DAVID BODER: O.K. Did you have blankets to cover yourselves?

[00:13:28]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We were given a blanket for two people.

[00:13:31]
DAVID BODER: Oh! You were given for two people...

[00:13:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: For two people, one blanket.

[00:13:33]
DAVID BODER: So, you...you slept practically together.

[00:13:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes. [We] slept together.

[00:13:39]
DAVID BODER: And how long were you in this lager?

[00:13:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Until...until the year forty-four, in May.

[00:13:46]
DAVID BODER: Aha. And what happened then? What was the name of this lager?

[00:13:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Posen.

[00:13:51]
DAVID BODER: Posen. And what happened then?

[00:13:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Then we went away to Auschwitz. The camp was disabanded, and we were taken to Auschwitz

[00:14:00]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:14:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In Auschwitz we came to Birkenau. There they made the ‘selections’. Who was good, who was able to work and was healthy, he went to work to the coal mines in Janina. And who wasn’t, he was taken away because he wasn’t able to work.

[00:14:19]
DAVID BODER: And what was done with them?

[00:14:20]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They went into the crematory. [Pause.] I went away to the coal mines in Janina. And in Janina the youngsters up to eighteen years, were taken out and taken to Monowitz—there to a rubber factory. We worked...

[00:14:39]
DAVID BODER: These were the ones under eighteen years...

[00:14:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:14:42]
DAVID BODER: ...were taken to the...

[00:14:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Where taken to the rubber factory in Monowitz. [Pause].

[00:14:51]
DAVID BODER: Yes. So, then you were in Monowitz in the rubber factory?

[00:14:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:14:55]
DAVID BODER: And the...

[00:14:55]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Work...

[00:14:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:14:56]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We worked in Monowitz in the rubber factory...we worked until the year forty-five, up to January the eighteenth. January the eighteenth...

[00:15:08]
DAVID BODER: January the eighteenth.

[00:15:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes. January the eighteenth we were taken away...we were evacuated to the Concentration Camp Buchenwald?

[00:15:17]
DAVID BODER: Oh! Were you in Buchenwald?

[00:15:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:15:19]
DAVID BODER: Tell me a little about Buchenwald.

[00:15:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We arrived in Buchenwald in January...

[00:15:26]
DAVID BODER: ...in January.

[00:15:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...in January. And then we were taken and first of all everybody was disinfected.

[00:15:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:15:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: At the time of disinfection, we had come from Auschwitz to...to Buchenwald. It took us twelve days. Three quarters had died from hunger. And we remained, from fourteen thousand, we only remained two-thousand eight hundred men, exactly. Because, I know precisely the numbers...there we were given numbers...everybody received a number...

[00:15:59]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:15:59]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...it was [starting] from a hundred and twenty thousand to a hundred twenty-two thousand eight hundred.

[00:16:04]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:16:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I know that exactly two thousand eight hundred have remained from our transport out of fourteen thousand people. The others were murdered...shot...in Slovakia...shot, and starved to death, and they were murdered...Then we came to Buchenwald. We were taken into the disinfection [hall], and there a quarter was murdered.

[00:16:27]
DAVID BODER: What does it mean, ‘they were murdered’?

[00:16:28]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They were taken into...the disinfection [chamber]. So they started...were dirty...so they rubbed so long till...they began to clip off the hair with machines...from all over...so long...we undressed...we were like the flies...food we didn’t get for six days...except what the civilian population in Czechoslovakie threw into the RR-cars. And the children who were going to school saw us from the bridges...it was so...they threw into the RR-cars a little piece of bread or anything they could...when they were going to school...and on this we endured a little...and snow helped...

[00:17:15]
DAVID BODER: What about the snow?

[00:17:15]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Snow....we ate the snow.

[00:17:17]
DAVID BODER: The white snow.

[00:17:17]
DAVID BODER: Oh, it was cold then?

[00:17:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:17:19]
DAVID BODER: Oh. That one ate for water?

[00:17:21]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It was eaten for bread and for water...for anything...we ate it from hunger.

[00:17:26]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:17:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: We didn’t have anything else to eat. The RR-cars were full of the dead...with the dead people...

[00:17:32]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, what does it mean dead...died of hunger...eh...

[00:17:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: From hunger, yes.

[00:17:37]
DAVID BODER: A man really...simply died...?

[00:17:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: He simply died...one simply murdered the other!

[00:17:43]
DAVID BODER: Why did you murder one another?

[00:17:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One another...so that...we took. One was hungry...

[00:17:49]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:17:49]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...the oth-...we couldn’t go out from the RR-cars because you were immediately shot...

[00:17:53]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:17:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and somebody saw there was a little snow...Snow was falling...

[00:17:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:17:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...on the sides of the RR-cars. We took off a little snow with the hands...and the other person saw it. So he wanted to take away the little snow so he could eat it. Then he took his wooden shoe off his foot...

[00:18:07]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:07]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...he gave it to him right over the head. He gave it to him over the head...he fell down...he was trambled on...he never used to get up any more.

[00:18:15]
DAVID BODER: One to the other?

[00:18:16]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, one to the other. So, there remained...a half of the RR-car were dead. We were a hundred and sixty-five men in a RR-car. We were a hundred and sixty-five persons to a RR-car. We were embarked in Gleiwitz. In the lager Gleiwitz we were embarked one hundred sixty-five people to a RR-car.

[00:18:32]
DAVID BODER: What kind of RR-cars were they?

[00:18:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Open ones.

[00:18:35]
DAVID BODER: Open ones? What do you mean by open RR-cars?

[00:18:37]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Completely open.

[00:18:38]
DAVID BODER: No roof?

[00:18:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No roof.

[00:18:40]
DAVID BODER: Oh, they were the railroad cars used for transportation of lumber and machinery.

[00:18:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Lumber...on these...

[00:18:45]
DAVID BODER: So how did people stand on the railroad cars while the train was in motion?

[00:18:48]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: That’s how they stood.

[00:18:50]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:18:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: That’s how they stood.

[00:18:53]
DAVID BODER: And this was where? This was already in Buch-...No?

[00:18:55]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No. From Auschwitz to Buchenwald, when we were taken...evacuated...

[00:18:58]
DAVID BODER: Uh-huh.

[00:18:59]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...from Auschwitz to Buchenwald.

[00:19:00]
DAVID BODER: Nu, and in Buchenwald, you tell me, they began to clip...

[00:19:03]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Began...

[00:19:03]
DAVID BODER: ...your hair...

[00:19:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The hair...there, when we came in, we hadn’t eaten for six days and then, when we came in there, until the names were written down, until everybody’s index card was made out. It also took three days till we entered the blocks...and we bathed. We only received a shirt and a piece of trousers and a pair of wooden shoes...and cold...it was so cold that nobody could...a person couldn’t...a person soon froze.

[00:19:33]
DAVID BODER: Which month was it in?

[00:19:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In January.

[00:19:34]
DAVID BODER: In January.

[00:19:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In January.

[00:19:36]
DAVID BODER: Now then...

[00:19:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And when one came out after bathing...he went outside improperly dressed in only...he only had something like a shirt...nothing...and when he stepped outside he immediately caught col...froze up, and remained lying outside near the blocks. Then every morning we threw the dead into the latrine...every morning we covered the dead with sand... [those] that have lain on the ground. Then in the morning we went out for appell...and we were given once a day to eat...we were given at twelve o’clock in the Kino of the quarantine...

[00:20:14]
DAVID BODER: What is a Kino? [The word appeard far out of context, hence the question.]

[00:20:15]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: There was a Kino...

[00:20:16]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:20:16]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: in the quarantine...

[00:20:18]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:20:18]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...there in Buchenwald...and...

[00:20:21]
DAVID BODER: What did you call a Kino?

[00:20:22]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It was a Kino. There they dispensed the food...there was a Kino.

[00:20:27]
David Boder: Oh, a Kino, a theater. [Footnote: The Kino was a large auditorium that had been used to show movies for the old-time political prisoners. It was located in the small lager called the ‘Quarantine’. At the time of Isakovitch’s arrival, the small lager was overcrowded and the movie house was used for dispensing the food rations to the newly arrived prisoners. B.W.]

[00:20:29]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A theater...a barrack...

[00:20:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:20:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...but it was only called so...and there was no food to be given to the people so they took them into the movie house... a line was formed in the morning from the appell square.

[00:20:42]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:20:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and till the evening...till ten o’clock...till everybody finished their food. One person doled out the food. We received once a day a piece of bread with a little soup. A hundred seventeen...a hundred and seventy grams of bread and a little piece of margarine and a half liter of soup.

[00:21:03]
DAVID BODER: Did one work in Buchenwald?

[00:21:05]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: One worked in the stone-quarry.

[00:21:07]
DAVID BODER: What did they...

[00:21:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the stone-quarries we worked.

[00:21:10]
DAVID BODER: What did one do? Carried out the stones?

[00:21:13]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Carried out the stones. We have...with the carts...with the wagons they were carried away...

[00:21:19]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:21:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Every day there remained in the stone quarry...every day ten, fifteen people...they were dead...they were murdered...in the quarry.

[00:21:30]
DAVID BODER: By whom?

[00:21:30]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The SS men...they couldn’t work; they were murdered in the quarries.

[00:21:35]
DAVID BODER: What, they were shot?

[00:21:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They were shot...if once it was said that one was of no use [no good], he was given a bullet in the head and left lying there.

[00:21:44]
DAVID BODER: And the...the others stood by?

[00:21:45]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And the others...were close by. Everybody was close by.

[00:21:47]
DAVID BODER: Did you see it yourself?

[00:21:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Sure. Everything I saw...we were there all together.

[00:21:54]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, but there were in Buchenwald...in Buchenwald others —there were Germans too...and...

[00:21:59]
Samuel Isakovitch: Yes. Yes. But they were already old prisoners...they were the old criminals...they had been there already for fifteen, sixteen years [Footnote: His statements are somewhat confused as to time.]...old criminals...and bandits...and they were the capos and the block elders... They did everything...they even made...we were simple prisoners...we had just arrived from the other lagers.

[00:22:18]
DAVID BODER: What do you mean by capos?

[00:22:20]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Capos were the overseers at work...

[00:22:23]
DAVID BODER: Hm. And they were what? Old criminals?

[00:22:26]
Samuel Isakovitch: They were old criminals...and bandits...and people who had committed sabotage. They had been in for fifteen, sixteen years...[?][Footnote: His statements are somewhat confused as to time.] political prisoners who were already for fifteen, sixteen years in the lager.

[00:22:37]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:22:38]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In concentration camps...they were the leaders. They murdered so. Much more than the SS men, than the ‘real’ Germans. And the SS men who were in reality Ukranians, Polacks, Magyars...the Magyars were even worse than the others. They were the Gestapo men with the black...

[00:23:01]
DAVID BODER: They were much worse?

[00:23:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Much worse than the Germans.

[00:23:04]
DAVID BODER: Hm. And that was in Buchenwald.

[00:23:07]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:23:08]
DAVID BODER: And where were you liberated?

[00:23:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In Buchenwald.

[00:23:10]
DAVID BODER: Who liberated you?

[00:23:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Americans.

[00:23:13]
DAVID BODER: Nu, tell me, what happened a few days before the liberation and [then] after?

[00:23:17]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Before the liberation...they took...when the Americans came...they took...we were sixty-five thousand men on the appell square. They started...First of all, was, ‘Jews, step forward.’ It was...

[00:23:28]
DAVID BODER: The Americans said that?

[00:23:30]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No! The Germans.

[00:23:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:23:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Before the Americans entered. It was ‘Jews, step forward.’ Then the Jews already knew exactly from other concentration camps what was going on. Then they began to dodge it.

[00:23:43]
DAVID BODER: The Jews?

[00:23:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Jews. They took, the old criminals and bandits, they began to throw out from theblocks...

[00:23:50]
DAVID BODER: Whom?

[00:23:51]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Jews.

[00:23:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:23:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...the prisoners...

[00:23:53]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:23:53]
Samuel Isakovitch: ...and the Jews...it was, ‘Get out.’ And he was immediately grabbed and taken to the D.K.V., and from the D.K.V. they never came out[Footnote: These were factories which had been bombed by the Americans at the end of 1944 and now were empty. To these buildings the Jews were taken. During the appell in the morning, the loudspeaker suddenly blared out, ‘Jews, fall out and line up to one side!’ Many started to run, I among them. I escaped fromm the appell square back to my original block and hid under a bunk. The others, those who remained on the appell square, were deported, destination unknown. B.W.].

[00:24:01]
DAVID BODER: The Jews were taken away?

[00:24:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes, the Jews.

[00:24:03]
DAVID BODER: Nu?

[00:24:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And when I saw what is going on, I immediately reported [hid] among the Frenchmen...

[00:24:08]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:24:09]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and...I knew no French. But the first who got out, these remained, and the others, these were taken right away and they remained there.

[00:24:18]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:24:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And these were...they went between the...between...there in the D.K.V., and they were shot and murdered...and then they, youngsters up to eighteen years, were taken into a youth block, block 66...

[00:24:35]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:24:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...in the quarantine, and we awaited...we had a very good man for a blokovy [Barrack chief in Polish] a Czech, a political prisoner...

[00:24:43]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:24:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: He was the block elder. He was...he worked for us, for the youngsters, so that we could remain alive. And so we awaited the Americans. And before the Americans came there, already [many] had left...there remained nineteen thousand prisoners, in Buchenwald.

[00:25:02]
DAVID BODER: Yes...and the others?

[00:25:03]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The others...the others have...no one knows whether they were shot, or...a stone was put up that fifty-nine thousand shot, murd-...murdered prisoners from among us.

[00:25:14]
DAVID BODER: In Buchenwald?

[00:25:15]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In Buchenwald.

[00:25:16]
DAVID BODER: Wait, so...when...before the Americans came did the SS leave, or what?

[00:25:24]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They left. Immediately. They left right away. They were caught. It was the...our...the prisoners of war, the Russians.

[00:25:34]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:25:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They immediately captured the weapons. They were still healthy and the Americans came from below, from the village...

[00:25:42]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:25:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They were held by the Americans from one side and the prisoners of war from the other side. They were immediately gathered together...they were captured, and after that we don’t know what the Americans did with them.

[00:25:55]
DAVID BODER: They weren’t...they weren’t punished?

[00:25:58]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: No, no, not punished. They were only taken away. Where, we don’t know.

[00:26:03]
DAVID BODER: The SS were taken away?

[00:26:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:26:05]
DAVID BODER: All right. And then who remained in...in...

[00:26:08]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: All of us remained in the lager, half...half-dead. And there came the Americans Red Cross machines...

[00:26:17]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:26:17]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...in automobiles. It began...took us out to the...led us into the SS barracks,

[00:26:24]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:26:24]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and there we recuperated a little...We were asked where everyone wants to go...We took and went to Italy...

[00:26:33]
DAVID BODER: You left for Italy?

[00:26:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:26:35]
DAVID BODER: Why did you decide to go to Italy?

[00:26:38]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Americans took us there to convalesce.

[00:26:40]
DAVID BODER: Oh, the Americans took you to convalesce.

[00:26:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...to convalesce...

[00:26:42]
DAVID BODER: to convalesce in Italy?

[00:26:43]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...in Italy.

[00:26:44]
DAVID BODER: Where did they take you?

[00:26:45]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They took us from Buchenwald and we went to Milan, and from Milan we went to Turin.

[00:26:51]
DAVID BODER: To Turin.

[00:26:51]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:26:52]
DAVID BODER: And who gave you to eat there?

[00:26:54]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Americans. The Americans units [?].

[00:26:59]
DAVID BODER: The Americans organizations?

[00:27:01]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:27:01]
DAVID BODER: And how long were you in Turin?

[00:27:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I was there four months.

[00:27:06]
DAVID BODER: And from there where did you go?

[00:27:08]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I came straight here, to Paris.

[00:27:09]
DAVID BODER: Why did you come to Paris?

[00:27:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I came here to Paris in order to...I want to learn a trade... I saw in Turin one can’t learn anything, and...

[00:27:20]
DAVID BODER: Is there no ORT in Turin?

[00:27:21]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: There is an ORT. There is a camp, a lager...

[00:27:25]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:27:25]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...but there is nothing else to learn. The Italians themselves don’t have...

[00:27:31]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:27:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and we wanted to learn something...

[00:27:33]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:27:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Now we are young, we have to learn something...

[00:27:38]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:27:39]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...so we came to Paris.

[00:27:40]
DAVID BODER: Nu, did you find out anything about your relatives, your family?

[00:27:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Till now I found nobody. I know of nobody...

[00:27:50]
DAVID BODER: Tell me, Moskovsky says that you were taken away to the same camp with his father.

[00:27:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:27:58]
DAVID BODER: What happened to him?

[00:28:00]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: About him I don’t kn-...nothing is known...I left with the youth block and he left...he wasn’t in the youth block. He was in the prisoner’s block where the other old people were. And there was a youth block and we were taken separately, in separate RR-cars, and he went separately...afterwards we didn’t see anybody from Auschwitz...we didn’t see him there any more. We left from Gleiwitz, from Gleiwitz l. We were put into RR-cars and I saw him no more. But I heard that he was taken away to Dora, and I went to...

[00:28:33]
DAVID BODER: Where is Dora?

[00:28:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: To Dora he went, to Germany, the father of Moskovitz...his father...

[00:28:39]
DAVID BODER: Is Dora a town in Germany?

[00:28:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A town.

[00:28:41]
DAVID BODER: Yes, and what was there, a lager?

[00:28:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Also a ‘camp,’ a lager.

[00:28:46]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:28:47]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And there the people were bombed.

[00:28:50]
DAVID BODER: Aha.

[00:28:51]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: There were bombings. Some people were shot in Dora[?].

[00:28:56]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:28:57]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: And where they went, I don’t know.

[00:28:59]
DAVID BODER: So, you have no relatives in Paris?

[00:29:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I have nobody here.

[00:29:03]
DAVID BODER: And where do you live here?

[00:29:05]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I live in Severn, on the Avenue Seguier, a youth home.

[00:29:10]
DAVID BODER: This is a youth home?

[00:29:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:29:12]
DAVID BODER: And your cousin lives...also there?

[00:29:14]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Also there. Yes.

[00:29:15]
DAVID BODER: How many young people live there?

[00:29:16]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: There are fifty young people.

[00:29:18]
DAVID BODER: Are they all Jewish young people?

[00:29:19]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: All Jewish, who learn all kinds of trades.

[00:29:23]
DAVID BODER: And you are learning during the day.

[00:29:25]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: During the day, yes.

[00:29:26]
DAVID BODER: What do you do in the evenings?

[00:29:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In the evening we learn French, and we learn English, whoever wants to.

[00:29:32]
DAVID BODER: Have all these young people been in concentration camps?

[00:29:35]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They have been. All have been in concentration camps.

[00:29:38]
DAVID BODER: Aha. Well, and if you have finished...are you learning radio here?

[00:29:49]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I am learning to be an electrician.

[00:29:52]
DAVID BODER: You are learning to be an electrician.

[00:29:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Electrician.

[00:29:54]
DAVID BODER: And when you will have completed your training, what do you want to do?

[00:29:56]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I want to continue working.

[00:29:58]
DAVID BODER: Do you want to remain in France?

[00:30:00]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I don’t know where I will remain...I have no home, I have nobody here...I don’t know what I will do...I am alone...

[00:30:08]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:30:08]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I don’t know myself what to do...

[00:30:11]
DAVID BODER: But for the time being you are here?

[00:30:13]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: For the time being I am here in the home [?].

[00:30:15]
DAVID BODER: [00:30:17]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Yes.

[00:30:20]
DAVID BODER: This concludes an interview with Isakovitch, what is your first name?

[00:30:25]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Samuel.

[00:30:26]
DAVID BODER: With Samuel Isakovitch, eighteen years old, who is taking a course in electro-technics in...at the ORT school in Paris.

[00:30:48]
DAVID BODER: Mr. Isakovitch, I have here a few pictures, and I want that you should tell me which of your experience of the last few years, do these pictures remind you of. [Aside:] This is #8. Hold it. Nu? What is this picture about? What does it remind you of?

[00:31:10]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: That is...

[00:31:11]
DAVID BODER: Make some kind of story out of it.

[00:31:13]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: This one...one of the women — prisoners who...they look like the women-prisoners who were in the lagers, who were ragged, in tatters...they are famished...they are emaciated...they have no...they are thinking when the liberation will come.

[00:31:33]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:31:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They have nothing to do...

[00:31:36]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:31:37]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...famished.

[00:31:39]
David Boder: And what is this? [Aside: #9.]

[00:31:45]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: This...so...the capo or the blokowy...[Polish for block-trusty]...the blokova [women block-trusty]sends the woman...

[00:31:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:31:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and drives to work...and makes with her...she should work...she should do everything.

[00:32:01]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:32:02]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ..all kind of hard things...

[00:32:05]
DAVID BODER: And...#12.M. And what is this?

[00:32:13]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: These are...the prisoners...they were taken to the lager. hey were looked over like this and...if one was sick, or what...they were taken and looked over if he still alive, or what...he lay there — the comrade. He saw that he lay so on the bed. He took him...he tested him with the hands if he is still alive...he should stay alive, or what...and he was already dead...he was thrown out on the heap [of bodies?].

[00:32:46]
David Boder: And what do you think is this? [Aside: #15.] Yes?

[00:32:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It is also a prisoner...a ‘Mussulman,’ who...simply a ‘Mussulman,’ He can’t walk any more to work...

[00:33:03]
DAVID BODER: What is a ‘Mussulman’?

[00:33:05]
Samuel Isakovitch: A ‘Mussulman’...who is quite emaciated and he can’t walk, he can’t talk...he is completely emaciated...worked out, used up, who can’t do anything any more. Then he becomes emaciated. Then he is a finished ‘Mussulman.’[Footnote: His description of a so-called mussulman is perefect. The origin of this nickname is not known. See the book by Odd Nansen: From Day to Day.]

[00:33:24]
DAVID BODER: What was done with the Mussulmen?

[00:33:26]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The Mussulmen were taken and sent to Birkenau.

[00:33:29]
DAVID BODER: And there?

[00:33:30]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: In Birkenau they were taken into the gas-chambers. Gassed.

[00:33:34]
DAVID BODER: What is this? [Card number not recorded.]

[00:33:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It could be some youth...it could be some youth from the ghetto or from somewhere...after the liberation.

[00:33:46]
DAVID BODER: And what is this? [Card number not recorded.]

[00:33:50]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: This is work...

[00:33:52]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:33:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: It is at work [some words not clear]...working in the fields...

[00:34:01]
DAVID BODER: Oh. Yes. Tell me, what is the most terrible story that you remember from the concentration camp?

[00:34:13]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: The most terrible...eh...it was when we came to Birkenau and they took the children with the women and they started to throw them into the fire, this was the most terrible...

[00:34:26]
DAVID BODER: Did you see it yourself?

[00:34:27]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I saw it with my [own] eyes.

[00:34:28]
DAVID BODER: What do you mean, in the fire? Before the gas?

[00:34:30]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Before the gas. Before everything. They took the dogs and with machine-guns they shot at the children and women...they were taken and thrown into the fire...

[00:34:39]
DAVID BODER: What kind of a fire did they have?

[00:34:41]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: A fire that was a pit and since many couldn’t be burned in the crematories, so a pit was made in Birkenau...a pit was made. On the bottom burned oil and coke and other such that burns, and there they took and threw in the people. They threw themselves in. They already saw it does not make any difference any more...they were thrown in so long...between the wires...pushed in so long...so long until they themselves had to jump into the fire...[long means continuously].

[00:35:09]
DAVID BODER: What kind of wires?

[00:35:11]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Between the electrical wires [the electrified fence]. The electric wires came right to the...near the pit.

[00:35:16]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:35:16]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: They were pushed so long toward the pit...with the dogs and machine guns....for so long till they came so near that they had to jump by themselves into the fire. And then...

[00:35:26]
DAVID BODER: I don’t understand. Where were the electrified wires?

[00:35:28]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: I will show you. Here was the pit, yes?

[00:35:31]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:35:31]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...and here came the electrified wires...

[00:35:33]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:35:34]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...thus. And here the people were driven...

[00:35:36]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:35:36]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Here was the fire. When the people came from this side, they then had no way out. Here they couldn’t. Here were the electrified wires...

[00:35:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:35:44]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: If they touched the electrified fence they were right away ‘kaput.’ [This adjective normally means the complete breakdown of inanimate objects, predominantly mechanisms such as clocks or machinery.]

[00:35:48]
DAVID BODER: Yes.

[00:35:48]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...went ‘kaput.’ And here they couldn’t but go into the fire. And here they were driven into...

[00:35:52]
DAVID BODER: Hm.

[00:35:52]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: ...with machine guns, with dogs, with...

[00:35:55]
DAVID BODER: With blookhounds?

[00:35:55]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Blood-hounds. The big dogs that the SS men had.

[00:35:59]
DAVID BODER: Hm. Anyone from the family had been there?

[00:36:04]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Everbody was there who...I have no means of knowing...I didn’t see...I only saw people...people are being led...such screams that...

[00:36:10]
DAVID BODER: And where did the men stand?

[00:36:12]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Everybody fell...everbody went in...and the men worked at it...worked...he was shot...he who didn’t want to enter, he was shot; he also had to be thrown in...at that time was full the whole...the whole court-yard of Birkenau was filled with...with dead.

[00:36:31]
DAVID BODER: When was that, in what year?

[00:36:33]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: That was in the year forty-four.

[00:36:35]
DAVID BODER: In what month?

[00:36:37]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: May...May on the...May, on the eighteenth of May...

[00:36:41]
DAVID BODER: Approximately.

[00:36:42]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: Approximately. [Long pause.]

[00:36:49]
DAVID BODER: What do you think should be done with Germany now?

[00:36:53]
SAMUEL ISAKOVITCH: What should be done? I can’t say anything. If there are no bigger heads [smarter people] who should that...who should do something, then I can’t say anything what...they didn’t...they had already visited the camps, they can...nobody can say it...such youth who remained without parents, without...and who have nobody...who can say anything?

[00:37:18]
DAVID BODER: Yes. This was the supplement to the same spool of the young Samuel Isakovitch. Spool#7.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Toba Schiver
entries.content:
[00:00:01]
DAVID BODER: Italy, September 2nd, Tradate. A little community of displaced people living in a old castle which later was a convent and then a armory between Milano and Como. Uh, there is a number of community of kibbutzim that are co-operative groups of specially young people that have gotten together, mostly young people who have lost all their whole family and could not, did not feel, or could not stay in their place where their families were, uh, perished. They are roaming through Europe and form various groups, leaving homes, cross borders illegally, and here is a, uh, group that entered Italy and is being supported by the UNRRA and by the Joint. Uh, the interviewee is now, uh, Miss Toba Schiver, uh, 22 years old, born in Czechoslovakia.

[00:00:55]
DAVID BODER: Well, Miss, are you mar-, are you married?

[00:00:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: No.

[00:00:58]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Well, Miss Schiver. Would you tell me again what your full name is, where were you born and how old are you?

[00:01:05]
TOBA SCHIVER: Born in Czechoslovakia.

[00:01:07]
DAVID BODER: Speak up and slow down. You were born in Czech-

[00:01:10]
TOBA SCHIVER: in Czechoslovakia. Born ’22.

[00:01:12]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Uh, what, and you are 22 years old?

[00:01:15]
TOBA SCHIVER: Old.

[00:01:16]
DAVID BODER: Old. Well, tell me. Where were you when the war began, and what has happened to you and with your family? At the time the war began.

[00:01:28]
TOBA SCHIVER: Well. Once, dro-, uh, driven to, uh, Mátészalka. In ghetto.

[00:01:34]
DAVID BODER: Now then, wait a minute. Did the Germans enter your place?

[00:01:37]
TOBA SCHIVER: No. Hungarians.

[00:01:38]
DAVID BODER: No?

[00:01:38]
TOBA SCHIVER: Hungarians to-, took us. In Mátészalka....

[00:01:40]
DAVID BODER: You were?

[00:01:41]
TOBA SCHIVER: in ghetto. This first together.

[00:01:43]
DAVID BODER: So you were in Czechoslovakia. How did you get to Hungary?

[00:01:47]
TOBA SCHIVER: That, that we were in Czechoslovakia and, uh, later came to Hungary for six years.

[00:01:51]
DAVID BODER: When?

[00:01:52]
TOBA SCHIVER: Hungary. For six years we were in Hungary.

[00:01:54]
DAVID BODER: And [?]. No, no, no.

[00:01:57]
TOBA SCHIVER: Czechoslovakia. Six years we were in Hungary.

[00:02:00]
DAVID BODER: That is, uh, the Hungarians annexed you?

[00:02:02]
TOBA SCHIVER: Annexed.

[00:02:03]
DAVID BODER: So that’s it. That was a place in Czechoslovakia, which when the, uh, when they started, the Hungarians annexed from the Czechs.

[00:02:11]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes

[00:02:11]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Well, what happened? A ghetto was created?

[00:02:14]
TOBA SCHIVER: A ghetto in Mátészalka.

[00:02:16]
DAVID BODER: In Mátészalka a ghetto was created. So tell me, when did they declare it a ghetto and how were you taken to the ghetto

[00:02:23]
TOBA SCHIVER: They began to confine the people in a ghetto and [?] camp. And, uh, they were together four weeks.

[00:02:30]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:02:30]
TOBA SCHIVER: Later, they did a roll call and made the whole family, uh, took them, all things and led everyone away to Auschwitz.

[00:02:39]
DAVID BODER: Who? The whole family?

[00:02:40]
TOBA SCHIVER: Whole family.

[00:02:41]
DAVID BODER: There were no selections who should stay?

[00:02:43]
TOBA SCHIVER: No, no. [Unintelligible]

[00:02:45]
DAVID BODER: What wa-, was a family, who were part of it. Father, mother?

[00:02:49]
TOBA SCHIVER: Father, mother, sister.

[00:02:51]
DAVID BODER: One sister?

[00:02:52]
TOBA SCHIVER: One sister. Bro-, brother in army.

[00:02:54]
DAVID BODER: The brother was in the Czech army.

[00:02:56]
TOBA SCHIVER: Czech army.

[00:02:57]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Now go on. So you came to where?

[00:03:00]
TOBA SCHIVER: To Auschwitz.

[00:03:01]
DAVID BODER: Now then, how many days did your journey to Auschwitz take?

[00:03:03]
TOBA SCHIVER: Four days. None, one bread had four days, one man.

[00:03:07]
DAVID BODER: Yes? Well, and?

[00:03:08]
TOBA SCHIVER: . Until Karshow we accom- the Hungarians. After Karshow too-, uh, was taken over by the Germans.

[00:03:15]
DAVID BODER: By the SS?

[00:03:16]
TOBA SCHIVER: The SS.

[00:03:17]
DAVID BODER: Or the Wehrmacht?

[00:03:18]
TOBA SCHIVER: The SS.

[00:03:19]
DAVID BODER: The SS took it over?

[00:03:20]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:16:07]
TOBA SCHIVER: . They beat us for ten days...

[00:16:15]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:16:15]
TOBA SCHIVER: in the car and no food and always beat us.

[00:16:18]
DAVID BODER: Now, wait a minute. How do you make it through ten days in a car without food?

[00:16:23]
TOBA SCHIVER: Many died.

[00:16:25]
DAVID BODER: And you really did not eat?

[00:16:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: We once got a small piece of bread.

[00:16:29]
DAVID BODER: Well. And your sister was with you?

[00:16:32]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, always together.

[00:16:33]
DAVID BODER: That is, once a day or once in these ten days?

[00:16:36]
TOBA SCHIVER: Once a day, o-, but, o- such a little [?] that is such a little.

[00:16:40]
DAVID BODER: She shows a piece of a few inches square.

[00:16:43]
TOBA SCHIVER: And then...

[00:16:44]
DAVID BODER: Well?

[00:16:44]
TOBA SCHIVER: Suddenly, there comes an, uh, American of, uh, well an American perhaps, of the Red Cross and he gives us a small package, a package [?].

[00:16:56]
DAVID BODER: I see. An America-, a man of the Red Cross and he gave a small package [?]. A small package to each?

[00:17:00]
TOBA SCHIVER: Each a small package and for each one, perhaps two kilos in it, one kilo.

[00:17:05]
DAVID BODER: What was inside?

[00:17:06]
TOBA SCHIVER: Milk, and then, uh, canned meat, chocolate, and, uh, soap, cigarettes, and, uh, butter,...

[00:17:14]
DAVID BODER: I see, uh

[00:17:15]
TOBA SCHIVER: and cane of sugar.

[00:17:16]
DAVID BODER: What sort of milk, milk-pul-, milk, uh, -powder?

[00:17:19]
TOBA SCHIVER: Powder.

[00:17:19]
DAVID BODER: Did they give water to, uh, mix with it?

[00:17:22]
TOBA SCHIVER: We had that already, water we could.

[00:17:24]
DAVID BODER: That was still with the Germans?

[00:17:26]
TOBA SCHIVER: With the Germans.

[00:17:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:17:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: And the SS-man that many received the order [?], so that the 3000 men, 3000 people should, should many in, uh, in forest shoot us out.

[00:17:41]
DAVID BODER: Uh, who told you that? [Unintelligible].

[00:17:43]
TOBA SCHIVER: We saw that. We saw that.

[00:17:45]
DAVID BODER: Saw what? The order?

[00:17:46]
TOBA SCHIVER: Order. Saw it.

[00:17:48]
DAVID BODER: What, did he write it down, you read it, yes?

[00:17:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: Became free ourselves.

[00:17:52]
DAVID BODER: Oh, you, you were freed?

[00:17:54]
TOBA SCHIVER: He showed it to me.

[00:17:55]
DAVID BODER: He showed it.

[00:17:56]
TOBA SCHIVER: Of the SS.

[00:17:57]
DAVID BODER: Yes and why did he show it [?]?

[00:17:59]
TOBA SCHIVER: No and later on another day we hear shooting and the Americans arrived. Stayed in the car. Then it was said that we should close the car, what to do everything with the many, uh, car?

[00:18:13]
DAVID BODER: You mean what?

[00:18:13]
TOBA SCHIVER: The, uh, SS" closed the, no, each car eighty people...

[00:18:20]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:20]
TOBA SCHIVER: and two SS had stayed in each car.

[00:18:23]
DAVID BODER: In the car!

[00:18:23]
TOBA SCHIVER: In the car. Two SS.

[00:18:25]
DAVID BODER: Together with the free people?

[00:18:25]
TOBA SCHIVER: With the free people.

[00:18:26]
DAVID BODER: Well?

[00:18:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: Always two SS.

[00:18:28]
DAVID BODER: Oh, so also while driving?

[00:18:29]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, it was always, always

[00:18:31]
DAVID BODER: Always two SS?

[00:18:31]
TOBA SCHIVER: Always. They didn’t tell us [Unintelligible] and all SS took out the, well these emblems, that they are with the SS, the uh

[00:18:40]
DAVID BODER: Took off their SS emblems.

[00:18:42]
TOBA SCHIVER: Did nothing, said nothing else, but we did see that [?]. Und suddenly we hear the shooting.

[00:18:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:50]
TOBA SCHIVER: And [?] so we closed the cars. They shouldn’t [?] the clothes...

[00:18:56]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:56]
TOBA SCHIVER: the [?] clothes.

[00:18:57]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:18:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: And received an, uh, order [?]. We were very afraid, hung up a dress on the car.

[00:19:07]
DAVID BODER: From the outside?

[00:19:08]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, that we are prisoners.

[00:19:10]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:19:10]
TOBA SCHIVER: And suddenly, came an, uh, an American and were freed.

[00:19:15]
DAVID BODER: Well, were arrested?

[00:19:17]
TOBA SCHIVER: No. And all SS [?], like this...

[00:19:21]
DAVID BODER: Raised the hands.

[00:19:21]
TOBA SCHIVER: raised the hands. And he had shown this scrap of paper, that there comes an order that he should shoot them out. That’s why he left free.

[00:19:31]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:19:31]
Toba Schiver: Left free, the SS [Note: In German, it is clear that by “the SS” she means only that one SS person].

[00:19:33]
DAVID BODER: The SS was freed?

[00:19:34]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:19:35]
DAVID BODER: Because he didn’t the

[00:19:36]
TOBA SCHIVER: Jews, uh

[00:19:37]
DAVID BODER: didn’t, uh, kill the Jews.

[00:19:38]
TOBA SCHIVER: Killed. But the others all killed.

[00:19:41]
DAVID BODER: Who?

[00:19:41]
TOBA SCHIVER: The SS. The Americans.

[00:19:43]
DAVID BODER: Did they shoot?

[00:19:44]
TOBA SCHIVER: Shot. [Inaudible, TS and DB speaking simultaneously]

[00:19:45]
DAVID BODER: The Americans shot the SS?

[00:19:47]
TOBA SCHIVER: The SS.

[00:19:48]
DAVID BODER: And the man, who had the letter, was what, the commander [?]

[00:19:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: Who commanded that the 3000, uh, people [?] in the cars should be shot out.

[00:19:56]
DAVID BODER: I see.

[00:19:56]
TOBA SCHIVER: Killed.

[00:19:57]
DAVID BODER: And you saw how the Americans shot the SS?

[00:20:00]
TOBA SCHIVER: The SS.

[00:20:00]
DAVID BODER: Did the SS say anything, did they beg [?]?

[00:20:03]
TOBA SCHIVER: Not at all [?].

[00:20:07]
DAVID BODER: I see. Well?

[00:20:08]
TOBA SCHIVER: apartment, to eat, but we, they did nothing for us.

[00:20:16]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:20:16]
TOBA SCHIVER: The Americans did nothing for us.

[00:20:18]
DAVID BODER: I see, What did they?

[00:20:19]
TOBA SCHIVER: we did by ourselves, alone.

[00:20:21]
DAVID BODER: What did they do, what did you do?

[00:20:23]
TOBA SCHIVER: The people, the Americans went away from us.

[00:20:25]
DAVID BODER: and you?

[00:20:26]
TOBA SCHIVER: We stayed alone. [Unintelligible].

[00:20:26]
DAVID BODER: Well, what did you do then?

[00:20:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: Some people went alone to supply themselves with food, but there were a lot who didn’t [?], provide accommodation, the Americans, heard they gave people clothes [?] had by themselves, took by themselves [?].

[00:20:43]
DAVID BODER: And what did they take? From where did you take?

[00:20:45]
TOBA SCHIVER: From the German apartments.

[00:20:46]
DAVID BODER: From the German. You went into the houses?

[00:20:48]
TOBA SCHIVER: And took.

[00:20:50]
DAVID BODER: Yes. Were the Germans at home, uh, the people?

[00:20:53]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:20:54]
DAVID BODER: And what did they say?

[00:20:55]
TOBA SCHIVER: Nothing at all. Were always crying.

[00:20:57]
DAVID BODER: The Germans were crying.

[00:20:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes. That they’re not guilty. It was the SS who did that. Were not guilty.

[00:21:02]
DAVID BODER: But you took what you could.

[00:21:04]
TOBA SCHIVER: No, took, but I did not take. I always thought that my parents [?].

[00:21:08]
DAVID BODER: You always what?

[00:21:09]
TOBA SCHIVER: Thought that my parents did not think, [corrects herself] did not take.

[00:21:12]
DAVID BODER: You did not take. And your sister was with you?

[00:21:14]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, together.

[00:21:15]
DAVID BODER: Well, go on?

[00:21:16]
TOBA SCHIVER: two weeks and were freed in Staltach

[00:21:21]
DAVID BODER: In Stahldach?

[00:21:22]
TOBA SCHIVER: Staltach.

[00:21:23]
DAVID BODER: Stalbach?

[00:21:24]
TOBA SCHIVER: Staltach.

[00:21:25]
DAVID BODER: Staltach. Well?

[00:21:26]
TOBA SCHIVER: we stayed there four weeks. We waited there to a Czech transporter [?] and we could drive a lot.

[00:21:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:21:32]
TOBA SCHIVER: And at once drove to Feldafing.

[00:21:35]
DAVID BODER: Feldafing?

[00:21:36]
TOBA SCHIVER: Feldafing. And there we then drove with Czech, Czech transport people. I had, I had a dress, I came with a pajama...

[00:21:44]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:21:45]
TOBA SCHIVER: To Czechia.

[00:21:46]
DAVID BODER: Without a dress?

[00:21:47]
TOBA SCHIVER: Without a dress [?], I didn’t have one.

[00:21:49]
DAVID BODER: And you didn’t, why didn’t you take from the Germans?

[00:21:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: I couldn’t.

[00:21:53]
DAVID BODER: And your sister?

[00:21:54]
TOBA SCHIVER: Sister couldn’t either.

[00:21:55]
DAVID BODER: Well?

[00:21:55]
TOBA SCHIVER: came home, no- met my father, only a brother.

[00:22:01]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:22:01]
TOBA SCHIVER: Czech army. A brother.

[00:22:03]
DAVID BODER: Yes, but the father you didn-

[00:22:04]
TOBA SCHIVER: Didn’t see. Died.

[00:22:05]
DAVID BODER: And the brother returned home from?

[00:22:08]
TOBA SCHIVER: He went in the army, Czech. From the Czech army.

[00:22:11]
DAVID BODER: Did you, where did you find him?

[00:22:12]
TOBA SCHIVER: In Czechia. In Prague.

[00:22:14]
DAVID BODER: Oh, was he there?

[00:22:15]
TOBA SCHIVER: Was he there.

[00:22:15]
DAVID BODER: And he was a soldier there?

[00:22:17]
TOBA SCHIVER: He was a soldier.

[00:22:17]
DAVID BODER: Now, go on?

[00:22:19]
TOBA SCHIVER: Well, after we came together we took a, an apartment. Came [?] in Ukraine...

[00:22:25]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:22:25]
TOBA SCHIVER: to Ukraine.

[00:22:27]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:22:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: Family wanted to stay there. Did no- want to go to Prague.

[00:22:30]
DAVID BODER: Yes. They didn’t want to go to Prague?

[00:22:32]
TOBA SCHIVER: Not stay at home [?] Ukraine. [Unintelligible]

[00:22:35]
DAVID BODER: [00:22:37]
TOBA SCHIVER: no- wanted to go back.

[00:22:39]
DAVID BODER: They didn’t want to go back.

[00:22:40]
TOBA SCHIVER: .

[00:22:42]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:22:42]
TOBA SCHIVER: .

[00:22:46]
DAVID BODER: You must be more precise. You came home to your ow-, own little town?

[00:22:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, but you couldn’t go back in the, uh, house there.

[00:22:54]
DAVID BODER: If you own the house?

[00:22:55]
TOBA SCHIVER: .

[00:22:56]
DAVID BODER: Was it your own house?

[00:22:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: Our own farm. Our own farm. We had eight houses there.

[00:23:01]
DAVID BODER: You had eight houses?

[00:23:02]
TOBA SCHIVER: But, but Ukraine, Ukraine that is kolkhoz. You can’t lose that. That is not mine but of the whole state.

[00:23:08]
DAVID BODER: I see. Ukraine turned communist.

[00:23:10]
TOBA SCHIVER: Communist. That I go to Ukraine [?]. My brother [?] in Prague.

[00:23:17]
DAVID BODER: Yes, well?

[00:23:18]
TOBA SCHIVER: And so I went to my brother.

[00:23:19]
DAVID BODER: You together with your sister?

[00:23:20]
TOBA SCHIVER: My sister and I, always together with my sister. We drove together to Prague and there we met my brother.

[00:23:26]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:23:26]
TOBA SCHIVER: And he [?]

[00:23:29]
DAVID BODER: How did you meet, where did you find it?

[00:23:31]
TOBA SCHIVER: In Prague.

[00:23:32]
DAVID BODER: Yes, did you know an address?

[00:23:34]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, he had sent us an address from, from home. He didn’t kno-, know where that address is.

[00:23:40]
DAVID BODER: Yes?

[00:23:41]
TOBA SCHIVER: He [?]

[00:23:45]
DAVID BODER: Yes, well?

[00:23:46]
TOBA SCHIVER: and so we to-, took an apartment and three people lived there. Brother, sister [?]. And later we worked in a chocolate factory.

[00:23:56]
DAVID BODER: Chocolate factory at the Czech?

[00:23:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: At the Czech. Very a good life was there.

[00:24:00]
DAVID BODER: Well, and then? Why, how, when did you decide to go away?

[00:24:04]
TOBA SCHIVER: We decided when it was said that you can’t, uh, stay, that Russian Jews can’t stay in Czechia.

[00:24:12]
DAVID BODER: Oh, who said that? The Czechs?

[00:24:15]
TOBA SCHIVER: They said.

[00:24:15]
DAVID BODER: Well, but not officially.

[00:24:17]
TOBA SCHIVER: Not officially.

[00:24:18]
DAVID BODER: .

[00:24:18]
TOBA SCHIVER: I decided, that I would go to Palestine.

[00:24:23]
DAVID BODER: Well, and your brother as well?

[00:24:24]
TOBA SCHIVER: No. Brother is to Czechia. He married [?]

[00:24:28]
DAVID BODER: He married a Jewish girl?

[00:24:30]
TOBA SCHIVER: Jewish girl.

[00:24:30]
DAVID BODER: And he stayed there?

[00:24:31]
TOBA SCHIVER: Stayed there.

[00:24:32]
DAVID BODER: Speak up. He stayed there. And you with the sister?

[00:24:35]
TOBA SCHIVER: We are here. The sister already married, uh, she already has a husband.

[00:24:39]
DAVID BODER: Here in?

[00:24:39]
TOBA SCHIVER: In Tradate.

[00:24:40]
DAVID BODER: In Tradate. Did she get married in Tradate?

[00:24:43]
TOBA SCHIVER: No, she got married in Venice.

[00:24:45]
DAVID BODER: I see. Well, wait, uh, wait a minute. Not so fast. You decided to go to Palestine now?

[00:24:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:24:52]
DAVID BODER: Well. How did you join, how did you become a member of the kibbutz? How did you?

[00:24:59]
TOBA SCHIVER: From Prague to Vienna.

[00:25:02]
DAVID BODER: In Vienna? You went from Prague to Vienna. And how did you find a kibbutz?

[00:25:06]
TOBA SCHIVER: These people were always taken, a few people, who were looking for a kibbutz.

[00:25:13]
DAVID BODER: I see. Well, and then you left Vienna again?

[00:25:16]
TOBA SCHIVER: To Enns. From Enns to Linz.

[00:25:19]
DAVID BODER: Enns?

[00:25:19]
TOBA SCHIVER: Ah, yes.

[00:25:20]
DAVID BODER: Well?

[00:25:21]
TOBA SCHIVER: To another kibbutz drove on weekend.

[00:25:23]
DAVID BODER: Drove or walked?

[00:25:24]
TOBA SCHIVER: Drove.

[00:25:25]
DAVID BODER: And then from Linz, from Linz to?

[00:25:27]
TOBA SCHIVER: To Salzburg.

[00:25:28]
DAVID BODER: To Salzburg. And from Salzburg?

[00:25:30]
TOBA SCHIVER: To, uh, Innsbruck. From Innsbruck to, uh, Milan.

[00:25:34]
DAVID BODER: To Milan. Well, uh, tell me, how did you eat on the way, what did you live on?

[00:25:39]
TOBA SCHIVER: Simply always there. From Enns to Salzburg simply always food there on the way.

[00:25:43]
DAVID BODER: Who?

[00:25:44]
TOBA SCHIVER: The...

[00:25:45]
DAVID BODER: The Joint, the UNRRA? Well and now, uh, uh, you plan to go to Palestine?

[00:25:51]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:25:52]
DAVID BODER: Your sister is a younger sister, yes?

[00:25:54]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, with one years.

[00:25:55]
DAVID BODER: And she has married already.

[00:25:56]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:25:57]
DAVID BODER: Why have you not married yet?

[00:25:58]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes, I, I [?] yet to marry, but I’d need a husband for that.

[00:26:03]
DAVID BODER: What?

[00:26:04]
TOBA SCHIVER: I do not have one!

[00:26:05]
DAVID BODER: You don’t have one. Well, and, uh, what are you planning to do in Palestine?

[00:26:10]
TOBA SCHIVER: .

[00:26:13]
DAVID BODER: Don’t you, don’t you have any relatives in America?

[00:26:16]
TOBA SCHIVER: [00:26:17]
DAVID BODER: Speak up! No?

[00:26:18]
TOBA SCHIVER: We have two cousins and an, uh, an, uh [?] an aunt...

[00:26:24]
DAVID BODER: An aunt, yes?

[00:26:26]
TOBA SCHIVER: to Palestine.

[00:26:27]
DAVID BODER: They’re going to Palestine now?

[00:26:28]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes. [Unintelligible].

[00:26:29]
DAVID BODER: Did they receive certificates?

[00:26:31]
TOBA SCHIVER: Yes.

[00:26:32]
DAVID BODER: Well, perhaps, you had better waited there, would have been better?

[00:26:35]
TOBA SCHIVER: That doesn’t matter.

[00:26:37]
DAVID BODER: That doesn’t matter.

[00:26:38]
TOBA SCHIVER: I’ve been through a lot already [?].

[00:26:41]
DAVID BODER: And what are doing here the whole day?

[00:26:44]
TOBA SCHIVER: Well, what, what other people do. Study and, uh, Hebrew and things like that.

[00:26:49]
DAVID BODER: This concludes the interview with Miss Toba Shiver who is rather very scarce on words. But we’ve got a, we think a significant story. We conclude this spool on 25 minutes.

[00:27:03]
DAVID BODER: Well, Mrs. Schiver, thank you very much. If you could please find the boy who brought you here and send him in. Thank you.

[00:27:07]
DAVID BODER: Tradate, Italy...a small locality between Como and Milano, with a community of displaced persons mainly consisting of young kibbutzim.

entries.title: David P. Boder Interviews Udel Stopnitsky
entries.content:
[00:00:01]
David Boder: France, September the 12th, 1946, at Hénonville, a chateau which has now given over to displaced Jews, a extremely religious Kibbutz in which the ORT has its school of agriculture and various trades. The interviewee is Mr. Udel Stopnitsky, 31 years old.

[00:00:30]
David Boder: Now, Mr. Stopnitsky, will you again tell me your full name...

[00:00:35]
Udel Stopnitsky: Stopnitsky, Udel

[00:00:36]
David Boder: Yes...

[00:00:37]
Udel Stopnitsky: Born in Bedzin, 1915

[00:00:40]
David Boder: Bedzin is not far from Sosnowiec?

[00:00:42]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes.

[00:00:00]
David Boder: Yes. In 1915, so how old are you now, 31?

[00:00:45]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, 31 years old.

[00:00:47]
David Boder: Now, Mr. Stopnitsky, what are you doing here? With what are you occupied here?

[00:00:51]
Udel Stopnitsky: I arrived here in order to get in the fastest way to the land of Israel.

[00:00:55]
David Boder: You are occupying some kind of a post here in the organization?

[00:00:57]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, I am the head of the Kibbutz, that means leader of the whole contingent.

[00:01:01]
David Boder: How many Kibbutzim [this is the plural form of Kibbutz] are here?

[00:01:03]
Udel Stopnitsky: One-hundred and twenty people.

[00:01:05]
David Boder: No, no I am not asking how many people. I want to know if there is only one Kibbutz here?

[00:01:08]
Udel Stopnitsky: One Kibbutz.

[00:01:09]
David Boder: And what is the name of this Kibbutz?

[00:01:10]
Udel Stopnitsky: Nezach Israel under the leadership of the Alya Agudahs Israel.

[00:01:15]
David Boder: . . . Agudahs Israel?

[00:01:16]
Udel Stopnitsky: Alya Agudahs Israel.

[00:01:17]
David Boder: And what does Alya mean?

[00:01:19]
Udel Stopnitsky: That is the youth organization of religious working men [the preceding Hebrew terms have to be re-checked].

[00:01:25]
David Boder: The youth organization of Jewish working men. And Rabbi Horwitz is with you?

[00:01:30]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, he is the religious leader of our Kibbutz.

[00:01:34]
David Boder: Yes. And to what organization belongs the Yeshiva, there upstairs?

[00:01:37]
Udel Stopnitsky: That is a Lituanian Yeshiva.

[00:01:39]
David Boder: They don’t belong to your group?

[00:01:40]
Udel Stopnitsky: No, that is a separate group which only dedicates itself to learning. The rest of the Kibbutz is organized to prepare working people for the land of Israel.

[00:01:48]
David Boder: And the others are a Yeshiva and it is not known whether they go to the land of Israel?

[00:01:51]
Udel Stopnitsky: They go to America.

[00:01:53]
David Boder: Yes. And do they have their own Rabbi?

[00:01:59]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, the Yeshiva has its own Rabbi.

[00:02:01]
David Boder: Has he arrived already?

[00:02:02]
Udel Stopnitsky: No, he will arrive tomorrow, on Friday. Every Sunday he leaves for Paris and he comes here for the Sabbath weekend.

[00:02:09]
David Boder: And what does he do in Paris during the whole week?

[00:02:11]
Udel Stopnitsky: He has to arrange various things, various formalities for the trip to America because the Yeshiva leaves for America.

[00:02:16]
David Boder: So he is busy the whole week in Paris?

[00:02:18]
Udel Stopnitsky: In Paris.

[00:02:19]
David Boder: Now, Mr. Stopnitsky, will you please tell me where you were when the war started and what happened to you?

[00:02:28]
Udel Stopnitsky: From 1939 to 1943, I was in Bedzin. In various ghettos. Sometimes in a large ghetto up to the end, to April, 1943, when there were established ghettos surrounded with wire fences.

[00:02:44]
David Boder: With wires?

[00:02:44]
Udel Stopnitsky: With wires. By that time there were in the ghetto seventeen thousand Jews.

[00:02:48]
David Boder: Now let us start again. Where and with whom were you? With whom did you live? I refer to your family at the time the Germans arrived in Bedzin.

[00:02:58]
Udel Stopnitsky: When the Germans arrived in Bedzin, I was at home. We were ten children.

[00:03:02]
David Boder: Were the Russians in Bedzin first?

[00:03:04]
Udel Stopnitsky: No.

[00:03:05]
David Boder: Oh...

[00:03:06]
Udel Stopnitsky: The Germans came in right from the start.

[00:03:07]
David Boder: the Germans came in before they were at war with the Russians?

[00:03:11]
Udel Stopnitsky: No, [they marched in] two years before.

[00:03:13]
David Boder: All right, go on.

[00:03:14]
Udel Stopnitsky: Also, when the Germans marched in—we were a family of ten children, and my father and my mother.

[00:03:20]
David Boder: Ten children and a father and mother in addition, together twelve?

[00:03:22]
Udel Stopnitsky: Together twelve.

[00:03:23]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:03:24]
Udel Stopnitsky: We lived [from the start] unmolested. The first few weeks various misfortunes happened to other Jews. They right away burned the synagogues and the prayer house, and a number of Jews were right away shot, they burned down various streets with Jews [possibly meaning where the Jews lived], but nothing so far happened to our family.

[00:03:38]
David Boder: Now wait a moment. [Do I understand that] the Germans were not yet at war with Russia, they marched into Poland, they marched into Bedzin?

[00:03:48]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes.

[00:03:48]
David Boder: Go on.

[00:03:49]
Udel Stopnitsky: So right away, the first day when they marched in, they took one hundred and seventy Jews and shot them.

[00:03:55]
David Boder: Where?

[00:03:55]
Udel Stopnitsky: In Bedzin.

[00:03:56]
David Boder: Did you see it?

[00:03:57]
Udel Stopnitsky: I have not seen it, but afterwards when we came outside we saw Jews sitting in poses like it would be Saturday night, they were sitting in their silk coats, with their heads [here one word not clear] leaning against the wall and in such a pose they were shot.

[00:04:10]
David Boder: So that you did see?

[00:04:11]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, I have seen it.

[00:04:12]
David Boder: One could see that they were shot?

[00:04:14]
Udel Stopnitsky: Shot, not once but several times shot.

[00:04:16]
David Boder: Yes?

[00:04:17]
Udel Stopnitsky: They were shot with so much suffering that one could not call it normal suffering. Entire pieces of flesh were torn away.

[00:04:23]
David Boder: H-um, and who buried them?

[00:04:27]
Udel Stopnitsky: The official Jewish undertakers.

[00:04:28]
David Boder: The official Jewish undertakers had to bury them? Some hundred seventy Jews?

[00:04:30]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes.

[00:04:31]
David Boder: Where were they buried?

[00:04:32]
Udel Stopnitsky: On the cemetery, under [one word is not clear] highway which [cemetery] exists until this day.

[00:04:36]
David Boder: Were they buried in separate graves? [the interviewer inquired whether they were buried in individual graves but Stopnitsky interpreted the word as separate graves.]

[00:04:38]
Udel Stopnitsky: In separate graves, four graves, women separately and men separately.

[00:04:41]
David Boder: Oh, in two graves?

[00:04:43]
Udel Stopnitsky: No, in four graves, two for the men and two for the women.

[00:04:46]
David Boder: So they did not bury everyone separately, in a nice...[The interviewer unexpectedly said this last three words in English; as in so many cases the interviewer could not help becoming perplexed by the story which accounts for not having heard about the four graves when he mentioned them first, and also accounts for forgetting himself as to the language he was to use. —D.P.B.]

[00:04:49]
Udel Stopnitsky: That they did not permit.

[00:04:51]
David Boder: The Germans did not permit?

[00:04:51]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . because it took too much time.

[00:04:53]
David Boder: Yes...

[00:04:53]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . to dig so many graves if each one would have been separately buried.

[00:04:56]
David Boder: Oh...and what explanation did they give? Why were they shot? What did they...

[00:04:59]
Udel Stopnitsky: There was no explanation of any kind...no explanation.

[00:05:03]
David Boder: Did you have a Jewish Community Council right from the start?

[00:05:06]
Udel Stopnitsky: The Jewish Community Council was created [here is either a short break in the wire or the machine was stopped for some reason but there isn’t much missing if any].

[00:05:08]
David Boder: . . . let us continue. Stopnitsky, there were at the time in Bedzin thirty-two thousand Jews in all the orders of the Gestapo, that means the German Secret Police, had to be executed by the Jewish Community Council. No matter how horrible [an order] they had to execute it. [A pause] Also you told me that at that time...

[00:05:30]
Udel Stopnitsky: There were thirty-two thousand Jews in Bedzin, because Bedzin is one of the oldest cities in Poland, but in time, beginning with 1940 the Germans got busy with the little bit of Jews, daily they record various actions, sometimes they were picked for lumber gangs with the help of the German police, sometimes they were just common order to deliver two thousand Jews. At that time it wasn’t yet known for what purpose the Jews were sent away. It was said that the Jews are being re-settled to other districts where they could continue to live. But in time obscure information came through that there was created such a thing as Auschwitz. Auschwitz is located 32 kilometers from Bedzin.

[00:06:13]
David Boder: Oh, that is where Auschwitz is located?

[00:06:14]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes. 32 kilometers.

[00:06:16]
David Boder: And Birkenau?

[00:06:17]
Udel Stopnitsky: That is the same thing. I was also in Birkenau. From then on it was “obscurely felt” that the Jews are not being re-settled but they are taken to be murdered. But to murder them openly, they still could not decide. But in time they record a case when a woman, a woman from Bedzin has managed to escape—in what way is not exactly known—but she escaped from that hell, and she reported exactly how things occurred there at the time. At that time transports of two thousand, three thousand Jews would arrive. Arriving at Auschwitz they were told that they proceed traveling to a place of work. They were told to take off all their clothes to get ready to go bathing. Each one was given a towel with a little piece of soap as is usually done when people go into a bathhouse. On the [door] leading to the gas chamber was a sign in German “bathhouse”. The people simply marched in and there occurred the gas-killing. Sometimes it would last fifteen minutes, five, minutes, sometimes an hour, sometimes two hours. This depended on the experimentation with various gases which were manufactured by the I. G. Farben Industries in Auschwitz. Because there in the lager [camp]—the lager occupied 40 kilometers square—and in this lager was a gigantic plant of that great world wide concern, the I. G. Farben Industries.

[00:07:29]
David Boder: H-um.

[00:07:30]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . where they were manufacturing poison gases and these gases...when they would prepare a new gas they would test it on the “sacrificial offering” [the word really means plural of the noun sacrifice] of Jews which were sent there from the the name is not clear [district] nearby, [he enumerates here a number of towns of that region but he speaks at such a pace that the names are not clear.]

[00:07:43]
David Boder: Katowice also?

[00:07:43]
Udel Stopnitsky: Katowice too, [correcting himself] Katowice was at that time already Jew-clean. As soon as the Germans got into Katowice it was called Upper Silesia, that means [as if] originally German territory and sent over to Zagrumbia [?] which formerly was called Dabrowa, it was called that since hundreds of years] I am not sure of the translation of the last few words.

[00:07:57]
David Boder: What did you call [that district]?

[00:07:58]
Udel Stopnitsky: Zagrumbia [?], there are the coal mines, it is a coal district.

[00:08:01]
David Boder: Yes...

[00:08:02]
Udel Stopnitsky: The Polish coal district.

[00:08:03]
David Boder: Yes...

[00:08:03]
Udel Stopnitsky: But otherwise it is called the coal district.

[00:08:07]
David Boder: Yes. And you say that the I.G. Farben were located in the lager?

[00:08:10]
Udel Stopnitsky: In the lager a gigantic factory [I am not sure of the adjective, neither here nor before when he mentions Farben, it’s the same adjective], and there worked the prisoners, you see the internees were called prisoners. I shall explain to you later what that all means. From the beginning of 1942, misfortune started to fall also over our family.

[00:08:22]
David Boder: Slower please.

[00:08:23]
Udel Stopnitsky: We were ten children. All of us...the youngest one was thirteen years old and the oldest one was thirty-five years old.

[00:08:29]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:08:30]
Udel Stopnitsky: They started sending away one by one...one brother was sent away to labor service. Labor service, that means he was sent away deep into Germany; he was getting hardly any food except for 20 to 30 deca bread a day, barely anything else, and so he had to work eight, ten or even twelve hours a day. This was not yet considered too terrible because after all the people were still alive. We still were able to maintain contact with our children, we were able to write letters to them. In 1942 my father died of a natural death, and the mother...

[00:08:57]
David Boder: at home?

[00:08:57]
Udel Stopnitsky: At home. The mother—that was the 12th, 8th, that is, the 12th of August, 1942—they ordered all the Jews of Bedzin to assemble on three squares. At that time they were 57,000 Jews. And all the Jews assembled...

[00:09:12]
David Boder: On three different squares?

[00:09:13]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes.

[00:09:13]
David Boder: Why on three different squares?

[00:09:14]
Udel Stopnitsky: Because it was impossible for all of them to assemble on one square...

[00:09:17]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:09:17]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . because the squares were surrounded and guarded by the Gestapo with machine guns. And they started a selection. In German it is called selection, meaning they were classifying: these shall live, and these shall not. It was called: one, two, three. To one were assigned such people who were working, they had such papers from the special authorities, and that meant that they may live. But to three were assigned older people, children or such people who he disliked in general, and these were set apart and from them were formed the transports, two, three thousand Jews, and they were sent away to Auschwitz. And...

[00:09:47]
David Boder: And what about two?

[00:09:48]
Udel Stopnitsky: Group two meant the doubtful [cases]. When the “selection man”, the German, was unable to decide from a person’s papers whether his work is sufficient [of sufficient importance], then these people were ordered aside for the time being, and by night would arrive the proprietor of the plant, and when he would report that he needs the people, then such people would be released and they would continue going to work.

[00:10:05]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:10:05]
Udel Stopnitsky: Because they have set up in Bedzin certain shops like in America [occupying] nine thousand, five thousand people, which worked for the German Wehrmacht. Such people still had the right to remain at home. That happened in 1942. From then on, from the 12th, 8th, they began to drag away various Jews. There even happened once a case when a message came that the Gestapo is in need of three thousand Jews. The then active Jewish Community Council with the director [?] Monich Morin [?], that was a [the adjective is not clear] Jew...

[00:10:30]
David Boder: Morin?

[00:10:31]
Udel Stopnitsky: Merin.

[00:10:32]
David Boder: Merin.

[00:10:32]
Udel Stopnitsky: Monek Merin, Monek Merin, he was the leader of the central office of the Jewish Community Councils. He maintained contact with Berlin, with the Gestapo, with [the authorities] everywhere. He had full rights to travel wherever he wanted to.

[00:10:43]
David Boder: Please write down for me his name.

[00:10:44]
Udel Stopnitsky: Gladly....He was a congenial Jew; he took it unto himself...he meant well from the beginning, but later he was the executor of all the orders of the Gestapo. He knew that the Jews were going to Auschwitz, and he would assemble these Jews. He would send the old people to Auschwitz because he judged that an old person is already useless, he won’t bring anybody [or possibly anything] into this world while young people can produce [or possibly reproduce]. But in time it revealed itself that he was simply a traitor to the Jewish people, to the Jews. If he wouldn’t have confused our minds, if he wouldn’t have talked into us that there is a chance for salvation, we possibly would have organized for resistance. But he lulled us into such a sleep, that we did not organize any resistance and we went like sheep to the slaughter. Without any resistance and whatsoever. And so things went on until April, 1943. In April, 1943, this same Monek Merin with his whole crew, for reasons which we could not ascertain, the Gestapo took this same Monek Merin with all the other [Jewish] authorities and sent them, too, to Auschwitz.

[00:11:42]
David Boder: H-um.

[00:11:43]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . and we Jews remained without leadership, without anything. From then on the great holocaust started. It happened once...the first holocaust took place the 22nd of June. They surrounded the whole ghetto, because we were already [settled] outside of the town...

[00:11:59]
David Boder: You say that Bedzin is only 20 kilometers away from Auschwitz?

[00:12:02]
Udel Stopnitsky: 32 kilometers...

[00:12:03]
David Boder: 32 kilometers.

[00:12:04]
Udel Stopnitsky: 32 kilometers from Auschwitz; it formerly was Oswiecim...

[00:12:07]
David Boder: And you didn’t know what was going on there?

[00:12:09]
Udel Stopnitsky: No, until 1942, it was not known...

[00:12:11]
David Boder: People say that the fires from the crematories were...

[00:12:14]
Udel Stopnitsky: But there were no Jews, and such information did not reach us. But beginning with 1942 we knew exactly what was going on there and how things were going on there, everything. But we were without arms and we were unable to defend ourselves. And that happened on account of Monek Merin and his crew. He lulled us into such a sleep that we didn’t think, we didn’t consider the possibility of resistance.

[00:12:35]
David Boder: Oh...Now go on.

[00:12:36]
Udel Stopnitsky: It happened the 22nd of June they started it by surrounding the ghetto, the ghetto was outside the town. There still lived seventeen thousand Jews. And they took four thousand of the most splendid young people, the Jewish youth, and they were sent immediately to Auschwitz.

[00:12:50]
David Boder: Why?

[00:12:52]
Udel Stopnitsky: . . . Nothing, they just made a kind of...

[00:12:53]
David Boder: Were there too many people in the ghetto?

[00:12:55]
Udel Stopnitsky: Nothing of the kind. There was no question about that, they were just Jews. The only reason was that they were Jews. The Jews worked, they made themselves useful, they worked for the Wehrmacht, but because they were Jews they had no right to live and that was the order of things. People just shot at ever action, they used to shoot a couple of hundred Jews. These couple of hundred Jews were lying around on the ground, afterwards they [the bodies] were gathered together.

[00:13:11]
David Boder: Have you see that, how it happened...?

[00:13:12]
Udel Stopnitsky: I was committing them to burial. I participated in burying them because I had a post of raid watchman because in German a “raid watchman” was active in air raids, and we too had to do that, so I had the right to take those people and to bury them. I still know to this day where the graves are located, because at the end I was the deputy [he says president] of the religious contingents of Bedzin, now...

[00:13:30]
David Boder: Now? [He apparently meant at the time of those occurrences]

[00:13:31]
Udel Stopnitsky: Yes, and we proceeded with the various things [rituals] burials, tombstones, on a small scale because of course we had no money but we marked everything wherever the people were lying [buried], these sacrifices [one word is not clear]. And then...

[00:13:44]
David Boder: And how can it be known who they are?

[00:13:46]
Udel Stopnitsky: I wrote it down. I was born in Bedzin and I knew their names...

[00:13:49]
David Boder: You wrote it down then? Right after it [happened]?

[00:13:51]
Udel Stopnitsky: It was written down in a memorandum, it was all written down but they took it away from me afterwards in Auschwitz; everything was written down.

[00:13:55]
David Boder: H-um.

[00:13:55]
Udel Stopnitsky: I shall return to it later...

[00:13:56]
David Boder: Yes.

[00:13:56]
Udel Stopnitsky: Also that happened the 22nd, 6th. And the lst, 8th, when we arose in the morning...I want to remark here, since we knew already of the danger, and we were prepared for it. And when I saw that the horror was imminent and there was no salvation of any kind so we made for ourselves so-called bunkers, hideouts. We for instance excavated stories deep in the ground, we constructed various kinds of cellars, we constructed [double] walls, so with the first threats of danger one could hide because we had...as soon as Russia entered the war, we had information that America and England have allied themselves with the European powers, so we thought that help is near and we will be able to hold out two, three, or even four months live through in the hideouts. But time has shown that that was a mistake and we were unable to hide. The 1st of August, 1943, we were informed that Bedzin is to become Jew-clean. No Jew should be found in Bedzin. I at that time still had with me a sister, a brother and a wife with a child of fourteen months, and an in-law [one cannot understand whether he means father or mother-in-law or brother or sister-in-law]. I had constructed a hideout and we were lying there for seven days.

[00:15:06]
